passages: Works with Apple Home and Matter certification have allowed a wide array of third-party accessories to connect with Apple’s smart home ecosystem for years, and Apple Home Collection takes it even further.
Apple worked closely with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric to create an integrated Apple Home experience across the new product lineup.
1 These new accessories are simple to set up starting with one tap with iPhone, and everything is managed through the Apple Home app — no separate app or account required.
Each accessory is encrypted end-to-end in Apple Home, so only users and the people they choose can access their home data.
Products also automatically update their network credentials if a customer changes their home Wi-Fi, eliminating a common smart home frustration.

“Schneider Home’s new Smart Thermostat is a true collaboration with Apple to give customers a seamless way to help manage their home’s energy use, effortlessly blending efficiency with everyday comfort and simplicity.”
LG’s lineup of four cameras gives users a private and intelligent way to monitor their homes when using a home hub like Apple HomeView, HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K.
Camera footage is securely processed locally on the customer’s own Apple Home hub or in Private Cloud Compute and, for users with iCloud+, stored encrypted in iCloud for 10 days.
“LG Electronics has spent decades developing technologies and products designed around the way people live,” said Kihyun Jung, LG Electronics’ executive vice president.
Controls in the Home app allow the doorbell and lock to work together as a front-door system — letting users see who’s there and unlock the door in a single view or by asking Siri.
The new smart lock is Matter compatible and supports Aliro, working entirely locally so core access functions continue even without an internet connection.
LG’s Smart Deadbolt Lock brings a new level of convenience to home access.

Apple worked closely with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric to create an integrated Apple Home experience across the new product lineup. These new Apple Home Collection products feature a clean, minimal aesthetic and premium materials, with every detail considered, from how they mount and adjust to how they look and feel alongside Apple products throughout the home. Every camera captures up to 2.5K resolution video and recognizes people, familiar faces, pets, vehicles, and packages, with video history securely stored in users’ supported iCloud+ plan, so there’s no separate camera subscription. 2 Each camera works with iCloud+, giving users access to 10 days’ worth of event video history. On eligible iCloud+ plans, Apple Intelligence adds automatic video descriptions that summarize what’s happening in a clip, along with the ability to search footage using natural, descriptive language. 3 Built-in storage keeps cameras recording even when Wi-Fi goes down, and improvements to the way footage is captured and stored ensure detected moments aren’t missed during a network outage. Users can view live footage and camera activity at any time right from the Home app on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple TV 4K, or HomeView — with quick live snapshots that give an at-a-glance view without needing to open a full livestream. LG’s Smart Deadbolt Lock brings a new level of convenience to home access. Using Ultra Wideband technology, the lock can tell how close a user is and when they’re approaching the door. As a user with a home key on a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch walks up, the door unlocks automatically, with no tapping required. For flexibility, users can also tap to unlock with an iPhone or Apple Watch, use an integrated PIN pad, or rely on a hidden backup key slot. The lock can sense if the door has been opened, closed, or tampered with, alerting users if it’s open even while locked. Guest access can also be shared directly through the Home app, making it simple to grant a dog walker, house sitter, or visiting family member their own way in. Controls in the Home app allow the doorbell and lock to work together as a front-door system — letting users see who’s there and unlock the door in a single view or by asking Siri. When a visitor rings the bell, a chime sounds through HomeView, HomePod, or HomePod mini, and a notification appears on the user’s Apple devices, like iPhone or iPad. From wherever they are, users can see who’s at the door, speak to the visitor, and unlock the door for them. The new smart lock is Matter compatible and supports Aliro, working entirely locally so core access functions continue even without an internet connection. Two new Smart Thermostats are available — one from LG Electronics and one from Schneider Electric — so users can choose the product that best fits their home’s broader energy ecosystem. Using on-device intelligence from iPhone, Adaptive Temperature in the Home app automatically adjusts the thermostats based on whether someone is at home, winding down at night, or away, ensuring the home is always at the right temperature without any manual scheduling. In the contiguous U.S., Clean Energy Guidance can shift heating and cooling to cleaner, lower-cost periods for users with a compatible utility plan, and the Home app displays usage insights over time, including peak and off-peak rate information. Products also automatically update their network credentials if a customer changes their home Wi-Fi, eliminating a common smart home frustration. The accessories are designed to work together, and users can control every product with Siri. A single “Good Morning” scene can simultaneously adjust the thermostat, tilt an indoor camera down while a user is getting ready, and start music on HomePod. Using on-device intelligence from iPhone or Apple Watch, users can set up Apple Home to recognize key moments throughout the day: As the last user leaves for work, the thermostat adjusts for an empty home, the door locks, and cameras begin monitoring again. Before they arrive home, the thermostat begins adjusting the temperature, and the front door unlocks automatically as they approach. Privacy is foundational to Apple Home. Camera footage and personal data in the Home app are stored end-to-end encrypted and never accessible to LG Electronics, Schneider Electric, or Apple. Camera footage is securely processed locally on the customer’s own Apple Home hub or in Private Cloud Compute and, for users with iCloud+, stored encrypted in iCloud for 10 days. Based on Apple’s video, if she’s home, my call can now ring on the HomeView.

She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home.

A lot of initial reactions to the $299 HomeView (which looks like a giant Apple Watch on a flatter metallic HomePod Mini) ask why you would want it when you can do most of what it offers on your iPhone or iPad.

extraction.body: I love the approach Apple has taken with the HomeView. I think it’s the shared, always-available household interface that my family might finally use. Is Apple’s first smart display my dream smart home dashboard? But is it the right product for Apple Home at this moment? A lot of initial reactions to the $299 HomeView (which looks like a giant Apple Watch on a flatter metallic HomePod Mini) ask why you would want it when you can do most of what it offers on your iPhone or iPad. HomeView gives you another interface for those things, but crucially one that is always powered, always unlocked, and always in the same spot in your home, making it easy to walk up to and interact with. I’ve tried using an iPad to control my smart home, run my family’s calendar, and be a shared device for controlling music. An iPad can’t be a hub for your Apple Home; HomeView can. An iPad famously isn’t a good multiuser device, and controlling home devices on one requires it staying logged in to your personal iCloud account; HomeView offers Apple’s first crack at easy multiuser switching. Apple designed HomeView as a communal device that sits in a fixed place in the home. Not having a battery or detachable screen is a feature for me, because devices that do inevitably wander off and die under a couch cushion. One feature I’m most interested in is HomeView’s role as a home video phone. Do you know how many times I’ve tried to call my daughter when I’m not home, and her phone is dead or on silent? Based on Apple’s video, if she’s home, my call can now ring on the HomeView. Smart displays and speakers from Amazon and Google already help with this to some extent, but Apple’s version comes without ads (see the Echo Show) and may have a longer lifespan (RIP Pixel Tablet). She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” she said. "As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in a natural way.”" - Lilian Rincon, Apple Siri AI made this possible because it’s “much more capable,” said Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI at Apple. As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way.” On why now, Rincon says the natural-language shift is the point where AI goes mainstream. “Because now it can be … my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who’s in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want.” Siri AI in the home has another big advantage over the competition: It doesn’t say too much. “A lot of these assistants out there are always asking questions because they want more information,” she said. I had hoped that, along with new hardware, Apple would bring more functionality and deeper Apple Intelligence integration to Apple Home to make the smart home smarter. Apple trying to make the smart home easier for everyone to use can only be a good thing. As always, the smart home’s most important goal is to come up with an easier way to turn on the lights. HomeView’s simplicity may put off hardcore home automation enthusiasts, but I’d argue it’s perfect for their long-suffering spouses. I’ve tried every version of physical smart home control interface in my home, and you know who hasn’t used any of them? Because my family all have iPhones, and because the HomeView will always be there and will feel familiar, I can see them actually using it. That means I could set up a full Home Assistant instance and run a detailed dashboard on a tablet in my office, then feed the scenes and devices into Apple Home so my husband and daughter can just tap to control them on a HomeView in the kitchen. HomeView may not be the smart home computer I want Apple to make, but it is the smart home device Apple needed to make. It doesn’t have to run all the iPad apps or try to be a bigger version of my iPhone; it just needs to make the smart home accessible to everyone in the house. If Apple has pulled that off, it could be more valuable than any new smart home feature I’ve been wishing for.

sources.title: The best feature of Apple’s HomeView might be its simplicity
passages: An iPad famously isn’t a good multiuser device, and controlling home devices on one requires it staying logged in to your personal iCloud account; HomeView offers Apple’s first crack at easy multiuser switching.
Based on Apple’s video, if she’s home, my call can now ring on the HomeView.
I love the approach Apple has taken with the HomeView.
Apple designed HomeView as a communal device that sits in a fixed place in the home.
HomeView may not be the smart home computer I want Apple to make, but it is the smart home device Apple needed to make.
She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home.

A lot of initial reactions to the $299 HomeView (which looks like a giant Apple Watch on a flatter metallic HomePod Mini) ask why you would want it when you can do most of what it offers on your iPhone or iPad.
An iPad can’t be a hub for your Apple Home; HomeView can.
One feature I’m most interested in is HomeView’s role as a home video phone.
Smart displays and speakers from Amazon and Google already help with this to some extent, but Apple’s version comes without ads (see the Echo Show) and may have a longer lifespan (RIP Pixel Tablet).
HomeView’s simplicity may put off hardcore home automation enthusiasts, but I’d argue it’s perfect for their long-suffering spouses.

That means I could set up a full Home Assistant instance and run a detailed dashboard on a tablet in my office, then feed the scenes and devices into Apple Home so my husband and daughter can just tap to control them on a HomeView in the kitchen.

HomeView gives you another interface for those things, but crucially one that is always powered, always unlocked, and always in the same spot in your home, making it easy to walk up to and interact with.
Because my family all have iPhones, and because the HomeView will always be there and will feel familiar, I can see them actually using it.
If Apple has pulled that off, it could be more valuable than any new smart home feature I’ve been wishing for.

extraction.body: I love the approach Apple has taken with the HomeView. I think it’s the shared, always-available household interface that my family might finally use. Is Apple’s first smart display my dream smart home dashboard? But is it the right product for Apple Home at this moment? A lot of initial reactions to the $299 HomeView (which looks like a giant Apple Watch on a flatter metallic HomePod Mini) ask why you would want it when you can do most of what it offers on your iPhone or iPad. HomeView gives you another interface for those things, but crucially one that is always powered, always unlocked, and always in the same spot in your home, making it easy to walk up to and interact with. I’ve tried using an iPad to control my smart home, run my family’s calendar, and be a shared device for controlling music. An iPad can’t be a hub for your Apple Home; HomeView can. An iPad famously isn’t a good multiuser device, and controlling home devices on one requires it staying logged in to your personal iCloud account; HomeView offers Apple’s first crack at easy multiuser switching. Apple designed HomeView as a communal device that sits in a fixed place in the home. Not having a battery or detachable screen is a feature for me, because devices that do inevitably wander off and die under a couch cushion. One feature I’m most interested in is HomeView’s role as a home video phone. Do you know how many times I’ve tried to call my daughter when I’m not home, and her phone is dead or on silent? Based on Apple’s video, if she’s home, my call can now ring on the HomeView. Smart displays and speakers from Amazon and Google already help with this to some extent, but Apple’s version comes without ads (see the Echo Show) and may have a longer lifespan (RIP Pixel Tablet). She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” she said. "As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in a natural way.”" - Lilian Rincon, Apple Siri AI made this possible because it’s “much more capable,” said Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI at Apple. As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way.” On why now, Rincon says the natural-language shift is the point where AI goes mainstream. “Because now it can be … my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who’s in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want.” Siri AI in the home has another big advantage over the competition: It doesn’t say too much. “A lot of these assistants out there are always asking questions because they want more information,” she said. I had hoped that, along with new hardware, Apple would bring more functionality and deeper Apple Intelligence integration to Apple Home to make the smart home smarter. Apple trying to make the smart home easier for everyone to use can only be a good thing. As always, the smart home’s most important goal is to come up with an easier way to turn on the lights. HomeView’s simplicity may put off hardcore home automation enthusiasts, but I’d argue it’s perfect for their long-suffering spouses. I’ve tried every version of physical smart home control interface in my home, and you know who hasn’t used any of them? Because my family all have iPhones, and because the HomeView will always be there and will feel familiar, I can see them actually using it. That means I could set up a full Home Assistant instance and run a detailed dashboard on a tablet in my office, then feed the scenes and devices into Apple Home so my husband and daughter can just tap to control them on a HomeView in the kitchen. HomeView may not be the smart home computer I want Apple to make, but it is the smart home device Apple needed to make. It doesn’t have to run all the iPad apps or try to be a bigger version of my iPhone; it just needs to make the smart home accessible to everyone in the house. If Apple has pulled that off, it could be more valuable than any new smart home feature I’ve been wishing for.

After years of phone-centric habits, Apple’s new smart home device points toward a more ambient future, according to hands-on first impressions from The Wall Street Journal ’s Nicole Nguyen .
HomeView is a $299, seven-inch square tablet and speaker designed for smart home control, hands-free FaceTime calls, and interaction with the recently revamped Siri AI assistant.
As Nguyen notes in her reporting from New York City, the device’s clearest advantage over long-standing rivals from Amazon and Google is its deep access to data already on a user’s iPhone.⁠
In Nasdaq trading today, shares of Apple Inc. rose to hit a new all-time closing high.

IF Apple had a brain they would have offered a AppleTV with a built in FaceTime Camera and the software that is in the Continuity Camera feature that is very cool, but totally kludgy and nobody uses it because he have to futz with the phone and make a few false move every time you try to make a call.
The best feature of this software is how the iPhone camera can capture the whole room or find the speaker and zoom in on them gracefully.
It would be brilliant and it would immediately make FaceTime calls HomeFaceTime calls that display on your big screen instead of the tiny phone screen.
But they are too stupid to do this killer feature.
Homeview serves no real purpose and Apple TV is vastly overpriced by double for nothing more than a streaming box.
An OpenAI employee who left the ChatGPT maker for Apple sent more than 100 files about an unreleased product to a personal account…
Apple positions the product as both central to the home and private for each user, with pre-orders open now and availability starting November 13th in select countries.
Early looks from the event emphasize the design’s adaptability for counters, nightstands, or walls, along with room-filling audio and glanceable interfaces that shift based on distance.
The square screen sits on a compact speaker base (with a wall-mount option also available), letting it function as a shared household hub that can personalize the experience.

It uses facial recognition to identify up to six people and surface individual content — such as messages, calendars, or widgets — while keeping personal information protected behind that recognition (or an iPhone unlock as a fallback).

Siri AI, powered by Apple Intelligence, can draw on personal context from linked Apple devices for more helpful responses about schedules, messages, music, or home controls, while supporting features like recipe guidance, timers, and multi-camera live views for compatible HomeKit or Matter devices.

HomeView is a $299, seven-inch square tablet and speaker designed for smart home control, hands-free FaceTime calls, and interaction with the recently revamped Siri AI assistant. As Nguyen notes in her reporting from New York City, the device’s clearest advantage over long-standing rivals from Amazon and Google is its deep access to data already on a user’s iPhone.⁠

The square screen sits on a compact speaker base (with a wall-mount option also available), letting it function as a shared household hub that can personalize the experience. It uses facial recognition to identify up to six people and surface individual content — such as messages, calendars, or widgets — while keeping personal information protected behind that recognition (or an iPhone unlock as a fallback). Siri AI, powered by Apple Intelligence, can draw on personal context from linked Apple devices for more helpful responses about schedules, messages, music, or home controls, while supporting features like recipe guidance, timers, and multi-camera live views for compatible HomeKit or Matter devices.

Apple positions the product as both central to the home and private for each user, with pre-orders open now and availability starting November 13th in select countries. Early looks from the event emphasize the design’s adaptability for counters, nightstands, or walls, along with room-filling audio and glanceable interfaces that shift based on distance.

Nguyen’s hands-on account highlights the integration edge while the broader product introduction underscores privacy and ecosystem strengths. At the same time, the closed nature of the setup — requiring Apple devices for full personalization and limited third-party flexibility — means households outside the ecosystem may see fewer benefits than those already invested in iPhones and related gear. Whether the combination of Siri AI, facial recognition, and iPhone data access is enough to draw users away from established smart displays remains to be seen once the devices reach real homes. ‎ MacDailyNews Take: At just $299, it’s relatively inexpensive to just take a flier on one and see how much use it gets in our household.

sources.title: New streaming app Coda Music is rolling out tools for labeling and blocking AI-generated tunes - Engadget
passages: As for the new features for reporting and filtering out AI music, Coda says they're available as of today in its iOS and Android apps.
The company doesn't have a web interface yet, but says it is coming soon.
If ducking AI-generated tunes is something that catches your attention, Coda currently costs $11 a month, or $17 per month for a family plan with up to four listeners.
For starters, any artist added to Coda will be reviewed for AI origins, and their profile will be labeled "AI Artist" so that listeners know what they're getting into.
Coda is also letting users flag profiles of artists if they suspect the music is AI-generated; the company will then review them and label them if necessary.
Today, the fledgling service is announcing a new feature that feels designed to answer another of the recent Spotify controversies: AI slop music flooding the platform .
In response, Coda Music is launching AI identification tools with the purpose of finding and labeling songs that weren't composed by actual humans.
Besides its stance on AI and the assurance that the company does not "invest in war," there are a few other differentiators about Coda Music.
At this point, the streaming music landscape feels pretty well settled.

Obviously, how useful this setting is will depend on how good Coda gets at labeling AI-created music as such, but I can definitely see the appeal in just flipping that to "off" and avoiding as much slop as possible.

extraction.body: Coda Music is also vetting all new artists on the platform and proactively labeling AI artists it finds. At this point, the streaming music landscape feels pretty well settled. Giants like Spotify, Amazon, Apple and YouTube duke it out at the top, while plenty of other players like Qobuz, Tidal, Deezer try their best to stand out from the pack. Somewhat surprisingly, though, a new player emerged in September. Coda Music used the recent backlash around Spotify co-founder Daniel Ek as a way to differentiate itself from the number one streamer, calling out Ek's controversial funding of defense technology firm Helsing earlier in the year. (Spotify's refusal to stop airing ICE recruitment ads certainly hasn't helped the platform, either.) Today, the fledgling service is announcing a new feature that feels designed to answer another of the recent Spotify controversies: AI slop music flooding the platform . In response, Coda Music is launching AI identification tools with the purpose of finding and labeling songs that weren't composed by actual humans. There are a few prongs to Coda's approach. For starters, any artist added to Coda will be reviewed for AI origins, and their profile will be labeled "AI Artist" so that listeners know what they're getting into. Coda is also letting users flag profiles of artists if they suspect the music is AI-generated; the company will then review them and label them if necessary. Finally, there's a toggle in settings that just lets you turn off AI artists entirely. Obviously, how useful this setting is will depend on how good Coda gets at labeling AI-created music as such, but I can definitely see the appeal in just flipping that to "off" and avoiding as much slop as possible. Besides its stance on AI and the assurance that the company does not "invest in war," there are a few other differentiators about Coda Music. The company says that it currently paying the "highest per-stream rate" in the industry — while at the same time, it acknowledges that no one is paying enough to artists. "The real problem isn't how much is paid per stream, it's that streaming alone doesn't pay enough," the company's website says . "And minor improvements to a fundamentally flawed per stream model will not help." To that end, the company also lets users pick an "independent or qualifying artist" who gets $1 of their monthly subscription fee. Sure, it's only a dollar, but it's the kind of thing that sweetens the pot at least a little bit for musicians. And Coda has good reason to want to make itself visible to users and artists alike. The last major differentiator for Coda is the company's ambitions to turn its app into a social, music-sharing feed where you get recommendations from humans rather than algorithms. To that end, users can share anything from the app in their feed, and it also allows you to share external links and photos as well (go ahead and post your blurry images from that NIN concert!). The app's home page prominently features fan-made playlists and recommended users to follow in addition to the usual suggestions based on what you're listening to already. And there's a social tab where you can see posts from people you follow; share songs, artists or albums; and see posts from artists you follow. That last part is key, as Coda wants artists interacting and sharing as well as just end users. It reminds me a little bit of the Fan Groups feature that Amazon Music just announced — and as with that feature, the problem facing Coda is getting people to start contributing to a new network rather than just posting things on whatever app they're already using. Fortunately, music nerds love a community, so it'll be interesting to see if this takes off at all. As for the new features for reporting and filtering out AI music, Coda says they're available as of today in its iOS and Android apps. The company doesn't have a web interface yet, but says it is coming soon. If ducking AI-generated tunes is something that catches your attention, Coda currently costs $11 a month, or $17 per month for a family plan with up to four listeners.

sources.title: YouTube Music launches new labels as AI-generated music floods streaming platforms
passages: The move comes as AI-generated music rapidly expands across streaming services, and many platforms are adopting their own approaches.
For instance, Apple Music has plans to introduce “Made With AI” labels as part of its AI Transparency Tags later this year.
Spotify also has AI labels, as well as a music spam filter.
Deezer has taken one of the stricter stances, reporting in July that it was receiving nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks daily.
According to its help page , partners using YouTube can declare their work’s use of generative AI through one of three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI, or No Gen AI.
YouTube, by contrast, is focusing on disclosure rather than blanket restrictions.
Its new labels are intended to inform listeners about AI’s role in music creation, but AI involvement alone doesn’t make a track ineligible for monetization.

YouTube even experiments with AI-powered music creation, including its tool Dream Track , which lets select creators generate soundtracks featuring AI-generated versions of participating artists’ voices.
Now listeners will be able to easily identify tracks created using AI, including those involved in composition and vocals.
TIDAL also labels recordings it identifies as entirely AI-generated, allows listeners to disable them, and excludes these recordings from royalty attribution.
Notably, these labels will also extend to the main YouTube app.
Lauren covers media, streaming, apps and platforms at TechCrunch.

Now listeners will be able to easily identify tracks created using AI, including those involved in composition and vocals. The label will appear on the player page. Clicking on this label provides additional information about the specific role of AI in the track’s creation. Notably, these labels will also extend to the main YouTube app. YouTube said it collaborated with various music partners and deployed its own detection tools to identify AI-generated music. Tracks edited using pitch-correction tools such as Auto-Tune fall under the “No Gen AI” category. sources.title: Apple Music Plans ‘Made With AI’ Labels as Artificial Music Floods Streaming Platforms - The Source Magazine
passages: The streaming service plans to introduce visible “Made With AI” labels later this year for songs that are materially generated through artificial intelligence.
The move expands on Apple’s tagging system introduced in March and will require record labels and distributors to identify tracks that are primarily derived from generative AI services.
AI music has moved well beyond the experimental stage and into the center of the streaming economy.
Nearly 40 percent of July releases reportedly involved AI in some form, while platforms like Deezer have said AI-generated tracks now account for roughly 44 percent of daily uploads.
Apple Music is preparing to make AI-generated music easier to spot.

15.3% of "human" submissions on submithub actually had ai involved somewhere in the audio!!! the line between ai music and human music got blurry way faster than the labels are admitting… we can't runaway anymore: ai music aint going nowhere!!! 🎸 pic.twitter.com/FG037Z9035
The company is separating music that is fundamentally generated by AI from tracks where artists use AI-assisted tools during production, such as mastering, EQ, or other technical workflows.
Developers are facing increasing scrutiny over how music is collected and used to train generative models, especially when material is pulled from platforms such as YouTube and Spotify.

The move expands on Apple’s tagging system introduced in March and will require record labels and distributors to identify tracks that are primarily derived from generative AI services. The timing is significant. AI music has moved well beyond the experimental stage and into the center of the streaming economy. Nearly 40 percent of July releases reportedly involved AI in some form, while platforms like Deezer have said AI-generated tracks now account for roughly 44 percent of daily uploads. 15.3% of "human" submissions on submithub actually had ai involved somewhere in the audio!!! the line between ai music and human music got blurry way faster than the labels are admitting… we can't runaway anymore: ai music aint going nowhere!!! 🎸 pic.twitter.com/FG037Z9035 Listener behavior tells a different story. AI-generated songs still represent less than 3 percent of total streams, and a large portion of those plays have reportedly been linked to fraudulent or automated traffic. Apple’s approach is focused on disclosure rather than removal. The company is separating music that is fundamentally generated by AI from tracks where artists use AI-assisted tools during production, such as mastering, EQ, or other technical workflows. Under that distinction, a human-written and performed song using AI production software would not necessarily receive the same designation as a track whose vocals and instrumentation were generated primarily through prompts. SAG-AFTRA has praised the push for greater transparency, while reaction from listeners has ranged from support for clearer labeling to demands that streaming services allow users to block AI-generated music entirely. The issue is also getting bigger in courtrooms. Sony, Universal and Warner Music have pursued infringement cases against AI music companies including Suno and Udio over the use of copyrighted recordings in training datasets. Developers are facing increasing scrutiny over how music is collected and used to train generative models, especially when material is pulled from platforms such as YouTube and Spotify. AI music is already here at scale. Apple’s next move is about making sure listeners know when they are hearing it. Your email address will not be published. Required fields are marked *

sources.title: Streaming Platforms Back AI Music Labels as Fraud Actors Exploit Self-Reporting Gap
passages: Self-Reporting Cannot Reach the Platforms' Biggest Problem Here is the structural gap in that logic: the primary reason AI-generated tracks are being uploaded to streaming platforms at scale is not artistic expression — it is royalty fraud.

Of the streams those tracks generated, Deezer found that up to 85 percent were fraudulent in 2025 — fake plays driven by automated bots designed to extract royalties from the streaming pool, as detailed in the platform's AI fraud detection data.

Streaming platforms including Spotify, Apple Music, Amazon Music, and YouTube Music use a pro-rata royalty model: all subscription and advertising revenue is pooled, then divided proportionally across all streams that month.

Apple Music VP Oliver Schusser confirmed to The Hollywood Reporter that Apple demonetized approximately two billion fraudulent streams in 2025 alone, protecting roughly $17 million in royalties that would otherwise have flowed to bad actors instead of legitimate artists.
Apple Music launched its own voluntary AI Transparency Tags in March 2026, with the same architecture: labels and distributors declare AI use, and the platform displays the result.

Melissa Morgia, IFPI's chief global content protection officer, described AI to a WIPO enforcement panel in February 2025 as "the ultimate enabler" of streaming fraud, because it allows bad actors to operate below detection thresholds while still generating enough royalties to be profitable.
Fraud detection specialists at Beatdapp estimated that at least 10 percent of global streaming activity is fraudulent, representing roughly $2 billion in misallocated royalties annually.

A bipartisan group of senators has introduced the AI Labeling Act of 2026 (S.4915), which would require visible and machine-readable disclosures on AI-generated audio from developers and platforms — and would be enforced by the Federal Trade Commission.

The endorsement came three days after a coalition led by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) — joined by the Recording Academy, SAG-AFTRA, A2IM, IMPALA, WIN, and the Human Artistry Campaign — announced a voluntary two-tier labeling system that would tag tracks as either "AI-Generated" or "AI-Assisted." The proposed icons would function similarly to the explicit-content "E" label that has traveled with music metadata for decades.

"DIMA has long advocated for the creators, owners, and distributors of music to provide accurate and timely metadata on all music released and distributed to streaming services," said Graham Davies, DIMA president and CEO, in the statement.

Thibault Roucou, Deezer's head of streaming, stated the dynamic plainly in a May 2026 Music Week interview: "Generating fake streams continues to be the main purpose for uploading AI-generated music." The economics of why are straightforward.

TIDAL, meanwhile, has announced a TIDAL AI policy effective July 15 that takes effect tomorrow, July 15: fully AI-generated tracks will be labeled on the platform and will be ineligible for royalty attribution — the first major DSP to directly connect AI disclosure to payment status.

Deezer's 99.8% detection tool identifies unique audio signatures produced by generative AI models including Suno and Udio, and Deezer has licensed the tool to other platforms including Billboard, which now uses it to flag AI-generated tracks in its charts.

He added that DIMA's members were eager to work with labels, producers, artists, distributors, and standards body DDEX to build what he described as "a robust supply chain in which consumers can trust." What the Two Labels Actually Mean Under the RIAA/IFPI proposal, an "AI-Generated" tag would apply when artificial intelligence created the entirety or primary portion of a recording's creative elements — including tracks produced entirely from AI prompts, along with recordings whose lead vocals or key instrumentals are AI-generated.

extraction.body: The music industry's most powerful trade group threw its weight behind a new AI labeling standard this week — and quietly revealed why the standard, as currently designed, may not reach the people who need it most. The Digital Media Association (DIMA), whose members include Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, Amazon Music, TIDAL, Pandora, Qobuz, and Feed.fm, issued a formal statement last Friday welcoming a coalition proposal to embed AI-disclosure tags directly into music metadata on streaming platforms. The endorsement came three days after a coalition led by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) — joined by the Recording Academy, SAG-AFTRA, A2IM, IMPALA, WIN, and the Human Artistry Campaign — announced a voluntary two-tier labeling system that would tag tracks as either "AI-Generated" or "AI-Assisted." The proposed icons would function similarly to the explicit-content "E" label that has traveled with music metadata for decades. "DIMA has long advocated for the creators, owners, and distributors of music to provide accurate and timely metadata on all music released and distributed to streaming services," said Graham Davies, DIMA president and CEO, in the statement. He added that DIMA's members were eager to work with labels, producers, artists, distributors, and standards body DDEX to build what he described as "a robust supply chain in which consumers can trust." What the Two Labels Actually Mean Under the RIAA/IFPI proposal, an "AI-Generated" tag would apply when artificial intelligence created the entirety or primary portion of a recording's creative elements — including tracks produced entirely from AI prompts, along with recordings whose lead vocals or key instrumentals are AI-generated. The labels are described as voluntary and designed to travel through existing distribution pipelines as new fields in the industry's standard metadata format, the DDEX Electronic Release Notification standard (ERN) schema. RIAA chairman and CEO Mitch Glazier, speaking jointly with IFPI CEO Vikki Oakley at the announcement, framed the system as a way to accommodate both human artists and AI-assisted creators. "Artists who want to use AI in the creative process should be able to do so," he said. "Transparency is just the best way to have it both ways." Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. said the initiative was designed to ensure that "creativity, authorship, and artistic intent remain at the center of every song," according to the RIAA IFPI joint announcement. How the Pipeline Actually Works — and Where It Breaks The reason DIMA's statement emphasized the upstream supply chain rather than simply pledging to display labels is a technical one. AI disclosure under this system is a metadata field, not a platform-level detection scan. When a creator uploads a track, the label or distributor populates the AI disclosure field in the DDEX metadata delivery pipeline — the XML-formatted packet of data that travels from the rights holder through aggregators and distributors to DSPs like Spotify and Apple Music. If that field is populated correctly and the distributor's system supports it, the tag reaches the platform, which can then surface it to listeners in song credits or search filters. If the field is left blank — whether through oversight, lack of distributor support, or deliberate omission — no tag travels downstream, and the platform has no automated fallback at the ingest stage. Spotify's AI Credits disclosure system, which launched April 16, 2026, using the DDEX standard, operates exactly this way: disclosure is surfaced in song credits, and the company has confirmed it does not penalize or down-rank music for being AI-assisted. Apple Music launched its own voluntary AI Transparency Tags in March 2026, with the same architecture: labels and distributors declare AI use, and the platform displays the result. Self-Reporting Cannot Reach the Platforms' Biggest Problem Here is the structural gap in that logic: the primary reason AI-generated tracks are being uploaded to streaming platforms at scale is not artistic expression — it is royalty fraud. In April 2026, Deezer reported receiving roughly 75,000 fully AI-generated tracks per day, representing more than 44 percent of all content uploaded to the platform. Of the streams those tracks generated, Deezer found that up to 85 percent were fraudulent in 2025 — fake plays driven by automated bots designed to extract royalties from the streaming pool, as detailed in the platform's AI fraud detection data. Thibault Roucou, Deezer's head of streaming, stated the dynamic plainly in a May 2026 Music Week interview: "Generating fake streams continues to be the main purpose for uploading AI-generated music." The economics of why are straightforward. Streaming platforms including Spotify, Apple Music, Amazon Music, and YouTube Music use a pro-rata royalty model: all subscription and advertising revenue is pooled, then divided proportionally across all streams that month. Every fraudulent stream siphons from that shared pool. Fraud detection specialists at Beatdapp estimated that at least 10 percent of global streaming activity is fraudulent, representing roughly $2 billion in misallocated royalties annually. Apple Music VP Oliver Schusser confirmed to The Hollywood Reporter that Apple demonetized approximately two billion fraudulent streams in 2025 alone, protecting roughly $17 million in royalties that would otherwise have flowed to bad actors instead of legitimate artists. A bipartisan group of senators has introduced the AI Labeling Act of 2026 (S.4915), which would require visible and machine-readable disclosures on AI-generated audio from developers and platforms — and would be enforced by the Federal Trade Commission. But the bill remains in the first stage of the legislative process, and no enforcement mechanism exists in the current voluntary standard. Melissa Morgia, IFPI's chief global content protection officer, described AI to a WIPO enforcement panel in February 2025 as "the ultimate enabler" of streaming fraud, because it allows bad actors to operate below detection thresholds while still generating enough royalties to be profitable. Fraudsters have evolved past the early strategy of replaying a handful of tracks with bots — a pattern platforms learned to detect. Instead, they now flood distribution pipelines with millions of AI-generated tracks and stream each one a few thousand times, staying below individual detection thresholds while extracting royalties in aggregate across a vast catalog. Platforms Are Not Waiting for the Standard The RIAA/IFPI proposal is gaining support in part because major platforms had already begun building their own disclosure infrastructure — but the approaches differ significantly in what they can actually detect. The French streaming service launched its own AI detection tool in January 2025 and has since tagged more than 13.4 million tracks as fully AI-generated. In June 2026, the company released a second-generation detector it claims achieves 99.8 percent accuracy and has applied for patents on the underlying detection methods. Deezer's 99.8% detection tool identifies unique audio signatures produced by generative AI models including Suno and Udio, and Deezer has licensed the tool to other platforms including Billboard, which now uses it to flag AI-generated tracks in its charts. Qobuz introduced its own AI Charter and detection system in early 2026, committing to tag and remove content found to impersonate artists or manufacture fake streams. TIDAL, meanwhile, has announced a TIDAL AI policy effective July 15 that takes effect tomorrow, July 15: fully AI-generated tracks will be labeled on the platform and will be ineligible for royalty attribution — the first major DSP to directly connect AI disclosure to payment status. Rather than attempting to detect AI at the audio level, the platform enforces against behavior: mass uploads, duplicate titles, ultra-short filler tracks, and unauthorized voice clones.

coreStoryFacts.text: As for the new features for reporting and filtering out AI music, Coda says they're available as of today in its iOS and Android apps.
The company doesn't have a web interface yet, but says it is coming soon.
If ducking AI-generated tunes is something that catches your attention, Coda currently costs $11 a month, or $17 per month for a family plan with up to four listeners.
For starters, any artist added to Coda will be reviewed for AI origins, and their profile will be labeled "AI Artist" so that listeners know what they're getting into.
Coda is also letting users flag profiles of artists if they suspect the music is AI-generated; the company will then review them and label them if necessary.
Today, the fledgling service is announcing a new feature that feels designed to answer another of the recent Spotify controversies: AI slop music flooding the platform .
In response, Coda Music is launching AI identification tools with the purpose of finding and labeling songs that weren't composed by actual humans.
Besides its stance on AI and the assurance that the company does not "invest in war," there are a few other differentiators about Coda Music.
At this point, the streaming music landscape feels pretty well settled.

Obviously, how useful this setting is will depend on how good Coda gets at labeling AI-created music as such, but I can definitely see the appeal in just flipping that to "off" and avoiding as much slop as possible.
The move comes as AI-generated music rapidly expands across streaming services, and many platforms are adopting their own approaches.
For instance, Apple Music has plans to introduce “Made With AI” labels as part of its AI Transparency Tags later this year.
Spotify also has AI labels, as well as a music spam filter.
Deezer has taken one of the stricter stances, reporting in July that it was receiving nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks daily.
According to its help page , partners using YouTube can declare their work’s use of generative AI through one of three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI, or No Gen AI.
YouTube, by contrast, is focusing on disclosure rather than blanket restrictions.
Its new labels are intended to inform listeners about AI’s role in music creation, but AI involvement alone doesn’t make a track ineligible for monetization.

YouTube even experiments with AI-powered music creation, including its tool Dream Track , which lets select creators generate soundtracks featuring AI-generated versions of participating artists’ voices.
Now listeners will be able to easily identify tracks created using AI, including those involved in composition and vocals.
TIDAL also labels recordings it identifies as entirely AI-generated, allows listeners to disable them, and excludes these recordings from royalty attribution.
Notably, these labels will also extend to the main YouTube app.
Lauren covers media, streaming, apps and platforms at TechCrunch.

If ducking AI-generated tunes is something that catches your attention, Coda currently costs $11 a month, or $17 per month for a family plan with up to four listeners.
For starters, any artist added to Coda will be reviewed for AI origins, and their profile will be labeled "AI Artist" so that listeners know what they're getting into.
Coda is also letting users flag profiles of artists if they suspect the music is AI-generated; the company will then review them and label them if necessary.
Today, the fledgling service is announcing a new feature that feels designed to answer another of the recent Spotify controversies: AI slop music flooding the platform .
In response, Coda Music is launching AI identification tools with the purpose of finding and labeling songs that weren't composed by actual humans.
Besides its stance on AI and the assurance that the company does not "invest in war," there are a few other differentiators about Coda Music.
At this point, the streaming music landscape feels pretty well settled.

Obviously, how useful this setting is will depend on how good Coda gets at labeling AI-created music as such, but I can definitely see the appeal in just flipping that to "off" and avoiding as much slop as possible.
The move comes as AI-generated music rapidly expands across streaming services, and many platforms are adopting their own approaches.
For instance, Apple Music has plans to introduce “Made With AI” labels as part of its AI Transparency Tags later this year.
Spotify also has AI labels, as well as a music spam filter.
Deezer has taken one of the stricter stances, reporting in July that it was receiving nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks daily.
According to its help page , partners using YouTube can declare their work’s use of generative AI through one of three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI, or No Gen AI.
YouTube, by contrast, is focusing on disclosure rather than blanket restrictions.
Its new labels are intended to inform listeners about AI’s role in music creation, but AI involvement alone doesn’t make a track ineligible for monetization.

YouTube even experiments with AI-powered music creation, including its tool Dream Track , which lets select creators generate soundtracks featuring AI-generated versions of participating artists’ voices.
Now listeners will be able to easily identify tracks created using AI, including those involved in composition and vocals.
TIDAL also labels recordings it identifies as entirely AI-generated, allows listeners to disable them, and excludes these recordings from royalty attribution.
Notably, these labels will also extend to the main YouTube app.
Lauren covers media, streaming, apps and platforms at TechCrunch.
The streaming service plans to introduce visible “Made With AI” labels later this year for songs that are materially generated through artificial intelligence.
The move expands on Apple’s tagging system introduced in March and will require record labels and distributors to identify tracks that are primarily derived from generative AI services.
AI music has moved well beyond the experimental stage and into the center of the streaming economy.
Nearly 40 percent of July releases reportedly involved AI in some form, while platforms like Deezer have said AI-generated tracks now account for roughly 44 percent of daily uploads.
Apple Music is preparing to make AI-generated music easier to spot.

15.3% of "human" submissions on submithub actually had ai involved somewhere in the audio!!! the line between ai music and human music got blurry way faster than the labels are admitting… we can't runaway anymore: ai music aint going nowhere!!! 🎸 pic.twitter.com/FG037Z9035
The company is separating music that is fundamentally generated by AI from tracks where artists use AI-assisted tools during production, such as mastering, EQ, or other technical workflows.
Developers are facing increasing scrutiny over how music is collected and used to train generative models, especially when material is pulled from platforms such as YouTube and Spotify.
The Magazine of Hip Hop Music, Culture and Politics

Self-Reporting Cannot Reach the Platforms' Biggest Problem Here is the structural gap in that logic: the primary reason AI-generated tracks are being uploaded to streaming platforms at scale is not artistic expression — it is royalty fraud.

Of the streams those tracks generated, Deezer found that up to 85 percent were fraudulent in 2025 — fake plays driven by automated bots designed to extract royalties from the streaming pool, as detailed in the platform's AI fraud detection data.

Streaming platforms including Spotify, Apple Music, Amazon Music, and YouTube Music use a pro-rata royalty model: all subscription and advertising revenue is pooled, then divided proportionally across all streams that month.

Apple Music VP Oliver Schusser confirmed to The Hollywood Reporter that Apple demonetized approximately two billion fraudulent streams in 2025 alone, protecting roughly $17 million in royalties that would otherwise have flowed to bad actors instead of legitimate artists.
Apple Music launched its own voluntary AI Transparency Tags in March 2026, with the same architecture: labels and distributors declare AI use, and the platform displays the result.

Melissa Morgia, IFPI's chief global content protection officer, described AI to a WIPO enforcement panel in February 2025 as "the ultimate enabler" of streaming fraud, because it allows bad actors to operate below detection thresholds while still generating enough royalties to be profitable.
Fraud detection specialists at Beatdapp estimated that at least 10 percent of global streaming activity is fraudulent, representing roughly $2 billion in misallocated royalties annually.

A bipartisan group of senators has introduced the AI Labeling Act of 2026 (S.4915), which would require visible and machine-readable disclosures on AI-generated audio from developers and platforms — and would be enforced by the Federal Trade Commission.

The endorsement came three days after a coalition led by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) — joined by the Recording Academy, SAG-AFTRA, A2IM, IMPALA, WIN, and the Human Artistry Campaign — announced a voluntary two-tier labeling system that would tag tracks as either "AI-Generated" or "AI-Assisted." The proposed icons would function similarly to the explicit-content "E" label that has traveled with music metadata for decades.

"DIMA has long advocated for the creators, owners, and distributors of music to provide accurate and timely metadata on all music released and distributed to streaming services," said Graham Davies, DIMA president and CEO, in the statement.

Thibault Roucou, Deezer's head of streaming, stated the dynamic plainly in a May 2026 Music Week interview: "Generating fake streams continues to be the main purpose for uploading AI-generated music." The economics of why are straightforward.

TIDAL, meanwhile, has announced a TIDAL AI policy effective July 15 that takes effect tomorrow, July 15: fully AI-generated tracks will be labeled on the platform and will be ineligible for royalty attribution — the first major DSP to directly connect AI disclosure to payment status.

Deezer's 99.8% detection tool identifies unique audio signatures produced by generative AI models including Suno and Udio, and Deezer has licensed the tool to other platforms including Billboard, which now uses it to flag AI-generated tracks in its charts.

He added that DIMA's members were eager to work with labels, producers, artists, distributors, and standards body DDEX to build what he described as "a robust supply chain in which consumers can trust." What the Two Labels Actually Mean Under the RIAA/IFPI proposal, an "AI-Generated" tag would apply when artificial intelligence created the entirety or primary portion of a recording's creative elements — including tracks produced entirely from AI prompts, along with recordings whose lead vocals or key instrumentals are AI-generated.

extraction.body: Coda Music is also vetting all new artists on the platform and proactively labeling AI artists it finds. At this point, the streaming music landscape feels pretty well settled. Giants like Spotify, Amazon, Apple and YouTube duke it out at the top, while plenty of other players like Qobuz, Tidal, Deezer try their best to stand out from the pack. Somewhat surprisingly, though, a new player emerged in September. Coda Music used the recent backlash around Spotify co-founder Daniel Ek as a way to differentiate itself from the number one streamer, calling out Ek's controversial funding of defense technology firm Helsing earlier in the year. (Spotify's refusal to stop airing ICE recruitment ads certainly hasn't helped the platform, either.) Today, the fledgling service is announcing a new feature that feels designed to answer another of the recent Spotify controversies: AI slop music flooding the platform . In response, Coda Music is launching AI identification tools with the purpose of finding and labeling songs that weren't composed by actual humans. There are a few prongs to Coda's approach. For starters, any artist added to Coda will be reviewed for AI origins, and their profile will be labeled "AI Artist" so that listeners know what they're getting into. Coda is also letting users flag profiles of artists if they suspect the music is AI-generated; the company will then review them and label them if necessary. Finally, there's a toggle in settings that just lets you turn off AI artists entirely. Obviously, how useful this setting is will depend on how good Coda gets at labeling AI-created music as such, but I can definitely see the appeal in just flipping that to "off" and avoiding as much slop as possible. Besides its stance on AI and the assurance that the company does not "invest in war," there are a few other differentiators about Coda Music. The company says that it currently paying the "highest per-stream rate" in the industry — while at the same time, it acknowledges that no one is paying enough to artists. "The real problem isn't how much is paid per stream, it's that streaming alone doesn't pay enough," the company's website says . "And minor improvements to a fundamentally flawed per stream model will not help." To that end, the company also lets users pick an "independent or qualifying artist" who gets $1 of their monthly subscription fee. Sure, it's only a dollar, but it's the kind of thing that sweetens the pot at least a little bit for musicians. And Coda has good reason to want to make itself visible to users and artists alike. The last major differentiator for Coda is the company's ambitions to turn its app into a social, music-sharing feed where you get recommendations from humans rather than algorithms. To that end, users can share anything from the app in their feed, and it also allows you to share external links and photos as well (go ahead and post your blurry images from that NIN concert!). The app's home page prominently features fan-made playlists and recommended users to follow in addition to the usual suggestions based on what you're listening to already. And there's a social tab where you can see posts from people you follow; share songs, artists or albums; and see posts from artists you follow. That last part is key, as Coda wants artists interacting and sharing as well as just end users. It reminds me a little bit of the Fan Groups feature that Amazon Music just announced — and as with that feature, the problem facing Coda is getting people to start contributing to a new network rather than just posting things on whatever app they're already using. Fortunately, music nerds love a community, so it'll be interesting to see if this takes off at all. As for the new features for reporting and filtering out AI music, Coda says they're available as of today in its iOS and Android apps. The company doesn't have a web interface yet, but says it is coming soon. At this point, the streaming music landscape feels pretty well settled. Giants like Spotify, Amazon, Apple and YouTube duke it out at the top, while plenty of other players like Qobuz, Tidal, Deezer try their best to stand out from the pack. Somewhat surprisingly, though, a new player emerged in September. Coda Music used the recent backlash around Spotify co-founder Daniel Ek as a way to differentiate itself from the number one streamer, calling out Ek's controversial funding of defense technology firm Helsing earlier in the year. (Spotify's refusal to stop airing ICE recruitment ads certainly hasn't helped the platform, either.)

Today, the fledgling service is announcing a new feature that feels designed to answer another of the recent Spotify controversies: AI slop music flooding the platform . In response, Coda Music is launching AI identification tools with the purpose of finding and labeling songs that weren't composed by actual humans.

There are a few prongs to Coda's approach. For starters, any artist added to Coda will be reviewed for AI origins, and their profile will be labeled "AI Artist" so that listeners know what they're getting into. Coda is also letting users flag profiles of artists if they suspect the music is AI-generated; the company will then review them and label them if necessary.

Finally, there's a toggle in settings that just lets you turn off AI artists entirely. Obviously, how useful this setting is will depend on how good Coda gets at labeling AI-created music as such, but I can definitely see the appeal in just flipping that to "off" and avoiding as much slop as possible.

Besides its stance on AI and the assurance that the company does not "invest in war," there are a few other differentiators about Coda Music. The company says that it currently paying the "highest per-stream rate" in the industry — while at the same time, it acknowledges that no one is paying enough to artists. "The real problem isn't how much is paid per stream, it's that streaming alone doesn't pay enough," the company's website says . "And minor improvements to a fundamentally flawed per stream model will not help."

To that end, the company also lets users pick an "independent or qualifying artist" who gets $1 of their monthly subscription fee. Sure, it's only a dollar, but it's the kind of thing that sweetens the pot at least a little bit for musicians.

And Coda has good reason to want to make itself visible to users and artists alike. The last major differentiator for Coda is the company's ambitions to turn its app into a social, music-sharing feed where you get recommendations from humans rather than algorithms. To that end, users can share anything from the app in their feed, and it also allows you to share external links and photos as well (go ahead and post your blurry images from that NIN concert!).

The app's home page prominently features fan-made playlists and recommended users to follow in addition to the usual suggestions based on what you're listening to already. And there's a social tab where you can see posts from people you follow; share songs, artists or albums; and see posts from artists you follow. That last part is key, as Coda wants artists interacting and sharing as well as just end users.

It reminds me a little bit of the Fan Groups feature that Amazon Music just announced — and as with that feature, the problem facing Coda is getting people to start contributing to a new network rather than just posting things on whatever app they're already using. Fortunately, music nerds love a community, so it'll be interesting to see if this takes off at all.

The company doesn't have a web interface yet, but says it is coming soon. If ducking AI-generated tunes is something that catches your attention, Coda currently costs $11 a month, or $17 per month for a family plan with up to four listeners.

sources.title: YouTube Music launches new labels as AI-generated music floods streaming platforms
passages: The move comes as AI-generated music rapidly expands across streaming services, and many platforms are adopting their own approaches.
For instance, Apple Music has plans to introduce “Made With AI” labels as part of its AI Transparency Tags later this year.
Spotify also has AI labels, as well as a music spam filter.
Deezer has taken one of the stricter stances, reporting in July that it was receiving nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks daily.
According to its help page , partners using YouTube can declare their work’s use of generative AI through one of three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI, or No Gen AI.
YouTube, by contrast, is focusing on disclosure rather than blanket restrictions.
Its new labels are intended to inform listeners about AI’s role in music creation, but AI involvement alone doesn’t make a track ineligible for monetization.

YouTube even experiments with AI-powered music creation, including its tool Dream Track , which lets select creators generate soundtracks featuring AI-generated versions of participating artists’ voices.
Now listeners will be able to easily identify tracks created using AI, including those involved in composition and vocals.
TIDAL also labels recordings it identifies as entirely AI-generated, allows listeners to disable them, and excludes these recordings from royalty attribution.
Notably, these labels will also extend to the main YouTube app.
Lauren covers media, streaming, apps and platforms at TechCrunch.

sources.title: Apple Music Plans ‘Made With AI’ Labels as Artificial Music Floods Streaming Platforms - The Source Magazine
passages: The streaming service plans to introduce visible “Made With AI” labels later this year for songs that are materially generated through artificial intelligence.
The move expands on Apple’s tagging system introduced in March and will require record labels and distributors to identify tracks that are primarily derived from generative AI services.
AI music has moved well beyond the experimental stage and into the center of the streaming economy.
Nearly 40 percent of July releases reportedly involved AI in some form, while platforms like Deezer have said AI-generated tracks now account for roughly 44 percent of daily uploads.
Apple Music is preparing to make AI-generated music easier to spot.

The company is separating music that is fundamentally generated by AI from tracks where artists use AI-assisted tools during production, such as mastering, EQ, or other technical workflows.

The move expands on Apple’s tagging system introduced in March and will require record labels and distributors to identify tracks that are primarily derived from generative AI services. AI-generated songs still represent less than 3 percent of total streams, and a large portion of those plays have reportedly been linked to fraudulent or automated traffic. Apple’s approach is focused on disclosure rather than removal. The company is separating music that is fundamentally generated by AI from tracks where artists use AI-assisted tools during production, such as mastering, EQ, or other technical workflows. Under that distinction, a human-written and performed song using AI production software would not necessarily receive the same designation as a track whose vocals and instrumentation were generated primarily through prompts. SAG-AFTRA has praised the push for greater transparency, while reaction from listeners has ranged from support for clearer labeling to demands that streaming services allow users to block AI-generated music entirely. The issue is also getting bigger in courtrooms. Sony, Universal and Warner Music have pursued infringement cases against AI music companies including Suno and Udio over the use of copyrighted recordings in training datasets. Developers are facing increasing scrutiny over how music is collected and used to train generative models, especially when material is pulled from platforms such as YouTube and Spotify. sources.title: Streaming Platforms Back AI Music Labels as Fraud Actors Exploit Self-Reporting Gap
passages: Self-Reporting Cannot Reach the Platforms' Biggest Problem Here is the structural gap in that logic: the primary reason AI-generated tracks are being uploaded to streaming platforms at scale is not artistic expression — it is royalty fraud.

Of the streams those tracks generated, Deezer found that up to 85 percent were fraudulent in 2025 — fake plays driven by automated bots designed to extract royalties from the streaming pool, as detailed in the platform's AI fraud detection data.

Streaming platforms including Spotify, Apple Music, Amazon Music, and YouTube Music use a pro-rata royalty model: all subscription and advertising revenue is pooled, then divided proportionally across all streams that month.

Apple Music VP Oliver Schusser confirmed to The Hollywood Reporter that Apple demonetized approximately two billion fraudulent streams in 2025 alone, protecting roughly $17 million in royalties that would otherwise have flowed to bad actors instead of legitimate artists.
Apple Music launched its own voluntary AI Transparency Tags in March 2026, with the same architecture: labels and distributors declare AI use, and the platform displays the result.

Melissa Morgia, IFPI's chief global content protection officer, described AI to a WIPO enforcement panel in February 2025 as "the ultimate enabler" of streaming fraud, because it allows bad actors to operate below detection thresholds while still generating enough royalties to be profitable.
Fraud detection specialists at Beatdapp estimated that at least 10 percent of global streaming activity is fraudulent, representing roughly $2 billion in misallocated royalties annually.

A bipartisan group of senators has introduced the AI Labeling Act of 2026 (S.4915), which would require visible and machine-readable disclosures on AI-generated audio from developers and platforms — and would be enforced by the Federal Trade Commission.

The endorsement came three days after a coalition led by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) — joined by the Recording Academy, SAG-AFTRA, A2IM, IMPALA, WIN, and the Human Artistry Campaign — announced a voluntary two-tier labeling system that would tag tracks as either "AI-Generated" or "AI-Assisted." The proposed icons would function similarly to the explicit-content "E" label that has traveled with music metadata for decades.

"DIMA has long advocated for the creators, owners, and distributors of music to provide accurate and timely metadata on all music released and distributed to streaming services," said Graham Davies, DIMA president and CEO, in the statement.

Thibault Roucou, Deezer's head of streaming, stated the dynamic plainly in a May 2026 Music Week interview: "Generating fake streams continues to be the main purpose for uploading AI-generated music." The economics of why are straightforward.

TIDAL, meanwhile, has announced a TIDAL AI policy effective July 15 that takes effect tomorrow, July 15: fully AI-generated tracks will be labeled on the platform and will be ineligible for royalty attribution — the first major DSP to directly connect AI disclosure to payment status.

Deezer's 99.8% detection tool identifies unique audio signatures produced by generative AI models including Suno and Udio, and Deezer has licensed the tool to other platforms including Billboard, which now uses it to flag AI-generated tracks in its charts.

He added that DIMA's members were eager to work with labels, producers, artists, distributors, and standards body DDEX to build what he described as "a robust supply chain in which consumers can trust." What the Two Labels Actually Mean Under the RIAA/IFPI proposal, an "AI-Generated" tag would apply when artificial intelligence created the entirety or primary portion of a recording's creative elements — including tracks produced entirely from AI prompts, along with recordings whose lead vocals or key instrumentals are AI-generated.

extraction.body: The music industry's most powerful trade group threw its weight behind a new AI labeling standard this week — and quietly revealed why the standard, as currently designed, may not reach the people who need it most. The Digital Media Association (DIMA), whose members include Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, Amazon Music, TIDAL, Pandora, Qobuz, and Feed.fm, issued a formal statement last Friday welcoming a coalition proposal to embed AI-disclosure tags directly into music metadata on streaming platforms. The endorsement came three days after a coalition led by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) — joined by the Recording Academy, SAG-AFTRA, A2IM, IMPALA, WIN, and the Human Artistry Campaign — announced a voluntary two-tier labeling system that would tag tracks as either "AI-Generated" or "AI-Assisted." The proposed icons would function similarly to the explicit-content "E" label that has traveled with music metadata for decades. "DIMA has long advocated for the creators, owners, and distributors of music to provide accurate and timely metadata on all music released and distributed to streaming services," said Graham Davies, DIMA president and CEO, in the statement. He added that DIMA's members were eager to work with labels, producers, artists, distributors, and standards body DDEX to build what he described as "a robust supply chain in which consumers can trust." What the Two Labels Actually Mean Under the RIAA/IFPI proposal, an "AI-Generated" tag would apply when artificial intelligence created the entirety or primary portion of a recording's creative elements — including tracks produced entirely from AI prompts, along with recordings whose lead vocals or key instrumentals are AI-generated. The labels are described as voluntary and designed to travel through existing distribution pipelines as new fields in the industry's standard metadata format, the DDEX Electronic Release Notification standard (ERN) schema. RIAA chairman and CEO Mitch Glazier, speaking jointly with IFPI CEO Vikki Oakley at the announcement, framed the system as a way to accommodate both human artists and AI-assisted creators. "Artists who want to use AI in the creative process should be able to do so," he said. "Transparency is just the best way to have it both ways." Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. said the initiative was designed to ensure that "creativity, authorship, and artistic intent remain at the center of every song," according to the RIAA IFPI joint announcement. How the Pipeline Actually Works — and Where It Breaks The reason DIMA's statement emphasized the upstream supply chain rather than simply pledging to display labels is a technical one. AI disclosure under this system is a metadata field, not a platform-level detection scan. When a creator uploads a track, the label or distributor populates the AI disclosure field in the DDEX metadata delivery pipeline — the XML-formatted packet of data that travels from the rights holder through aggregators and distributors to DSPs like Spotify and Apple Music. If that field is populated correctly and the distributor's system supports it, the tag reaches the platform, which can then surface it to listeners in song credits or search filters. If the field is left blank — whether through oversight, lack of distributor support, or deliberate omission — no tag travels downstream, and the platform has no automated fallback at the ingest stage. Spotify's AI Credits disclosure system, which launched April 16, 2026, using the DDEX standard, operates exactly this way: disclosure is surfaced in song credits, and the company has confirmed it does not penalize or down-rank music for being AI-assisted. Apple Music launched its own voluntary AI Transparency Tags in March 2026, with the same architecture: labels and distributors declare AI use, and the platform displays the result.
