sources.title: Apple releases HomeView smart home hub with screen as showcase for Siri AI - CNBC
passages: Apple said its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.
Apple on Tuesday announced a home hub called HomeView, marking CEO John Ternus' first launch outside of iPhones since he took over from Tim Cook at the start of September.
Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad.

"It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's marketing head Greg Joswiak said in a statement.
The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch.

The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month.
Apple is emphasizing privacy, and said on Tuesday that its Apple Home Collection accessories encrypt data so that only the user and people they share with can see it.
Other smart home cameras, for example, maintain limited access to user video, or store it on servers.
Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence.
People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone.

"Apple always waits for an ecosystem to develop first until they are positive they can provide a stellar user experience," said Jennifer Kent, principal analyst at Parks Associates, which conducts research on the connected home.
Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday.
Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price.
Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories.
But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage.
It also comes as Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster.

extraction.body: Apple on Tuesday announced a home hub called HomeView, marking CEO John Ternus' first launch outside of iPhones since he took over from Tim Cook at the start of September. Apple said the device with a 7-inch screen was designed to be mounted on a wall or placed on a table. It's designed for multiple people in a household, and will recognize the user by their face to display pertinent information. It starts at $299 and ships on Nov. 13. Tuesday's launch event is the second under Ternus, who was the company's longtime hardware boss before being promoted to CEO. Last month, Apple announced new models of its most important product, the iPhone, including a foldable model called the Duo that retails for nearly $2,000. Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday. The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and has a redesigned remote that can play a sound if it is lost. Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price. The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month. Apple said HomeView features Siri AI, which can answer a broad range of questions. Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad. It has a built-in speaker for playing music. "It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's marketing head Greg Joswiak said in a statement. Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence. It can also be used to make FaceTime calls and as a digital photo frame. It's equipped with an Apple A18 chip. It supports up to six users. Apple TV, HomePods, and HomeView are included in Apple's Wearables, Home, and Accessories category, which reported $7.88 billion in sales in the most recent quarter ended June, which was about 7% of the company's total revenue. The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch. But while Apple has dabbled in home products and platforms in the past, Tuesday's announcement shows Apple is making its home products a higher priority under Ternus. "Apple always waits for an ecosystem to develop first until they are positive they can provide a stellar user experience," said Jennifer Kent, principal analyst at Parks Associates, which conducts research on the connected home. Apple said its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple is emphasizing privacy, and said on Tuesday that its Apple Home Collection accessories encrypt data so that only the user and people they share with can see it. Other smart home cameras, for example, maintain limited access to user video, or store it on servers. "They are going above and beyond what a lot of other companies do when it comes to privacy and security protections," Kent said. Apple's integration with the smart home is not just about sales, but also helps further lock customers into its ecosystem. People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone. HomeView can also become a smart home dashboard, Apple said. It can be used to view camera feeds, adjust the thermostat, or lock connected doors around the house. Apple said that setting up a new smart home device takes one tap from the user's iPhone. Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories. But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage. It also comes as Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster. Apple's new Apple TV 4K got a price hike from $199 to $299, and follows a similar price increase earlier this year, after Cook said that memory costs for Apple were unsustainable. extraction.body: Apple has opened preorders for HomeView, a $299 smart display intended to sit at the center of a connected household. The 7-inch device combines touch controls for lights, locks and cameras with FaceTime, speakers, personalized household screens and Siri AI. It goes on sale Nov. 13 in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, India and New Zealand. The launch gives Apple a direct answer to screen-equipped home hubs from Amazon and Google, a category where Apple has largely relied on iPads, HomePods and third-party accessories. Apple says HomeView can recognize up to six people, while its most sensitive personalized functions require an eligible, nearby and recently unlocked iPhone or iPad. According to Apple’s HomeView announcement , the device has a 7-inch Liquid Retina display and an A18 chip. It is available as a tabletop model or a wall-mounted model, both listed at $299 in the United States. The wall version requires a separate Schneider Home mount. Apple lists USB-C and AC-wired mounts at $59.95 and $79.95, respectively, while a Power over Ethernet mount priced at $129.95 is not expected until early 2027. Apple says HomeView can recognize up to six people and show personalized calendars, reminders, photo collections and home controls. CNBC’s launch coverage also describes the device as a showcase for the company’s Siri AI effort and household-profile system. Recognition does not by itself open a person’s private material. Apple says personal content requires that user’s paired iPhone or iPad to be nearby and recently unlocked. Personal-context Siri requests also require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. Apple describes HomeView as a shared device for household tasks while keeping personal content tied to a user’s paired device. Apple also says camera and microphone information is processed in protected hardware runtimes unavailable to HomeView software, apps, users or Apple itself. The company presents those protections as part of its privacy approach. HomeView is a touch-and-voice controller for compatible Apple Home and Matter accessories. Apple says users can view as many as nine live camera feeds at once and control connected devices through the screen or Siri. Apple is also using HomeView to promote its Apple Home Collection, a group of accessories developed with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. CNET’s launch coverage cites Ben Wood, chief analyst at CCS Insight, saying Apple has made setup for the new home products simpler than alternatives that require separate apps and QR-code scanning. Apple’s announcement says HomeView works with Apple TV and compatible third-party audio and video apps. The release does not provide a service-by-service list or clearly state which video apps run directly on HomeView and which require an iPhone, iPad or another Apple device. WIRED’s hands-on report says HomeView has no App Store and that YouTube, Netflix and Disney+ were not available as native apps at the time of its briefing. AppleInsider reported that video playback may depend on AirPlay from an iPhone or iPad or on CarPlay-related functionality. The available reporting does not resolve which services Apple considers compatible video apps. Preorders began Oct. 13 in the first group of markets. Apple says Singapore preorders begin Oct. 15. South Africa is scheduled to receive HomeView on Nov. 13 through authorized resellers. Apple says HomeView will not be sold in the European Union at launch because Siri AI is unavailable in iOS there. Siri AI is labeled beta in HomeView software version 27.2, and Apple says its personal-context capabilities require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. HomeView becomes available Nov. 13 in Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Apple says HomeView can recognize up to six people, while its most sensitive personalized functions require an eligible, nearby and recently unlocked iPhone or iPad.

According to Apple’s HomeView announcement , the device has a 7-inch Liquid Retina display and an A18 chip. It is available as a tabletop model or a wall-mounted model, both listed at $299 in the United States. The wall version requires a separate Schneider Home mount. Apple lists USB-C and AC-wired mounts at $59.95 and $79.95, respectively, while a Power over Ethernet mount priced at $129.95 is not expected until early 2027.

Apple says HomeView can recognize up to six people and show personalized calendars, reminders, photo collections and home controls. CNBC’s launch coverage also describes the device as a showcase for the company’s Siri AI effort and household-profile system.

Recognition does not by itself open a person’s private material. Apple says personal content requires that user’s paired iPhone or iPad to be nearby and recently unlocked. Personal-context Siri requests also require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. Apple describes HomeView as a shared device for household tasks while keeping personal content tied to a user’s paired device.

Apple also says camera and microphone information is processed in protected hardware runtimes unavailable to HomeView software, apps, users or Apple itself. The company presents those protections as part of its privacy approach.

HomeView is a touch-and-voice controller for compatible Apple Home and Matter accessories. Apple says users can view as many as nine live camera feeds at once and control connected devices through the screen or Siri.

Apple is also using HomeView to promote its Apple Home Collection, a group of accessories developed with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. CNET’s launch coverage cites Ben Wood, chief analyst at CCS Insight, saying Apple has made setup for the new home products simpler than alternatives that require separate apps and QR-code scanning.

Apple’s announcement says HomeView works with Apple TV and compatible third-party audio and video apps. The release does not provide a service-by-service list or clearly state which video apps run directly on HomeView and which require an iPhone, iPad or another Apple device.

WIRED’s hands-on report says HomeView has no App Store and that YouTube, Netflix and Disney+ were not available as native apps at the time of its briefing. AppleInsider reported that video playback may depend on AirPlay from an iPhone or iPad or on CarPlay-related functionality. The available reporting does not resolve which services Apple considers compatible video apps.

Preorders began Oct. 13 in the first group of markets. Apple says Singapore preorders begin Oct. 15. South Africa is scheduled to receive HomeView on Nov. 13 through authorized resellers. Apple says HomeView will not be sold in the European Union at launch because Siri AI is unavailable in iOS there.

Siri AI is labeled beta in HomeView software version 27.2, and Apple says its personal-context capabilities require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. HomeView becomes available Nov. 13 in Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States.

passages: Apple said its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.
Apple on Tuesday announced a home hub called HomeView, marking CEO John Ternus' first launch outside of iPhones since he took over from Tim Cook at the start of September.
Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad.

"It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's marketing head Greg Joswiak said in a statement.
The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch.

The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month.
Apple is emphasizing privacy, and said on Tuesday that its Apple Home Collection accessories encrypt data so that only the user and people they share with can see it.
Other smart home cameras, for example, maintain limited access to user video, or store it on servers.
Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence.
People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone.

"Apple always waits for an ecosystem to develop first until they are positive they can provide a stellar user experience," said Jennifer Kent, principal analyst at Parks Associates, which conducts research on the connected home.
Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday.
Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price.
Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories.
But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage.
It also comes as Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster.

13 in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, India and New Zealand.

Apple also says camera and microphone information is processed in protected hardware runtimes unavailable to HomeView software, apps, users or Apple itself.

extraction.body: Apple has opened preorders for HomeView, a $299 smart display intended to sit at the center of a connected household. The 7-inch device combines touch controls for lights, locks and cameras with FaceTime, speakers, personalized household screens and Siri AI. It goes on sale Nov. 13 in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, India and New Zealand. The launch gives Apple a direct answer to screen-equipped home hubs from Amazon and Google, a category where Apple has largely relied on iPads, HomePods and third-party accessories. Apple says HomeView can recognize up to six people, while its most sensitive personalized functions require an eligible, nearby and recently unlocked iPhone or iPad. According to Apple’s HomeView announcement , the device has a 7-inch Liquid Retina display and an A18 chip. It is available as a tabletop model or a wall-mounted model, both listed at $299 in the United States. The wall version requires a separate Schneider Home mount. Apple lists USB-C and AC-wired mounts at $59.95 and $79.95, respectively, while a Power over Ethernet mount priced at $129.95 is not expected until early 2027. Apple says HomeView can recognize up to six people and show personalized calendars, reminders, photo collections and home controls. CNBC’s launch coverage also describes the device as a showcase for the company’s Siri AI effort and household-profile system. Recognition does not by itself open a person’s private material. Apple says personal content requires that user’s paired iPhone or iPad to be nearby and recently unlocked. Personal-context Siri requests also require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. Apple describes HomeView as a shared device for household tasks while keeping personal content tied to a user’s paired device. Apple also says camera and microphone information is processed in protected hardware runtimes unavailable to HomeView software, apps, users or Apple itself. The company presents those protections as part of its privacy approach. HomeView is a touch-and-voice controller for compatible Apple Home and Matter accessories. Apple says users can view as many as nine live camera feeds at once and control connected devices through the screen or Siri. Apple is also using HomeView to promote its Apple Home Collection, a group of accessories developed with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. CNET’s launch coverage cites Ben Wood, chief analyst at CCS Insight, saying Apple has made setup for the new home products simpler than alternatives that require separate apps and QR-code scanning. Apple’s announcement says HomeView works with Apple TV and compatible third-party audio and video apps. The release does not provide a service-by-service list or clearly state which video apps run directly on HomeView and which require an iPhone, iPad or another Apple device. WIRED’s hands-on report says HomeView has no App Store and that YouTube, Netflix and Disney+ were not available as native apps at the time of its briefing. AppleInsider reported that video playback may depend on AirPlay from an iPhone or iPad or on CarPlay-related functionality. The available reporting does not resolve which services Apple considers compatible video apps. Preorders began Oct. 13 in the first group of markets. Apple says Singapore preorders begin Oct. 15. South Africa is scheduled to receive HomeView on Nov. 13 through authorized resellers. Apple says HomeView will not be sold in the European Union at launch because Siri AI is unavailable in iOS there. Siri AI is labeled beta in HomeView software version 27.2, and Apple says its personal-context capabilities require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. HomeView becomes available Nov. 13 in Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States.

extraction.body: If you are trying to do some online grocery shopping with Giant, Stop & Shop or Food Lion, you may notice that their websites and apps are currently unavailable. Dutch supermarket giant Ahold Delhaize said Tuesday it was working to restore systems it had shut down following what it described as a security issue. The company said its stores — including Albert Heijn in the Netherlands, Delhaize in Belgium and Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Giant in the United States — remained open, but the websites for those brands remained offline. There are published reports of a cybersecurity incident at the company that owns the chains. Each chains' website says they are "working to restore service as quickly as possible," adding that customers can still place delivery orders through Instacart, DoorDash and Uber Eats. Any unfulfilled web and app orders will be refunded. The chains' pharmacies and fueling stations are also still open. Ahold Delhaize said it had no evidence that customer or employee data had been stolen. This comes as cyberattacks disrupted European supermarket chains, affecting refrigeration systems at hundreds of stores in France and forcing a major grocer to shut down websites serving customers in Europe and the United States. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on Tuesday that about 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets were affected. He said there was no risk to France's food supplies but acknowledged that the attack "touches the heart of our food security." "It was a wake-up call for everyone," he said. The French government's cybersecurity agency said Tuesday it was "aware of numerous compromises" involving refrigeration system remote control modules made by Danish company Danfoss as well as U.S.-based Copeland. Danfoss said Monday that most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates, and that it was working with affected customers to limit the damage. "Danfoss has long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware, as well as to operate behind a firewall," the company said. In an August report, U.S. cybersecurity firm Claroty identified vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Copeland XWeb Pro platforms, which are used to manage refrigeration infrastructure in supermarkets, warehouses and other facilities. For example, Claroty said "numerous controllers" using the Danfoss system were directly accessible from the public internet, leaving them wide open for cyberattacks. But it noted that Danfoss and Copeland had since fixed the vulnerabilities. Copeland said Tuesday that a vulnerability had been identified in "a discontinued, end-of-life generation of controllers," and that it was working with impacted customers. Christopher Whyte, an associate professor of homeland security and emergency preparedness at Virginia Commonwealth University, said it's "not too difficult" to carry out such an attack. "It looks like almost certainly what happened here was these controls were left open to the broader network being used by the supermarket," Whyte said. Similar attacks on water systems, power infrastructure and other kinds of physical operations have been fairly common for years, often coming from Iran and other state actors, Whyte said. Over the summer, Minnesota and Michigan reported cyberattacks on their states' water systems. Whyte said attacks on refrigerator systems are not unprecedented. Last month, Stars and Stripes reported that three military agencies were investigating refrigeration outages at U.S. military commissaries that occurred within days of each other. The Associated Press left a message Tuesday seeking comment on that case with the U.S. Army's Criminal Investigation Division Cyber Field Office. But Whyte said the scale of the French attack, and the fact that there appeared to be no ransom demand or stealing of information, made this situation unusual. It was unclear Tuesday whether the French cyberattack involved artificial intelligence. But advances in AI have contributed to an increase in cybersecurity incidents, said Varun Chandrasekaran, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Illinois' Grainger College of Engineering. Chandrasekaran said there's also a possibility that the attack happened because of an experiment an AI lab was doing — like what happened with OpenAI's breach of an Australian health department website last month. He said people should absolutely expect an increase in such cyberattacks in the future thanks to AI. But Chandrasekaran said AI could also be useful in preventing such hacks. "Right now it seems like a lot of the defensive countermeasures people have are quite passive," Chandrasekaran said. "What we need is a proactive defender, like another AI model sitting on the defender side that's trying to counter whatever the attacker AI is doing."
passages: If you are trying to do some online grocery shopping with Giant, Stop & Shop or Food Lion, you may notice that their websites and apps are currently unavailable.

Dutch supermarket giant Ahold Delhaize said Tuesday it was working to restore systems it had shut down following what it described as a security issue. The company said its stores — including Albert Heijn in the Netherlands, Delhaize in Belgium and Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Giant in the United States — remained open, but the websites for those brands remained offline.
There are published reports of a cybersecurity incident at the company that owns the chains.

Each chains' website says they are "working to restore service as quickly as possible," adding that customers can still place delivery orders through Instacart, DoorDash and Uber Eats. Any unfulfilled web and app orders will be refunded.
The chains' pharmacies and fueling stations are also still open.
Ahold Delhaize said it had no evidence that customer or employee data had been stolen.

This comes as cyberattacks disrupted European supermarket chains, affecting refrigeration systems at hundreds of stores in France and forcing a major grocer to shut down websites serving customers in Europe and the United States.

French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on Tuesday that about 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets were affected. He said there was no risk to France's food supplies but acknowledged that the attack "touches the heart of our food security."
"It was a wake-up call for everyone," he said.

The French government's cybersecurity agency said Tuesday it was "aware of numerous compromises" involving refrigeration system remote control modules made by Danish company Danfoss as well as U.S.-based Copeland.
Danfoss said Monday that most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates, and that it was working with affected customers to limit the damage.
"Danfoss has long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware, as well as to operate behind a firewall," the company said.

In an August report, U.S. cybersecurity firm Claroty identified vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Copeland XWeb Pro platforms, which are used to manage refrigeration infrastructure in supermarkets, warehouses and other facilities.

For example, Claroty said "numerous controllers" using the Danfoss system were directly accessible from the public internet, leaving them wide open for cyberattacks. But it noted that Danfoss and Copeland had since fixed the vulnerabilities.
Copeland said Tuesday that a vulnerability had been identified in "a discontinued, end-of-life generation of controllers," and that it was working with impacted customers.
Christopher Whyte, an associate professor of homeland security and emergency preparedness at Virginia Commonwealth University, said it's "not too difficult" to carry out such an attack.
"It looks like almost certainly what happened here was these controls were left open to the broader network being used by the supermarket," Whyte said.

Similar attacks on water systems, power infrastructure and other kinds of physical operations have been fairly common for years, often coming from Iran and other state actors, Whyte said. Over the summer, Minnesota and Michigan reported cyberattacks on their states' water systems.

Whyte said attacks on refrigerator systems are not unprecedented. Last month, Stars and Stripes reported that three military agencies were investigating refrigeration outages at U.S. military commissaries that occurred within days of each other. The Associated Press left a message Tuesday seeking comment on that case with the U.S. Army's Criminal Investigation Division Cyber Field Office.
But Whyte said the scale of the French attack, and the fact that there appeared to be no ransom demand or stealing of information, made this situation unusual.

It was unclear Tuesday whether the French cyberattack involved artificial intelligence. But advances in AI have contributed to an increase in cybersecurity incidents, said Varun Chandrasekaran, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Illinois' Grainger College of Engineering.

Chandrasekaran said there's also a possibility that the attack happened because of an experiment an AI lab was doing — like what happened with OpenAI's breach of an Australian health department website last month. He said people should absolutely expect an increase in such cyberattacks in the future thanks to AI.
But Chandrasekaran said AI could also be useful in preventing such hacks.

"Right now it seems like a lot of the defensive countermeasures people have are quite passive," Chandrasekaran said. "What we need is a proactive defender, like another AI model sitting on the defender side that's trying to counter whatever the attacker AI is doing."

extraction.body:
Websites and apps for grocery chains Stop & Shop, Hannaford, and Giant Food were offline Monday and Tuesday after their Dutch parent company experienced a cyber incident. Ahold Delhaize said in a statement Tuesday that it was experiencing a cyberattack within its network and took some systems offline “to help protect them.” The company said stores continued to be open while teams worked to assess and mitigate the security issue. While customers cannot purchase groceries online and have them delivered through Peapod, they could place orders through third-party sites like DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Instacart. Other store operations like refrigeration and sale systems are unaffected, a spokesperson confirmed to the Globe. “We recognize that these actions have caused disruption for customers, associates and partners, but protecting our infrastructure in the best interest of our customers, associates and partners is a top priority,” they said in a statement. “Our teams are working with urgency to investigate the incident and restore affected systems safely. “As they make progress in assessing and mitigating the issues, we are in the process of starting a controlled re-launch of certain systems,” the statement added. The company said there has been no indication that client data has been stolen in the incident. The regional stores’ webpages and apps were offline both Monday and Tuesday, and maintenance messages were in place, alerting customers that stores, pharmacies, and fuel stations were operating as normal. The maintenance message said that any unfulfilled orders placed online or through the app would be refunded. “As a result, our website and app are not available at this time — but we are working as quickly as possible to restore them,” a spokesperson said in a statement. Hannaford Supermarkets said in a statement that its website, mobile app, and To Go pickup and delivery services have been affected by the security issue. “Hannaford stores remain open and continue to welcome customers,” a spokesperson said. “We apologize for the inconvenience and appreciate our customers’ patience and understanding. We’ll provide an update once the issue has been resolved.” Ahold Delhaize has five brands in the United States: Stop & Shop, Hannaford, Giant Food, The GIANT Company, and Food Lion. The company is based in the Netherlands and has 17 local brands across nine countries. Separately, cyberattacks have disrupted other European supermarket chains, which have affected refrigeration systems at hundreds of stores in France. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on Tuesday that roughly 700 supermarkets were impacted. He said that while there was no risk to France’s supplies, the attack “touches the heart of our food security.” Alexa Gagosz can be reached at alexa.gagosz@globe.com . Follow her @alexagagosz and on Instagram @AlexaGagosz . Madyline Swearing can be reached at madyline.swearing@globe.com .

We apologize for any inconvenience this issue may have caused customers and partners.” As of publication, a timetable for all the sites and apps to be back up and running has not been released. So for now, it’s a wait-and-see game. In the meantime, you’re more than welcome to physically go to these stores to get the items you need. extraction.body: If you are trying to do some online grocery shopping with Giant, Stop & Shop or Food Lion, you may notice that their websites and apps are currently unavailable. Dutch supermarket giant Ahold Delhaize said Tuesday it was working to restore systems it had shut down following what it described as a security issue. The company said its stores — including Albert Heijn in the Netherlands, Delhaize in Belgium and Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Giant in the United States — remained open, but the websites for those brands remained offline. There are published reports of a cybersecurity incident at the company that owns the chains. Each chains' website says they are "working to restore service as quickly as possible," adding that customers can still place delivery orders through Instacart, DoorDash and Uber Eats. Any unfulfilled web and app orders will be refunded. The chains' pharmacies and fueling stations are also still open. Ahold Delhaize said it had no evidence that customer or employee data had been stolen. This comes as cyberattacks disrupted European supermarket chains, affecting refrigeration systems at hundreds of stores in France and forcing a major grocer to shut down websites serving customers in Europe and the United States. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on Tuesday that about 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets were affected. He said there was no risk to France's food supplies but acknowledged that the attack "touches the heart of our food security." "It was a wake-up call for everyone," he said. The French government's cybersecurity agency said Tuesday it was "aware of numerous compromises" involving refrigeration system remote control modules made by Danish company Danfoss as well as U.S.-based Copeland. Danfoss said Monday that most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates, and that it was working with affected customers to limit the damage. "Danfoss has long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware, as well as to operate behind a firewall," the company said. In an August report, U.S. cybersecurity firm Claroty identified vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Copeland XWeb Pro platforms, which are used to manage refrigeration infrastructure in supermarkets, warehouses and other facilities. For example, Claroty said "numerous controllers" using the Danfoss system were directly accessible from the public internet, leaving them wide open for cyberattacks. But it noted that Danfoss and Copeland had since fixed the vulnerabilities. Copeland said Tuesday that a vulnerability had been identified in "a discontinued, end-of-life generation of controllers," and that it was working with impacted customers. Christopher Whyte, an associate professor of homeland security and emergency preparedness at Virginia Commonwealth University, said it's "not too difficult" to carry out such an attack. "It looks like almost certainly what happened here was these controls were left open to the broader network being used by the supermarket," Whyte said. Similar attacks on water systems, power infrastructure and other kinds of physical operations have been fairly common for years, often coming from Iran and other state actors, Whyte said. Over the summer, Minnesota and Michigan reported cyberattacks on their states' water systems. Whyte said attacks on refrigerator systems are not unprecedented. Last month, Stars and Stripes reported that three military agencies were investigating refrigeration outages at U.S. military commissaries that occurred within days of each other. The Associated Press left a message Tuesday seeking comment on that case with the U.S. Army's Criminal Investigation Division Cyber Field Office. But Whyte said the scale of the French attack, and the fact that there appeared to be no ransom demand or stealing of information, made this situation unusual. It was unclear Tuesday whether the French cyberattack involved artificial intelligence. But advances in AI have contributed to an increase in cybersecurity incidents, said Varun Chandrasekaran, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Illinois' Grainger College of Engineering. Chandrasekaran said there's also a possibility that the attack happened because of an experiment an AI lab was doing — like what happened with OpenAI's breach of an Australian health department website last month. He said people should absolutely expect an increase in such cyberattacks in the future thanks to AI. But Chandrasekaran said AI could also be useful in preventing such hacks. "Right now it seems like a lot of the defensive countermeasures people have are quite passive," Chandrasekaran said. "What we need is a proactive defender, like another AI model sitting on the defender side that's trying to counter whatever the attacker AI is doing."

extraction.body:
Websites and apps for grocery chains Stop & Shop, Hannaford, and Giant Food were offline Monday and Tuesday after their Dutch parent company experienced a cyber incident. Ahold Delhaize said in a statement Tuesday that it was experiencing a cyberattack within its network and took some systems offline “to help protect them.” The company said stores continued to be open while teams worked to assess and mitigate the security issue. While customers cannot purchase groceries online and have them delivered through Peapod, they could place orders through third-party sites like DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Instacart. Other store operations like refrigeration and sale systems are unaffected, a spokesperson confirmed to the Globe. “We recognize that these actions have caused disruption for customers, associates and partners, but protecting our infrastructure in the best interest of our customers, associates and partners is a top priority,” they said in a statement. “Our teams are working with urgency to investigate the incident and restore affected systems safely. “As they make progress in assessing and mitigating the issues, we are in the process of starting a controlled re-launch of certain systems,” the statement added. The company said there has been no indication that client data has been stolen in the incident. The regional stores’ webpages and apps were offline both Monday and Tuesday, and maintenance messages were in place, alerting customers that stores, pharmacies, and fuel stations were operating as normal. The maintenance message said that any unfulfilled orders placed online or through the app would be refunded. “As a result, our website and app are not available at this time — but we are working as quickly as possible to restore them,” a spokesperson said in a statement. Hannaford Supermarkets said in a statement that its website, mobile app, and To Go pickup and delivery services have been affected by the security issue. “Hannaford stores remain open and continue to welcome customers,” a spokesperson said. “We apologize for the inconvenience and appreciate our customers’ patience and understanding. We’ll provide an update once the issue has been resolved.” Ahold Delhaize has five brands in the United States: Stop & Shop, Hannaford, Giant Food, The GIANT Company, and Food Lion. The company is based in the Netherlands and has 17 local brands across nine countries. Separately, cyberattacks have disrupted other European supermarket chains, which have affected refrigeration systems at hundreds of stores in France. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on Tuesday that roughly 700 supermarkets were impacted. He said that while there was no risk to France’s supplies, the attack “touches the heart of our food security.” Alexa Gagosz can be reached at alexa.gagosz@globe.com . extraction.body: Colossal Biosciences announced Wednesday a new AI platform to help accelerate its efforts to bring back extinct species, TechCrunch can exclusively report. The platform, called GenoMorph, uses advanced 3D morphology, comparative genomics, and developmental biology to identify genes that could be edited in de-extinction projects with limited gene data. sources.title: Colossal Biosciences Unveils AI Platform for De-Extinction
passages: Colossal Biosciences is making a smart pivot from pure research play to platform provider, creating immediate revenue opportunities while advancing their long-term de-extinction goals.
Colossal Biosciences just dropped its most ambitious tech play yet - an AI platform designed to fast-track the company's moonshot mission of bringing extinct species back to life.
De-extinction timelines are measured in decades, but platform revenue can start flowing immediately.
The AI platform could accelerate research into everything from crop resilience to rare disease treatments.

While companies like Ginkgo Bioworks have built platforms for synthetic biology, Colossal's focus on extinct species has forced them to solve uniquely challenging problems around incomplete genetic data and cellular compatibility.
For Colossal, the platform launch solves a critical business model question.
Colossal's platform could compress that timeline from years to months, potentially unleashing a wave of innovation across multiple sectors.

extraction.body: Colossal Biosciences just dropped its most ambitious tech play yet - an AI platform designed to fast-track the company's moonshot mission of bringing extinct species back to life. The Dallas-based startup, already valued at $1.5 billion, is betting that artificial intelligence can solve the complex genetic puzzles that have slowed de-extinction research for decades. Peter Diamandis has backed the move with a new fund specifically targeting startups that leverage the platform. The de-extinction game just got its biggest tech upgrade. Colossal Biosciences, the company trying to bring back woolly mammoths and Tasmanian tigers, announced today it's opening up its AI-powered research platform to the broader scientific community - and investors are already lining up. While Colossal has raised over $225 million since 2021, the company's core mission - literally resurrecting extinct species - faces massive technical hurdles that could take decades to overcome. By platformizing its AI tools, the startup is creating a new revenue stream while positioning itself as the infrastructure backbone for next-generation biotech. Peter Diamandis, the XPRIZE founder who's been bullish on longevity and biotech investments, didn't waste time. He's launching a dedicated fund to back startups that build on Colossal's platform, essentially betting that the company's AI tools will spawn an entire ecosystem of genetic engineering applications. The platform leverages machine learning to tackle some of the most complex challenges in genetic engineering - from predicting how ancient DNA sequences might function in modern cellular environments to optimizing CRISPR edits for maximum accuracy. What took Colossal's team months of trial and error can now be modeled and tested virtually before any lab work begins. The AI platform could accelerate research into everything from crop resilience to rare disease treatments. By making these tools available to smaller research teams and startups, Colossal is essentially democratizing access to cutting-edge genetic engineering capabilities that were previously locked behind massive R&D budgets. While companies like Ginkgo Bioworks have built platforms for synthetic biology, Colossal's focus on extinct species has forced them to solve uniquely challenging problems around incomplete genetic data and cellular compatibility. Those solutions now become competitive advantages in the broader biotech market. Diamandis's fund signals that investors see Colossal as more than a science experiment. The company is building the picks and shovels for a new gold rush in genetic engineering, where the real money might not be in the headline-grabbing de-extinction projects but in the infrastructure that makes thousands of smaller innovations possible. For Colossal, the platform launch solves a critical business model question. De-extinction timelines are measured in decades, but platform revenue can start flowing immediately. Every startup that uses their AI tools to design better gene therapies or engineer more resilient crops validates the underlying technology while generating cash flow to fund the moonshot projects. The biotech industry has been waiting for this kind of infrastructure play. Most genetic engineering startups spend years building basic computational tools before they can focus on their core research. Colossal's platform could compress that timeline from years to months, potentially unleashing a wave of innovation across multiple sectors. Colossal Biosciences is making a smart pivot from pure research play to platform provider, creating immediate revenue opportunities while advancing their long-term de-extinction goals. With Diamandis backing the ecosystem play, we're likely seeing the emergence of a new category in biotech infrastructure. The real test will be whether the platform can deliver the promised acceleration in genetic engineering timelines - and whether enough startups adopt it to create the network effects that make platforms truly valuable.

extraction.body: Colossal Biosciences , the world’s first de-extinction company, announced new scientific milestones that will accelerate dodo de-extinction efforts — or bringing back the extinct dodo bird. Building on last year’s advances in pigeon primordial germ cells, gene-edited chicken surrogates and comparative avian genomes, today Colossal unveiled GenoMorph, its AI platform developed to identify potential gene-editing targets from limited genomic data. Applied to the dodo program, the platform identified an estimated 2,300 candidate regulatory elements associated with avian beak size and shape. It’s a pretty ambitious effort, and the company said once before it was making better progress than expected . And the firm has convinced investors to give it hundreds of millions of dollars to develop the science to bring back lost species. There are skeptics, but it is interesting to note that the company has already claimed success in bringing back dire wolves . The company has raised $615 million and it has 270 employees. And previously, Colossal said it had figured out how to make artificial eggs to breed avian species. The artificial egg will be useful for the purpose of hatching eggs, but the company still has to make progress on the genetics behind making new birds. Colossal also announced advances across its avian de-extinction pipeline, including substantially improving the dodo genome assembly through the use of technology from its dire wolf project, an expanded Nicobar pigeon colony, newly derived Nicobar primordial germ cells, chicken embryonic-stem-cell chimeras and a breakthrough lipid-nanoparticle system for gene editing delivery in avian embryos. Together, these capabilities provide the genomic, cellular and reproductive foundation required to translate predicted dodo traits into experimentally validated edits. Colossal has developed GenoMorph, an AI-powered platform that identifies potential gene-editing targets for de-extinction projects with limited genomic data. The platform combines comparative genomics, developmental biology and high-resolution 3D morphology to predict which regulatory elements may be active during development and identifies those most strongly associated with differences in physical form. Unlike protein-coding genes, which provide instructions for building an animal, regulatory DNA controls when, where and how strongly those instructions are activated. These genetic “switches” help shape traits such as the size and structure of a bird’s skull and beak. “De-extinction is as much a data problem as a biology problem,” said Ben Lamm, CEO and cofounder of Colossal, in a statement. “Because so few dodo genomes survive, we cannot rely on the population-level comparisons available for many living species. Our GenoMorph platform provides another path: it learns how regulatory DNA shapes living birds, then identifies the genetic switches that may have contributed to the dodo’s distinctive anatomy. This is more than a solution for the dodo. It provides a repeatable approach for extinct species whose genomic records are similarly limited.” To build GenoMorph, Colossal’s avian team created an avian regulatory atlas using hundreds of samples from chickens, quail, ducks and pigeons. The samples covered six stages of embryonic development and three regions of the developing face. Elements confirmed to influence craniofacial development may then be considered for precision genome editing in the Nicobar pigeon, providing a data-driven path toward reconstructing key aspects of the dodo’s distinctive anatomy. “The dodo’s defining anatomy emerged from networks of regulatory instructions that are difficult to interpret from ancient DNA alone,” said Beth Shapiro, Colossal’s Chief Science Officer, in a statement. “The answer turned out to be comparative: use the breadth of living bird diversity, combined with AI, to identify candidate loci for the next phase of testing. By learning how skulls and beaks develop across living birds, GenoMorph allows us to prioritize the regulatory changes most likely to have shaped the dodo and move them into functional validation. It establishes a repeatable framework for connecting ancient genomes to extinct traits.” “You cannot train AI to answer a precise developmental question using just generic data,” said Anna Keyte, Avian Species Director at Colossal., in a statement “We needed to capture how regulatory activity changes across species, developmental stages and different regions of the face. Building that dataset required more than a year of focused experimental work, and it is what allows GenoMorph to generate biologically meaningful predictions.” Candidate elements are now entering functional-validation studies. Those confirmed to influence craniofacial development may be prioritized for precision editing in the Nicobar pigeon genome. Preliminary findings have been presented at the Craniofacial Gordon Research Conference and the Society for Molecular Biology and Evolution annual conference and the 2026 Society for Molecular Biology and Evolution annual meeting. While this work advances the dodo de-extinction program, its scientific implications extend well beyond a single species. The ability to predict developmentally active regulatory DNA from genome sequence alone, and to validate that against quantitative morphological data across a broad comparative sample, provides a scalable framework for studying the genetic basis of complex anatomical traits in any bird lineage. This includes endangered species for which large population genomic datasets are unlikely ever to exist, where identifying functionally relevant regulatory variants has previously been intractable. The dodo genome assembly that Colossal’s team is using is of extremely high quality for ancient DNA, thanks to the excellent preservation of the dodo specimen from which the genomic data was extracted. However, the fragmented nature of ancient DNA means that, despite this excellent preservation, gaps in the genome sequence remain that can impact analysis. Through the dire wolf program, the company developed a computational genome-assembly method that, applied to improve the dodo genome assembly, demonstrates how technologies created for one de-extinction project can be refined and applied across Colossal’s broader species portfolio. Ancient DNA is fragmented into short strands of surviving DNA, damaged due to degradation, and the genome sequence is often substantially different from that of its closest living relative. Conventional assembly methods map ancient DNA fragments against a living reference genome—in this case, the Nicobar pigeon—and may discard fragments that are too divergent to align. This can leave gaps in the assembly and bias the reconstructed genome toward the living species. Colossal’s published iterative assembly method addresses this limitation by using newly mapped dodo DNA to progressively update the reference genome. The updated reference is then used to map the ancient DNA again, allowing previously unmatched fragments to “walk” into gaps with each successive round. After repeating this process until the number of newly recovered dodo sequences reached a plateau, the result is a substantially more complete assembly than would have been possible through a conventional single-pass approach. Our dodo genome has, for example, 95% of bases covered at least 5-fold (meaning that at least five unique ancient DNA molecules map to more than 95% of letters in the genome), and an average coverage of 65-fold. “We are in the final stages of our analysis of the dodo genome, with much more to come after the genome paper goes through peer review. In the meantime, it’s been rewarding to see that an approach developed for the dire wolf is now producing value across another species program. That repeatability is central to Colossal’s model: every scientific breakthrough becomes part of a scalable technology platform that can accelerate the programs that follow,” said Beth Shapiro. Colossal has expanded its Texas colony of Nicobar pigeons—the dodo’s closest living relative—to 36 birds following successful breeding among established pairs. The growing colony provides an increasingly robust foundation for studying Nicobar pigeon development, reproduction, and genetics while supporting the company’s dodo de-extinction program. Eggs collected during the latest breeding season were used to derive Nicobar pigeon primordial germ cells, or PGCs. These are the cells that eventually develop into sperm and eggs. Establishing these cells is essential to our path of creating heritable genome edits and producing future generations of birds carrying selected dodo traits. Colossal is also working to develop a telomere-to-telomere Nicobar pigeon genome, improving on the existing chromosome-level assembly. This will provide a stronger foundation for identifying potential edits and for improving the genome of the Rodrigues solitaire, an extinct relative of the dodo. Colossal plans to add newly available solitaire sequence data and remap it against the improved Nicobar reference to increase its coverage and completeness. Colossal scientists have also developed a new platform using avian embryonic stem cells to generate chimeric chickens, and have successfully hatched the first chimeras produced through the platform. Embryonic stem cells offer a route to introduce engineered cells into a developing embryo and observe how those cells contribute to the phenotype of the bird. Hatching viable chimeric chickens confirms that the cultured cells retain the developmental potential needed to integrate into a host embryo and contribute to its various tissues. Colossal is also expanding their embryonic stem cell culture system to pigeons to support the dodo de-extinction program. By editing embryonic stem cells and using these edited cells to create chimeric pigeons, scientists can test whether the edits have the predicted effect on phenotype before editing PGCs. This establishes a platform for phenotype screening, allowing the team to test candidate edits and evaluate their effects before combining them on the path to a dodo. In another world’s first, Colossal has also developed a lipid-nanoparticle delivery platform that efficiently introduces DNA, RNA, and CRISPR gene-editing tools into developing bird embryos while improving embryo viability over traditional delivery methods. In experiments, editing the bone-development regulator Runx2 produced a clear craniofacial phenotype, demonstrating the platform’s ability to test how specific genetic changes affect avian development. The system has also been used successfully in rock dove and duck embryos, supporting its application across bird species. Colossal scientists are now using the lipid-nanoparticle delivery platform to validate regulatory elements identified by GenoMorph in near real time. The strongest candidates are being engineered into Nicobar pigeon primordial germ cells for further precision-editing studies. Colossal’s dodo de-extinction update focuses primarily on a new AI platform called GenoMorph. In conjunction with this announcement, the avian team is post a new paper to bioRxiv about an innovation in gene-editing tool delivery. The team developed a lipid-nanoparticle delivery method that allows us to use gene-editing tools on developing bird embryos, and we proved that it worked across three different avian species. GenoMorph is an internal AI platform that identifies gene-editing targets in genomic data. The tool uses comparative genomics, developmental biology, and high-resolution 3D morphology to help us understand which genes are important to the development of physical features like the shape of a beak or the size of a skull. “To recreate the dodo’s iconic beak size and skull shape, we can’t just write instructions for a final outcome. We need to build the instructions for how to get there,” the company said. “So we’re studying beak development across a range of different bird species, and we’re using AI to identify which regulatory elements to target. So far, GenoMorph has identified 653 candidate regulatory elements associated with beak size, and 1,698 associated with beak thickness and breadth. In over a billion base pairs of DNA, that’s major progress for narrowing our search.” But this isn’t just about software. This announcement is full of updates about dodo de-extinction. Colossal is making major progress on the de-extinction of the dodo. Colossal said it has decoded more of the dodo’s genome, and it has a growing colony of its closest living relative, and we’ve been able to derive critically important cells that will one day help us hatch dodos. The method usited to assemble the dire wolf genome, published in Cell this year, helped the company generate a substantially more complete dodo genome than ever. And its colony of Nicobar pigeons, the dodo’s closest living relative, is growing and thriving. The firm has successfully hatched chicken chimeras using avian embryonic stem cells, helping us confirm that our genetic edits result in the changes it wants.

“De-extinction is as much a data problem as a biology problem,” said Ben Lamm, CEO and cofounder of Colossal, in a statement. “Because so few dodo genomes survive, we cannot rely on the population-level comparisons available for many living species. Our GenoMorph platform provides another path: it learns how regulatory DNA shapes living birds, then identifies the genetic switches that may have contributed to the dodo’s distinctive anatomy. This is more than a solution for the dodo. It provides a repeatable approach for extinct species whose genomic records are similarly limited.”

To build GenoMorph, Colossal’s avian team created an avian regulatory atlas using hundreds of samples from chickens, quail, ducks and pigeons. The samples covered six stages of embryonic development and three regions of the developing face.

Elements confirmed to influence craniofacial development may then be considered for precision genome editing in the Nicobar pigeon, providing a data-driven path toward reconstructing key aspects of the dodo’s distinctive anatomy.

“The dodo’s defining anatomy emerged from networks of regulatory instructions that are difficult to interpret from ancient DNA alone,” said Beth Shapiro, Colossal’s Chief Science Officer, in a statement. “The answer turned out to be comparative: use the breadth of living bird diversity, combined with AI, to identify candidate loci for the next phase of testing. By learning how skulls and beaks develop across living birds, GenoMorph allows us to prioritize the regulatory changes most likely to have shaped the dodo and move them into functional validation. It establishes a repeatable framework for connecting ancient genomes to extinct traits.”

“You cannot train AI to answer a precise developmental question using just generic data,” said Anna Keyte, Avian Species Director at Colossal., in a statement “We needed to capture how regulatory activity changes across species, developmental stages and different regions of the face. Building that dataset required more than a year of focused experimental work, and it is what allows GenoMorph to generate biologically meaningful predictions.”

Candidate elements are now entering functional-validation studies. Those confirmed to influence craniofacial development may be prioritized for precision editing in the Nicobar pigeon genome. Preliminary findings have been presented at the Craniofacial Gordon Research Conference and the Society for Molecular Biology and Evolution annual conference and the 2026 Society for Molecular Biology and Evolution annual meeting.

While this work advances the dodo de-extinction program, its scientific implications extend well beyond a single species. The ability to predict developmentally active regulatory DNA from genome sequence alone, and to validate that against quantitative morphological data across a broad comparative sample, provides a scalable framework for studying the genetic basis of complex anatomical traits in any bird lineage. This includes endangered species for which large population genomic datasets are unlikely ever to exist, where identifying functionally relevant regulatory variants has previously been intractable.

The dodo genome assembly that Colossal’s team is using is of extremely high quality for ancient DNA, thanks to the excellent preservation of the dodo specimen from which the genomic data was extracted. However, the fragmented nature of ancient DNA means that, despite this excellent preservation, gaps in the genome sequence remain that can impact analysis. Through the dire wolf program, the company developed a computational genome-assembly method that, applied to improve the dodo genome assembly, demonstrates how technologies created for one de-extinction project can be refined and applied across Colossal’s broader species portfolio.

Ancient DNA is fragmented into short strands of surviving DNA, damaged due to degradation, and the genome sequence is often substantially different from that of its closest living relative. Conventional assembly methods map ancient DNA fragments against a living reference genome—in this case, the Nicobar pigeon—and may discard fragments that are too divergent to align. This can leave gaps in the assembly and bias the reconstructed genome toward the living species.

Colossal’s published iterative assembly method addresses this limitation by using newly mapped dodo DNA to progressively update the reference genome. The updated reference is then used to map the ancient DNA again, allowing previously unmatched fragments to “walk” into gaps with each successive round. After repeating this process until the number of newly recovered dodo sequences reached a plateau, the result is a substantially more complete assembly than would have been possible through a conventional single-pass approach. Our dodo genome has, for example, 95% of bases covered at least 5-fold (meaning that at least five unique ancient DNA molecules map to more than 95% of letters in the genome), and an average coverage of 65-fold.

“We are in the final stages of our analysis of the dodo genome, with much more to come after the genome paper goes through peer review. In the meantime, it’s been rewarding to see that an approach developed for the dire wolf is now producing value across another species program. That repeatability is central to Colossal’s model: every scientific breakthrough becomes part of a scalable technology platform that can accelerate the programs that follow,” said Beth Shapiro.

Colossal has expanded its Texas colony of Nicobar pigeons—the dodo’s closest living relative—to 36 birds following successful breeding among established pairs. The growing colony provides an increasingly robust foundation for studying Nicobar pigeon development, reproduction, and genetics while supporting the company’s dodo de-extinction program.

Eggs collected during the latest breeding season were used to derive Nicobar pigeon primordial germ cells, or PGCs. These are the cells that eventually develop into sperm and eggs. Establishing these cells is essential to our path of creating heritable genome edits and producing future generations of birds carrying selected dodo traits.

Colossal is also working to develop a telomere-to-telomere Nicobar pigeon genome, improving on the existing chromosome-level assembly. This will provide a stronger foundation for identifying potential edits and for improving the genome of the Rodrigues solitaire, an extinct relative of the dodo. Colossal plans to add newly available solitaire sequence data and remap it against the improved Nicobar reference to increase its coverage and completeness.

Colossal scientists have also developed a new platform using avian embryonic stem cells to generate chimeric chickens, and have successfully hatched the first chimeras produced through the platform. Embryonic stem cells offer a route to introduce engineered cells into a developing embryo and observe how those cells contribute to the phenotype of the bird. Hatching viable chimeric chickens confirms that the cultured cells retain the developmental potential needed to integrate into a host embryo and contribute to its various tissues.

Colossal is also expanding their embryonic stem cell culture system to pigeons to support the dodo de-extinction program. By editing embryonic stem cells and using these edited cells to create chimeric pigeons, scientists can test whether the edits have the predicted effect on phenotype before editing PGCs. This establishes a platform for phenotype screening, allowing the team to test candidate edits and evaluate their effects before combining them on the path to a dodo.

In another world’s first, Colossal has also developed a lipid-nanoparticle delivery platform that efficiently introduces DNA, RNA, and CRISPR gene-editing tools into developing bird embryos while improving embryo viability over traditional delivery methods. In experiments, editing the bone-development regulator Runx2 produced a clear craniofacial phenotype, demonstrating the platform’s ability to test how specific genetic changes affect avian development. The system has also been used successfully in rock dove and duck embryos, supporting its application across bird species.

Colossal scientists are now using the lipid-nanoparticle delivery platform to validate regulatory elements identified by GenoMorph in near real time. The strongest candidates are being engineered into Nicobar pigeon primordial germ cells for further precision-editing studies.

Colossal’s dodo de-extinction update focuses primarily on a new AI platform called GenoMorph. In conjunction with this announcement, the avian team is post a new paper to bioRxiv about an innovation in gene-editing tool delivery.
The team developed a lipid-nanoparticle delivery method that allows us to use gene-editing tools on developing bird embryos, and we proved that it worked across three different avian species.

GenoMorph is an internal AI platform that identifies gene-editing targets in genomic data. The tool uses comparative genomics, developmental biology, and high-resolution 3D morphology to help us understand which genes are important to the development of physical features like the shape of a beak or the size of a skull.

“To recreate the dodo’s iconic beak size and skull shape, we can’t just write instructions for a final outcome. We need to build the instructions for how to get there,” the company said. “So we’re studying beak development across a range of different bird species, and we’re using AI to identify which regulatory elements to target. So far, GenoMorph has identified 653 candidate regulatory elements associated with beak size, and 1,698 associated with beak thickness and breadth. In over a billion base pairs of DNA, that’s major progress for narrowing our search.”
But this isn’t just about software. This announcement is full of updates about dodo de-extinction. Colossal is making major progress on the de-extinction of the dodo.

Colossal said it has decoded more of the dodo’s genome, and it has a growing colony of its closest living relative, and we’ve been able to derive critically important cells that will one day help us hatch dodos.
The method usited to assemble the dire wolf genome, published in Cell this year, helped the company generate a substantially more complete dodo genome than ever.

And its colony of Nicobar pigeons, the dodo’s closest living relative, is growing and thriving. The firm has successfully hatched chicken chimeras using avian embryonic stem cells, helping us confirm that our genetic edits result in the changes it wants.

Meanwhile, Colossal Biosciences’ latest technology has already obtained a vote of confidence from XPRIZE founder Peter Diamandis.

To build GenoMorph, Lamm said the company collected a bunch of developmental data from “chickens, quail, ducks, and pigeons,” and combined it with the “genetic information and 3D skull measurements from more than 70 bird species.” He said it took more than a year of work to build this platform, which also builds on the company’s years of work in de-extinction.
Colossal Biosciences is making a smart pivot from pure research play to platform provider, creating immediate revenue opportunities while advancing their long-term de-extinction goals.
Colossal Biosciences just dropped its most ambitious tech play yet - an AI platform designed to fast-track the company's moonshot mission of bringing extinct species back to life.
De-extinction timelines are measured in decades, but platform revenue can start flowing immediately.
The AI platform could accelerate research into everything from crop resilience to rare disease treatments.

While companies like Ginkgo Bioworks have built platforms for synthetic biology, Colossal's focus on extinct species has forced them to solve uniquely challenging problems around incomplete genetic data and cellular compatibility.

Colossal's platform could compress that timeline from years to months, potentially unleashing a wave of innovation across multiple sectors.

extraction.body: Colossal Biosciences announced Wednesday a new AI platform to help accelerate its efforts to bring back extinct species, TechCrunch can exclusively report. The platform, called GenoMorph, uses advanced 3D morphology, comparative genomics, and developmental biology to identify genes that could be edited in de-extinction projects with limited gene data. The company is using it as part of its effort to bring back the dodo bird, for which there are limited genomes to work with. For example, the company is working with only one dodo genome compared to the 100 genomes it has been able to obtain as part of its woolly mammoth de-extinction project. DNA from the woolly mammoth is more plentiful because the colder climates the animal lived in preserve the DNA better than the tropics where the dodo lived, the company said. “Normally, scientists can compare many genomes to understand which genetic differences are responsible for certain traits,” Colossal CEO and co-founder Ben Lamm told TechCrunch. “We don’t have that luxury with ancient DNA from extinct species whose DNA is severely limited, and we can only get a small number of complete genomes.” To build GenoMorph, Lamm said the company collected a bunch of developmental data from “chickens, quail, ducks, and pigeons,” and combined it with the “genetic information and 3D skull measurements from more than 70 bird species.” He said it took more than a year of work to build this platform, which also builds on the company’s years of work in de-extinction. “The AI learns which regions of DNA are active as different birds develop their beaks and facial structures, and uses that information to predict which genetic switches may have given the dodo its iconic appearance.” He said to think of the platform as a “treasure map for the dodo genome,” where, rather than searching through a bunch of potential genetic differences, GenoMorph can help the Colossal team find only the genetic differences that matter. “So far we’ve identified approximately 2,300 promising DNA editing targets for the dodo cranial facial morphology that we can now test in the lab,” he continued. He said GenoMorph will help the company tackle one of its biggest bottlenecks in trying to de-extinct animals — finding out which changes actually make an extinct species unique. But Lamm said scientists also need to test whether those edits can create the physical traits they need. “We’ve developed a new system that uses lipid nanoparticles to deliver gene-editing tools directly into developing bird embryos,” he said. This will help the team see how certain genetic changes impact the development of a bird “without having to wait through an entire breeding cycle that requires birds to reach sexual maturity.” The company also announced Wednesday that its Nicobar pigeon colony now has 36 birds and that it has successfully created the essential cells that become eggs and sperm. “Because the Nicobar pigeon is the dodo’s closest living relative, those cells are a critical part of our strategy for creating birds that carry dodo traits,” he said. Next, the company is hoping to prove what GenoMorph predicts in a lab. “What’s most exciting is that we’re reaching a point where the different technologies we’ve been developing are starting to converge together and help other projects we are working on in a completely different part of the tree of life,” Lamm continued. When asked whether it was safe to edit genes this way, Lamm said the point of developing a technology like GenoMorph is to make genetic engineering “more precise, controlled, and testable.” He said the product doesn’t edit genes itself, but helps their team identify which genetic changes are worth investigating. “Identifying a potential edit doesn’t mean we immediately introduce it into an animal or assume it’s safe,” he continued. “The more precisely we can identify and validate these changes, the more informed our decisions become throughout the process.” Meanwhile, Colossal Biosciences’ latest technology has already obtained a vote of confidence from XPRIZE founder Peter Diamandis. Diamandis, who is an investor in Colossal, announced on Wednesday that he has founded a new VC firm, NeoGenesis Capital, to back companies using Colossal Biosciences’ programmable biology platform across health, agriculture, and conservation. To build GenoMorph, Lamm said the company collected a bunch of developmental data from “chickens, quail, ducks, and pigeons,” and combined it with the “genetic information and 3D skull measurements from more than 70 bird species.” He said it took more than a year of work to build this platform, which also builds on the company’s years of work in de-extinction.

passages: Colossal Biosciences is making a smart pivot from pure research play to platform provider, creating immediate revenue opportunities while advancing their long-term de-extinction goals.
Colossal Biosciences just dropped its most ambitious tech play yet - an AI platform designed to fast-track the company's moonshot mission of bringing extinct species back to life.
De-extinction timelines are measured in decades, but platform revenue can start flowing immediately.
The AI platform could accelerate research into everything from crop resilience to rare disease treatments.

While companies like Ginkgo Bioworks have built platforms for synthetic biology, Colossal's focus on extinct species has forced them to solve uniquely challenging problems around incomplete genetic data and cellular compatibility.
For Colossal, the platform launch solves a critical business model question.
Colossal's platform could compress that timeline from years to months, potentially unleashing a wave of innovation across multiple sectors.
