extraction.body: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new Android banking trojan called Hirudo that works by replacing legitimate banking apps with purpose-built patched versions designed to bypass security checks from inside the app itself, marking a new escalation in financial fraud. Dutch mobile security company ThreatFabric said it identified replacements for eight Indonesian banking apps, while credential targeting in the malware spans Indonesia, China, India, Mexico, Morocco and Thailand. "The operation combines credential theft, device takeover, screen and camera capture, and SMS theft, in combination with a fairly mature backend," Eward Driehuis, vice president of fraud engineering at ThreatFabric, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News. Hirudo facilitates on-device credential theft and live remote control. The malware is delivered by shopping, adult video, and entertainment dropper apps that carry the trojan as a separate installation package, which is then served as an in-app update. "The lure is functional, loading real content in a WebView, a storefront, a video catalogue or short dramas, so the experience looks legitimate," ThreatFabric explained. "Behind that content the dropper runs a fixed startup routine: it collects promotion-tracking data, fetches its campaign configuration, and checks whether the payload, the Hirudo RAT, is already installed with its accessibility service and notification access enabled." If it's not present, it displays a fake in-app update prompt to trigger the installation of the malware. It's worth emphasizing that Hirudo is installed as a second app and must be granted its own permissions before it can carry out the malicious activities. As observed in the case of StreamRat , the malware implements an anti-detection technique based on blocking Internet access by configuring a deliberately non-functional VPN connection prior to the payload installation. This is seen as an attempt to prevent other apps and services, like Google Play Protect, from carrying out cloud-based checks of the payload. "However, Play Protect also provides offline detection for known potentially harmful applications, meaning that the mechanism does not completely disable its protection," ThreatFabric noted last month. "We therefore assess that the technique is more likely intended to reduce the effectiveness of online reputation and code-analysis mechanisms rather than bypass Play Protect entirely." Depending on the nature of the lure app used, the dropper is also designed to serve bogus screens to capture payment PINs, serve fake screens requesting login credentials for banks and wallet apps, display fake lock screen pattern and PIN overlays, and facilitate total remote control of the device. While all this behavior is par for the course when it comes to Android banking trojans, it's their attempts to replace the target banking app with a tampered copy that stand out. Specifically, the purpose-built replacements embed a hooking engine to blind signature, accessibility, screen-capture, and Play Integrity checks from within the app. The replacement targets eight Indonesian apps. "For these, the RAT detects the installed banking app through accessibility, checks its signing certificate against a stored reference, [and] then shows a fake 'update' prompt," ThreatFabric explained. "It opens Android's uninstaller for the genuine app without waiting for the user to tap, and downloads the bank-specific replacement in parallel." While the need for having to remove the app before installing its near-identical malicious copy is a "real constraint," the mechanism offers the ability to bypass the banking app's own security checks by returning responses fed by the attacker beforehand. This involves returning the genuine app signing certificate, returning an empty list when querying for enabled accessibility services, and stripping the FLAG_SECURE flag so that the app's screens can be viewed and recorded remotely. "Key-attestation certificates are re-signed with a bundled keybox, and Play Integrity requests are relayed over plain HTTP to an operator-controlled server, which returns a verdict for the app to accept," the mobile security company said. "Two details are worth underlining for defenders. First, the attestation keybox the engine ships is not the operators' own: it is a publicly leaked keybox. Second, because the Integrity request is relayed rather than genuinely produced, a valid Integrity response alone is not evidence of an untampered app." Evidence indicates that the malware is distributed via fake web pages masquerading as Google Play Store landing pages for shopping, short drama, and football apps. Unsuspecting users are assessed to be directed to these websites through ads on Meta-owned social media platforms. The entire operation rests on a backend that combines device control with the ability to manage different campaigns and stolen data, including device records, lock-screen history, and financial profiles containing monthly income and risk-score fields. "Hirudo marks a deliberate escalation in how Android bankers approach hardened applications," ThreatFabric said. "By moving its tampering inside the target app, the operation shifts the contest from the device to the application's own integrity checks, and from a bespoke patch to a reusable engine that can be retargeted at other apps and regions." "Once an app can be replaced, its locally produced signals, signature, accessibility list, and integrity verdict, must be treated as attacker-influenced and verified server-side," ThreatFabric said. Last month, the findings came a little over a month after the cybersecurity firm revealed StreamRat's targeting of Spanish-speaking users via Meta and TikTok advertisements impersonating a free TV streaming service named Streamtv Esp to enable control over compromised Android devices. "StreamRat abuses accessibility services and MediaProjection to provide operators with near-complete control over infected devices, combining VNC and hidden-screen control, UI-tree collection, keylogging, credential-stealing overlays, internet and screen-blocking capabilities," ThreatFabric said. sources.title: Can you sue over targeted ads? 'Blockbuster' Supreme Court case to decide - Yahoo
passages: This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Can you sue over targeted ads? 'Blockbuster' Supreme Court case to decide
WASHINGTON – A 1988 video tape-era privacy law will collide with the modern digital age at the Supreme Court on Oct.
The outrage surrounding disclosure prompted Congress to create stiff penalties for any video tape service provider who discloses personally identifying information about a customer.
Almost 40 years later, the court must decide whether and how that law applies to websites.
Chamber of Commerce told the court that the case could abolish the targeted-advertising model that funds much of the internet.
Paramount contends that Salazar is suing to get a "massive windfall" by transforming a "Blockbuster-era statute" about video rental history into an unworkable internet-privacy regime.
An appeals court dismissed Salazar's lawsuit, ruling that subscribing to an online newsletter giving Salazar access to videos is not the same as subscribing to actual audiovisual content.

Salazar is seeking to bring a class action suit against Paramount under the Video Privacy Protection Act, arguing the law bars Paramount from sharing his video watching history and other personal information with Meta to create targeted advertising in his feed.

Any content Salazar viewed was available for free, Paramount's lawyers wrote in a filing, making 247Sports "a completely different business from renting video cassette tapes." Essentially, they're arguing that watching a free video doesn't make someone a "consumer" under the law so the privacy protections don't apply.

Privacy advocates, on the other hand, say the law is even more important today because video streaming services have become ubiquitous, vastly expanding the amount and types of personal data that can be collected about viewers.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON – A 1988 video tape-era privacy law will collide with the modern digital age at the Supreme Court on Oct. 14. How the justices approach the case being argued could have far-reaching consequences for the large swaths of the internet that rely on targeted advertising — and for the internet users who are the target of those ads. The law at issue, the Video Privacy Protection Act, was enacted in response to the decision by the Washington City Paper to release a list of 146 movies rented from a local video store by Robert Bork, who had been nominated by President Ronald Reagan to serve on the Supreme Court . The outrage surrounding disclosure prompted Congress to create stiff penalties for any video tape service provider who discloses personally identifying information about a customer. Almost 40 years later, the court must decide whether and how that law applies to websites. The California man at the center of the case says it does. Michael Salazar used his free digital subscription for 247Sports.com, which is owned by Paramount Global, to watch videos about college sports. He was logged into Facebook at the time. Like many websites that provide content outside a paywall, 247Sports makes money through advertising. Online tracking tools inserted in the webpage send information about the user to a third party – in this case, Facebook's parent company, Meta. Salazar is seeking to bring a class action suit against Paramount under the Video Privacy Protection Act, arguing the law bars Paramount from sharing his video watching history and other personal information with Meta to create targeted advertising in his feed. The case pits privacy advocates against major corporations and a widely used business model. Paramount contends that Salazar is suing to get a "massive windfall" by transforming a "Blockbuster-era statute" about video rental history into an unworkable internet-privacy regime. Any content Salazar viewed was available for free, Paramount's lawyers wrote in a filing, making 247Sports "a completely different business from renting video cassette tapes." Essentially, they're arguing that watching a free video doesn't make someone a "consumer" under the law so the privacy protections don't apply. News media organizations said in filings supporting Paramount that tracking video viewers is a routine part of their business model that allows them to offer content to the public for free. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce told the court that the case could abolish the targeted-advertising model that funds much of the internet. Privacy advocates, on the other hand, say the law is even more important today because video streaming services have become ubiquitous, vastly expanding the amount and types of personal data that can be collected about viewers. Data from the Pew Research Center show Americans are confused and concerned about how their online data is being used. More than seven in ten Americans surveyed in 2023 said they have little to no control over what companies do with their data. "We have had a massive proliferation in online tracking and profiling in the last few decades," said Sara Geoghegan, a lawyer with the Electronic Privacy Information Center, which filed a brief supporting Salazar. "We don't have a general, federal comprehensive privacy law. But we do have this specific law that protects video viewing habits." Geoghegan said there's still plenty of other data valuable to businesses that website operators can collect. Companies can also use their own information about customers to pitch ads or can get viewers' consent for targeted ads. "There are many ways of serving ads online that don't require these unlawful disclosures," she said. The legal debate centers on whether the privacy protections kick in only when someone signs up or pays money specifically to watch a video. An appeals court dismissed Salazar's lawsuit, ruling that subscribing to an online newsletter giving Salazar access to videos is not the same as subscribing to actual audiovisual content. The law protects "any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider." Salazar's lawyers argue that the phrase "goods or services" covers everything offered by a company, including a free newsletter. Paramount's lawyers say that when the phrase "goods and services" is read in context with the rest of the law, it's clear the protections apply only to renting, purchasing or subscribing to audiovisual materials. Josh Robbins, an attorney with the Libertarian Pacific Legal Foundation, said Paramount's theory could be compelling to a court that has often been opposed to broad interpretations of the law. "I expect there will probably be a continued push towards this narrower, more contextual reading of statutes to confine their reach," he said. A decision in Salazar v. Paramount Global is expected by the end of June. This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Can you sue over targeted ads? Nearly four decades later, the court is weighing how the Blockbuster-era statute fits into the modern age of digital commerce. The Supreme Court heard arguments Wednesday in a case exploring the extent to which companies from an array of sectors are obligated to protect the privacy of customers’ video-viewing data. A ruling could resolve a lower-court split over how a consumer qualifies for the law's protections. Consumer advocates say the Video Privacy Protection Act of 1988 was broadly written to adapt to inevitable advances in technology and safeguard consumers' personal information. Critics of the law view it as a relic that plaintiffs' lawyers are trying to exploit in a way that Congress could not have anticipated before the internet revolutionized commerce. They are urging the justices to reject an interpretation of the law that deprives companies of a vital source of revenue from targeted online advertising. The current case was brought by a customer who subscribed to Paramount Global's online newsletter to view videos on its website 247Sports.com. Michael Salazar claims Paramount violated the law by disclosing his video-watching history to Facebook without his consent, allowing companies to use his personal information to create and display targeted advertising. Justice Elena Kagan, who said the language of the statute is “relatively clear," stressed that it is easy for companies to obtain consent from customers to use their digital data. “Going forward, you have two very simple solutions," Kagan told Paramount lawyer Paul Clement. “One is to get consent. Easy enough. People do it every day. And the other is to stop selling people's private information. Take your pick.” “Well, I think that's one way that people would try to deal with this,” Clement said. The law at issue, the Video Privacy Protection Act, was enacted in response to the decision by the Washington City Paper to release a list of 146 movies rented from a local video store by Robert Bork, who had been nominated by President Ronald Reagan to serve on the Supreme Court . The outrage surrounding disclosure prompted Congress to create stiff penalties for any video tape service provider who discloses personally identifying information about a customer. Almost 40 years later, the court must decide whether and how that law applies to websites. The California man at the center of the case says it does. Michael Salazar used his free digital subscription for 247Sports.com, which is owned by Paramount Global, to watch videos about college sports. He was logged into Facebook at the time. Like many websites that provide content outside a paywall, 247Sports makes money through advertising. Online tracking tools inserted in the webpage send information about the user to a third party – in this case, Facebook's parent company, Meta. Salazar is seeking to bring a class action suit against Paramount under the Video Privacy Protection Act, arguing the law bars Paramount from sharing his video watching history and other personal information with Meta to create targeted advertising in his feed. The case pits privacy advocates against major corporations and a widely used business model. Paramount contends that Salazar is suing to get a "massive windfall" by transforming a "Blockbuster-era statute" about video rental history into an unworkable internet-privacy regime. Any content Salazar viewed was available for free, Paramount's lawyers wrote in a filing, making 247Sports "a completely different business from renting video cassette tapes." Essentially, they're arguing that watching a free video doesn't make someone a "consumer" under the law so the privacy protections don't apply. News media organizations said in filings supporting Paramount that tracking video viewers is a routine part of their business model that allows them to offer content to the public for free. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce told the court that the case could abolish the targeted-advertising model that funds much of the internet. Privacy advocates, on the other hand, say the law is even more important today because video streaming services have become ubiquitous, vastly expanding the amount and types of personal data that can be collected about viewers. Data from the Pew Research Center show Americans are confused and concerned about how their online data is being used. More than seven in ten Americans surveyed in 2023 said they have little to no control over what companies do with their data. "We have had a massive proliferation in online tracking and profiling in the last few decades," said Sara Geoghegan, a lawyer with the Electronic Privacy Information Center, which filed a brief supporting Salazar. "We don't have a general, federal comprehensive privacy law. But we do have this specific law that protects video viewing habits." Geoghegan said there's still plenty of other data valuable to businesses that website operators can collect. Companies can also use their own information about customers to pitch ads or can get viewers' consent for targeted ads. "There are many ways of serving ads online that don't require these unlawful disclosures," she said. The legal debate centers on whether the privacy protections kick in only when someone signs up or pays money specifically to watch a video. An appeals court dismissed Salazar's lawsuit, ruling that subscribing to an online newsletter giving Salazar access to videos is not the same as subscribing to actual audiovisual content. The law protects "any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider." Salazar's lawyers argue that the phrase "goods or services" covers everything offered by a company, including a free newsletter. Paramount's lawyers say that when the phrase "goods and services" is read in context with the rest of the law, it's clear the protections apply only to renting, purchasing or subscribing to audiovisual materials. Josh Robbins, an attorney with the Libertarian Pacific Legal Foundation, said Paramount's theory could be compelling to a court that has often been opposed to broad interpretations of the law. "I expect there will probably be a continued push towards this narrower, more contextual reading of statutes to confine their reach," he said. A decision in Salazar v. Paramount Global is expected by the end of June. This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Can you sue over targeted ads? extraction.body: WASHINGTON -- In 1988, Congress enacted a law to protect the privacy of video rentals after a journalist published details of Supreme Court nominee Robert Bork’s movie rental history during his Senate hearings. Nearly four decades later, the court is weighing how the Blockbuster-era statute fits into the modern age of digital commerce. The Supreme Court heard arguments Wednesday in a case exploring the extent to which companies from an array of sectors are obligated to protect the privacy of customers’ video-viewing data. A ruling could resolve a lower-court split over how a consumer qualifies for the law's protections. Consumer advocates say the Video Privacy Protection Act of 1988 was broadly written to adapt to inevitable advances in technology and safeguard consumers' personal information. Critics of the law view it as a relic that plaintiffs' lawyers are trying to exploit in a way that Congress could not have anticipated before the internet revolutionized commerce. They are urging the justices to reject an interpretation of the law that deprives companies of a vital source of revenue from targeted online advertising. The current case was brought by a customer who subscribed to Paramount Global's online newsletter to view videos on its website 247Sports.com. Michael Salazar claims Paramount violated the law by disclosing his video-watching history to Facebook without his consent, allowing companies to use his personal information to create and display targeted advertising. Justice Elena Kagan, who said the language of the statute is “relatively clear," stressed that it is easy for companies to obtain consent from customers to use their digital data. “Going forward, you have two very simple solutions," Kagan told Paramount lawyer Paul Clement. “One is to get consent. Easy enough. People do it every day. And the other is to stop selling people's private information. Take your pick.” “Well, I think that's one way that people would try to deal with this,” Clement said. Congress passed the law a year after a video store clerk provided a Washington City Paper reporter with a list of 146 movies rented by Bork, a federal appeals court judge at the time of his nomination by Republican President Ronald Reagan. The reporter's publication of “The Bork Tapes," on the eve of Bork's hearings in 1987 that ended with the Senate rejecting the nominee, fueled bipartisan outrage and led to the law's enactment. Paramount's lawyers say lower courts have overwhelmingly rejected other attempts to expand the law’s reach, with district court judges dismissing most cases. “And why do you think that is?” Justice Samuel Alito asked Salazar’s lawyer, Joshua Hammack. “Why do you think these smart lower court judges have rejected the kind of very literal interpretation of the statutory language that you’re presenting to us today?” “I think there is, unfortunately, some reluctance to believe that Congress actually meant what it said in the context of this statute,” Hammack responded. “It wrote a broad law that is very protective of personally identifiable information.” Paramount argues that Salazar does not meet the definition of a “consumer” under the law to qualify for its protections. Rulings in two appeals courts defined a consumer, under this law, as anybody who purchases, rents or subscribes to any good or service from a videotape service provider. Two other appeals courts adopted a narrower definition of consumer limited to goods and services with audiovisual content. Only the Supreme Court "can resolve the split and bring uniformity to this important area of federal law,” Salazar’s lawyers wrote. Paramount says Salazar has no basis to broaden the scope of the law. The company says the law merely prohibits video rental stores from disclosing customers' rental histories without consent. “Salazar seeks to transmogrify it into a prohibition against targeted advertising on the Internet,” Paramount attorneys wrote. Paramount says 247Sports is a sports news website that posts video clips with articles and photos free of charge. “That is a completely different business from renting video cassette tapes. In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms.

Additionally, Attorney General Josh Kaul in August announced Wisconsin could receive up to $313 million in a settlement social media company Meta made with 47 states in a case that alleged addictive components of its platforms threatened teens’ mental health.

In a statement, Tiffany also said Wisconsin needs “commonsense guardrails” to protect children and older adults, including holding companies accountable for platforms that allow creation of sexually explicit images or engage minors in inappropriate chatbot conversations.
Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025.

“Like so many parents, Ericka and I are raising our three girls in the age of social media and AI, and we’re navigating things no generation before us has ever had to, worrying about whether a stranger is messaging our kids, or a fake picture of our daughter is going around school, or even scammers trying to drain a grandparent’s life savings,” Crowley said.
The proposals in Crowley’s regulatory plan would require state legislative action.

extraction.body: In a governor’s race that has focused more on data center construction than artificial intelligence technology, Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Tuesday announced a plan for state regulations on AI aimed at protecting vulnerable Wisconsinites. In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms. Some key components of the plan include: Limiting access to AI chatbot apps for children under 13. Prohibiting addictive design features, such as infinite scrolling and autoplay, on accounts of minors. Increasing penalties for circulating AI-generated sexual images of minors. Allowing families to sue AI platforms if their content harms children, such as by promoting suicide or eating disorders. More funding for adult protective services and resource centers that can help victims of scams or fraud. Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, is running for governor against Republican U.S. Tom Tiffany in what polling from Marquette University Law School shows could be another close governor’s race in Wisconsin. AI policy debates between the two candidates in the months since the August primary have mostly been focused on the planning and construction of AI data centers, rather than the technology itself. In a statement, Tiffany also said Wisconsin needs “commonsense guardrails” to protect children and older adults, including holding companies accountable for platforms that allow creation of sexually explicit images or engage minors in inappropriate chatbot conversations. Tiffany said he also wants to prevent personal data from “falling into the hands of foreign adversaries, including Communist China.” “As governor, I will also support commonsense age-verification requirements for app providers, strengthen parental-consent protections, and give parents greater control over their children’s online activity,” Tiffany said. Crowley’s proposed state-level AI regulations land as President Donald Trump has dismissed calls for guardrails and warnings from technology company leaders asking for government oversight as their platforms become more advanced. Trump in May 2025 signed the Take it Down Act, which criminalized the online publication of real and AI-generated intimate images and requires social media platforms to remove them once notified of their existence. Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025. Other proposed federal legislation has not advanced, including bills requiring public reporting of safety incidents by AI companies and requiring labels on any AI-generated content. Crowley in a statement said he would not “wait around for DC to act” on additional AI regulations if he is elected. “Like so many parents, Ericka and I are raising our three girls in the age of social media and AI, and we’re navigating things no generation before us has ever had to, worrying about whether a stranger is messaging our kids, or a fake picture of our daughter is going around school, or even scammers trying to drain a grandparent’s life savings,” Crowley said. The proposals in Crowley’s regulatory plan would require state legislative action. In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms.
Some key components of the plan include: Limiting access to AI chatbot apps for children under 13.
Prohibiting addictive design features, such as infinite scrolling and autoplay, on accounts of minors.
Increasing penalties for circulating AI-generated sexual images of minors.
Allowing families to sue AI platforms if their content harms children, such as by promoting suicide or eating disorders.
More funding for adult protective services and resource centers that can help victims of scams or fraud.
Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, is running for governor against Republican U.S.
Tom Tiffany in what polling from Marquette University Law School shows could be another close governor’s race in Wisconsin.
AI policy debates between the two candidates in the months since the August primary have mostly been focused on the planning and construction of AI data centers, rather than the technology itself.

In a statement, Tiffany also said Wisconsin needs “commonsense guardrails” to protect children and older adults, including holding companies accountable for platforms that allow creation of sexually explicit images or engage minors in inappropriate chatbot conversations.

Tiffany said he also wants to prevent personal data from “falling into the hands of foreign adversaries, including Communist China.” “As governor, I will also support commonsense age-verification requirements for app providers, strengthen parental-consent protections, and give parents greater control over their children’s online activity,” Tiffany said.

sources.title: As data centers remain potent political issue, David Crowley offers plan to regulate artificial intelligence in Wisconsin
passages: In a governor’s race that has focused more on data center construction than artificial intelligence technology, Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Tuesday announced a plan for state regulations on AI aimed at protecting vulnerable Wisconsinites.
In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms.

Additionally, Attorney General Josh Kaul in August announced Wisconsin could receive up to $313 million in a settlement social media company Meta made with 47 states in a case that alleged addictive components of its platforms threatened teens’ mental health.

In a statement, Tiffany also said Wisconsin needs “commonsense guardrails” to protect children and older adults, including holding companies accountable for platforms that allow creation of sexually explicit images or engage minors in inappropriate chatbot conversations.
Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025.

“Like so many parents, Ericka and I are raising our three girls in the age of social media and AI, and we’re navigating things no generation before us has ever had to, worrying about whether a stranger is messaging our kids, or a fake picture of our daughter is going around school, or even scammers trying to drain a grandparent’s life savings,” Crowley said.
The proposals in Crowley’s regulatory plan would require state legislative action.

In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms. Some key components of the plan include: Limiting access to AI chatbot apps for children under 13. Prohibiting addictive design features, such as infinite scrolling and autoplay, on accounts of minors. Increasing penalties for circulating AI-generated sexual images of minors. Allowing families to sue AI platforms if their content harms children, such as by promoting suicide or eating disorders. More funding for adult protective services and resource centers that can help victims of scams or fraud. Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, is running for governor against Republican U.S. Tom Tiffany in what polling from Marquette University Law School shows could be another close governor’s race in Wisconsin. AI policy debates between the two candidates in the months since the August primary have mostly been focused on the planning and construction of AI data centers, rather than the technology itself. In a statement, Tiffany also said Wisconsin needs “commonsense guardrails” to protect children and older adults, including holding companies accountable for platforms that allow creation of sexually explicit images or engage minors in inappropriate chatbot conversations. Tiffany said he also wants to prevent personal data from “falling into the hands of foreign adversaries, including Communist China.” “As governor, I will also support commonsense age-verification requirements for app providers, strengthen parental-consent protections, and give parents greater control over their children’s online activity,” Tiffany said. Crowley’s proposed state-level AI regulations land as President Donald Trump has dismissed calls for guardrails and warnings from technology company leaders asking for government oversight as their platforms become more advanced. Trump in May 2025 signed the Take it Down Act, which criminalized the online publication of real and AI-generated intimate images and requires social media platforms to remove them once notified of their existence. Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025. Other proposed federal legislation has not advanced, including bills requiring public reporting of safety incidents by AI companies and requiring labels on any AI-generated content. Crowley in a statement said he would not “wait around for DC to act” on additional AI regulations if he is elected. “Like so many parents, Ericka and I are raising our three girls in the age of social media and AI, and we’re navigating things no generation before us has ever had to, worrying about whether a stranger is messaging our kids, or a fake picture of our daughter is going around school, or even scammers trying to drain a grandparent’s life savings,” Crowley said. extraction.body: Stubbornly hot inflation in August could push up the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security recipients, according to a new estimate from AARP. The 2027 COLA is now projected at 3.6%, based on the August Consumer Price Index figures released on Wednesday, according to the advocacy group. AARP had forecast a 3.5% increase a month ago.Other groups are forecasting a slightly lower COLA, with the Senior Citizens League, an advocacy group for older Americans, projecting a 3.5% adjustment, down from its prior estimate of 3.6%.A benefit increase of 3.6% would represent the biggest annual adjustment in Social Security payments since 2023. The program's more than 70 million recipients rely on the annual cost-of-living adjustment to ensure their benefits keep up with inflation, although some critics say the measure has failed to offset the price pressures facing older Americans and people with disabilities, including rising healthcare costs."No matter if the COLA announcement comes in slightly higher or slightly lower than our prediction, seniors will probably end up disappointed in the long run," said Shannon Benton, executive director of the Senior Citizens League, in a statement. "The reality is that older Americans allocate their budgets differently than people still in the workforce, so inflation hits them differently."The average retired worker received $2,071 a month in Social Security benefits as of January, according to the Social Security Administration. That means a 3.6% COLA would increase the average monthly benefit by about $75, raising it to roughly $2,146 a month at the start of 2027. When will the official COLA be announced?The official COLA won't be announced until next month, when the Social Security Administration will calculate next year's inflation adjustment based on the July, August and September inflation data. The September CPI report will be released on Oct. 14, with the Social Security Administration set to announce the 2027 COLA the same day.Inflation remained elevated in August, with consumer prices rising 3.4% from a year ago. Economists are concerned that the rise in diesel, which powers the trucks and railroads that transport goods around the U.S., could trickle through the economy as businesses hike prices to offset their higher energy costs.Seniors, in the meantime, can feel that their COLA isn't keeping up with current inflation, experts say. For instance, the 2026 COLA, which went into effect in January's benefit payments, was set at 2.8%. "The COLA only happening once a year puts life on hold for a lot of seniors. When prices rise, they don't rise next January when your benefit check goes up," Benton said.

Baltimore, MD - The Social Security Administration (SSA) today announced a 3.6 percent benefit increase for 2027. Social Security benefits include Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI), and Supplemental Security Income (SSI). On average, Social Security retirement benefits will increase by $75 per month. Nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see a 3.6 percent cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) beginning in January 2027. Increased payments to about 7.3 million people receiving SSI will begin on December 31, 2026. (Note: Some people receive both Social Security benefits and SSI). “Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability,” said Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano . “Under President Donald J. Trump, Social Security is delivering better, faster, higher-quality service for the American people." Individuals with personal my Social Security accounts can view their COLA notice online starting in late November—up to three weeks earlier than receiving a paper notice in the mail. Account holders can also choose to receive text or email alerts when a new message, including their COLA notice, is available in their personal my Social Security account’s Message Center. Individuals who do not have a personal account will need to create one and enroll in paperless notices by November 18 to see their COLA notice online. Create an account today at www.ssa.gov/myaccount . Individuals who have not enrolled in paperless notices in my Social Security will receive their COLA notice by mail in December. Social Security beneficiaries will receive a simplified, one-page COLA notice, which uses plain and personalized language, and provides exact dates and dollar amounts of an individual’s new benefit amount and any deductions. Information about Medicare changes for 2027 will be available at www.medicare.gov . For Medicare enrollees, the 2027 premium amount will be available via my Social Security Message Center starting in late November. Individuals who have not opted to receive messages online will receive their COLA notice by mail in December. The Social Security Act provides for how the COLA is calculated. The Social Security Act ties the annual COLA to the increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) as determined by the Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics. For additional information, visit www.ssa.gov/cola . NOTE TO CORRESPONDENTS: Here is the COLA 2027 Fact Sheet showing an easy-to-understand overview of all the various automatic adjustments for 2027. For more information about Social Security’s services, visit www.ssa.gov . For more Social Security news, follow the agency on X @SocialSecurity .

Baltimore, MD - The Social Security Administration (SSA) today announced a 3.6 percent benefit increase for 2027. Social Security benefits include Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI), and Supplemental Security Income (SSI). On average, Social Security retirement benefits will increase by $75 per month. Nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see a 3.6 percent cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) beginning in January 2027. Increased payments to about 7.3 million people receiving SSI will begin on December 31, 2026. (Note: Some people receive both Social Security benefits and SSI). “Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability,” said Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano . “Under President Donald J. Trump, Social Security is delivering better, faster, higher-quality service for the American people." Individuals with personal my Social Security accounts can view their COLA notice online starting in late November—up to three weeks earlier than receiving a paper notice in the mail. Account holders can also choose to receive text or email alerts when a new message, including their COLA notice, is available in their personal my Social Security account’s Message Center. Individuals who do not have a personal account will need to create one and enroll in paperless notices by November 18 to see their COLA notice online. Create an account today at www.ssa.gov/myaccount . Individuals who have not enrolled in paperless notices in my Social Security will receive their COLA notice by mail in December. Social Security beneficiaries will receive a simplified, one-page COLA notice, which uses plain and personalized language, and provides exact dates and dollar amounts of an individual’s new benefit amount and any deductions. The Social Security Act ties the annual COLA to the increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) as determined by the Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics. For additional information, visit www.ssa.gov/cola . NOTE TO CORRESPONDENTS: Here is the COLA 2027 Fact Sheet showing an easy-to-understand overview of all the various automatic adjustments for 2027. extraction.body: Stubbornly hot inflation in August could push up the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security recipients, according to a new estimate from AARP. The 2027 COLA is now projected at 3.6%, based on the August Consumer Price Index figures released on Wednesday, according to the advocacy group. AARP had forecast a 3.5% increase a month ago.Other groups are forecasting a slightly lower COLA, with the Senior Citizens League, an advocacy group for older Americans, projecting a 3.5% adjustment, down from its prior estimate of 3.6%.A benefit increase of 3.6% would represent the biggest annual adjustment in Social Security payments since 2023. The program's more than 70 million recipients rely on the annual cost-of-living adjustment to ensure their benefits keep up with inflation, although some critics say the measure has failed to offset the price pressures facing older Americans and people with disabilities, including rising healthcare costs."No matter if the COLA announcement comes in slightly higher or slightly lower than our prediction, seniors will probably end up disappointed in the long run," said Shannon Benton, executive director of the Senior Citizens League, in a statement. "The reality is that older Americans allocate their budgets differently than people still in the workforce, so inflation hits them differently."The average retired worker received $2,071 a month in Social Security benefits as of January, according to the Social Security Administration. That means a 3.6% COLA would increase the average monthly benefit by about $75, raising it to roughly $2,146 a month at the start of 2027. When will the official COLA be announced?The official COLA won't be announced until next month, when the Social Security Administration will calculate next year's inflation adjustment based on the July, August and September inflation data. The September CPI report will be released on Oct. 14, with the Social Security Administration set to announce the 2027 COLA the same day.Inflation remained elevated in August, with consumer prices rising 3.4% from a year ago. Economists are concerned that the rise in diesel, which powers the trucks and railroads that transport goods around the U.S., could trickle through the economy as businesses hike prices to offset their higher energy costs.Seniors, in the meantime, can feel that their COLA isn't keeping up with current inflation, experts say. For instance, the 2026 COLA, which went into effect in January's benefit payments, was set at 2.8%. "The COLA only happening once a year puts life on hold for a lot of seniors. When prices rise, they don't rise next January when your benefit check goes up," Benton said.

The 2027 COLA is now projected at 3.6%, based on the August Consumer Price Index figures released on Wednesday, according to the advocacy group.

AARP had forecast a 3.5% increase a month ago.Other groups are forecasting a slightly lower COLA, with the Senior Citizens League, an advocacy group for older Americans, projecting a 3.5% adjustment, down from its prior estimate of 3.6%.A benefit increase of 3.6% would represent the biggest annual adjustment in Social Security payments since 2023.

The program's more than 70 million recipients rely on the annual cost-of-living adjustment to ensure their benefits keep up with inflation, although some critics say the measure has failed to offset the price pressures facing older Americans and people with disabilities, including rising healthcare costs."No matter if the COLA announcement comes in slightly higher or slightly lower than our prediction, seniors will probably end up disappointed in the long run," said Shannon Benton, executive director of the Senior Citizens League, in a statement.

"The reality is that older Americans allocate their budgets differently than people still in the workforce, so inflation hits them differently."The average retired worker received $2,071 a month in Social Security benefits as of January, according to the Social Security Administration.

extraction.body: Social Security benefits and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payments for 76 million Americans will increase 3.6 percent in 2027. On average, Social Security retirement benefits will increase by about $75 per month starting in January. Nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see a 3.6 percent cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) beginning in January 2027. Increased payments to about 7.3 million people receiving SSI will begin on December 31, 2026. Several other adjustments that take effect in January of each year are based on increases in average wages. For example, the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security tax, known as taxable maximum, is slated to increase to $192,300 from $184,500 in 2027. People with personal my Social Security accounts can view their COLA notices online starting in late November. Accessing the notice online is secure, convenient, and often faster than waiting for a mailed notice. Account holders can also choose to receive text or email alerts when a new message, including their COLA notice, is available in their personal my Social Security account Message Center. If you do not have a personal account, you will need to create one by November 18 to see your COLA notice online. Social Security will mail notices with updated benefit amounts to recipients not enrolled in paperless notices during the month of December. Information about Medicare changes for 2027 will be available on the Medicare website. For Social Security beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare, the 2027 benefit amount will be available in their personal my Social Security ’s Message Center starting in late November. Those who do not have an online my Social Security account will receive their COLA notice by mail in December. The Social Security Act establishes the annual COLA is calculated. The adjustment is based on changes in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) as determined by the Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Statistics. You can find more information about the 2027 COLA here .

extraction.body: U.S. inflation sped up more than expected in September, perhaps putting multiple Federal Reserve rate hikes back into play. The September Consumer Price Index rose 0.6%, according to a Wednesday morning report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That’s up from 0.4% in August, and in line with economist forecasts for 0.6%. On a year-over-year basis, however, CPI rose 3.7% versus 3.4% in August and above estimates for 3.6%. Core CPI — which strips out food and energy costs — also disappointed, rising 0.3% in September. That was the same pace as August, but above consensus forecasts for 0.2%. Year-over-year core CPI was higher by 2.6% versus 2.4% the previous month and above estimates for 2.5%. Bitcoin BTC $83,212.45 dropped $1,000 on the news, now trading at $82,800. The 10-year Treasury yield has shot higher by 6.5 basis points to 5.284%. U.S. stock index futures are all lower, the Nasdaq 100 leading with a 0.65% decline. Ahead of the data, a string of Fed speakers had hinted that the central bank was likely to raise interest rates another 25 basis points before year-end. Market pricing reflected that information, with most expecting the central bank to pause at its upcoming meeting later this month, but hike at its final meeting of the year in early December.

The crypto market cap stood at $2.53 trillion last Wednesday. As of this morning, it has dropped to $2.25 trillion, with Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) testing $61,500 overnight before rebounding to $63K. There’s quite a few reasons for the market plunge. Strategy broke a years-long rule and sold Bitcoin for the first time in nearly four years, while U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs are now on their longest outflow streak ever. On top of that, $1.76 billion in leveraged positions got liquidated in 24 hours, and fresh U.S. strikes on Iran have rattled the fragile ceasefire that had been holding since April. Every major coin is now down double digits on the month. Below is the breakdown of how Bitcoin, Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ), and Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ) are performing right now. Bitcoin is showing the worst of the market downturn. The largest cryptocurrency by market cap is now trading at $63,436, down 3.2% in 24 hours and down 22.3% on the month. The bigger picture is even worse, with Bitcoin trading more than 50% below its $126,000 all-time high. Meanwhile, Ethereum and XRP are doing no better. ETH is trading at $1,768 after a 25.8% slide on the month, and XRP at $1.17 has hit a 15-week low, down 17.3% on the month. Both followed Bitcoin’s slide and ended up losing even more ground. Solana took the hardest single-day hit of the four cryptocurrencies. SOL is down 4.6% in 24 hours alone and 20.9% over the past month, now trading at $68.38. High-beta altcoins like Solana and XRP amplify Bitcoin’s moves, and on the way down, that means they fall steeper than the rest of the market. Beyond the price drops, the leverage washout was also ugly. $1.76 billion in leveraged positions got liquidated in 24 hours, with $1.50 billion of that from long positions getting forced out. Bitcoin took $773 million of the damage, Ethereum $482 million, and Solana $88 million. Traders went into this week heavily long, and the market punished them for it. For nearly four years, Strategy (the company formerly known as MicroStrategy) was the loudest voice in Bitcoin, telling everyone to buy and never sell. The company built its corporate identity around accumulation, stacking 843,706 BTC over five years and turning Michael Saylor into the face of the institutional bullish thesis on Bitcoin. On Monday, that changed. Strategy disclosed in an SEC 8-K filing on June 1 that it had sold 32 Bitcoin between May 26 and May 31 for $2.5 million, at an average price of $77,135. The amount represents 0.004% of the company’s holdings. That is not a number that moves markets on its own, but the signal it sent did. That said, this was actually not panic selling. Saylor pre-announced the move on May 5, telling investors that Strategy would probably sell some bitcoin to pay a dividend just to inoculate the market and send the message that “we did it.” The 32 BTC went to fund distributions on STRC, which is the company’s perpetual preferred stock. So, the whole sequence was planned and telegraphed for weeks. However, none of that planning protected the stock. MSTR fell nearly 6% on Monday, then dropped another 7% on Wednesday as Bitcoin slid below $62,000. Two Wall Street analysts called the sale economically immaterial, but the narrative break was the bigger damage. For years, the “Saylor never sells” rule had been one of the arguments for holding Bitcoin through volatility. But the recent sale has made that argument look weaker, and the timing came right in the middle of the Bitcoin ETF outflow streak and a macro shock. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs were already on a record streak when last week ended, and they have now extended it further. The 10-day outflow run that closed May has stretched to 13 trading days as of June 3, deepening what was already the longest withdrawal streak since the funds launched in January 2024. The structural bid that had supported Bitcoin through every previous selloff is now selling instead of buying. The pace has been intense. On June 3 alone, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $396.6 million, led by BlackRock’s IBIT at $342.3 million and Fidelity’s FBTC at $54.3 million. And the day before, outflows hit $519 million. Since May 20, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost over $3 billion in cumulative net outflows, or roughly 40,000 BTC by holdings. Bitcoin ETF assets under management have dropped from around $109 billion to $85 billion during the streak, marking a 22% decline in three weeks. Ethereum ETFs have run their own parallel bleed, posting their 17th consecutive outflow day on June 3, with cumulative net inflows shrinking to $11.24 billion. The selling is not only happening in ETFs either. According to on-chain data, whales holding between 10 and 10,000 Bitcoin sold roughly 25,000 BTC in the past week alone. So it’s not just an ETF problem, but a wider sell-off happening across the board. Macro conditions have only made things worse for crypto. Inflation came in at 3.8% year-over-year in April, the hottest reading since May 2023, while wholesale prices jumped 6%, the largest increase since December 2022. Energy prices are up 17.9% on the year and gasoline is up 28.4%, which has pushed real wages negative for the first time since 2023. The Federal Reserve’s response has been to hold. The April FOMC vote was 8-4 to keep rates at 3.50%-3.75%, marking the most dissents since 1992. Markets are now pricing a 68.8% probability of zero rate cuts in all of 2026, according to Polymarket . New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, sworn in on May 22, has not had time to establish his own approach yet, which adds even more uncertainty. Then on Tuesday, June 2, Iran fired missiles at Kuwait and Bahrain, and the U.S. retaliated late that night with strikes on an Iranian military facility on Qeshm Island. Iranian drones hit Kuwait International Airport on Wednesday, killing one and injuring 63. Three days later, neither side has clarified whether the ceasefire still holds. The result keeps the inflation loop intact. WTI crude is at $94.99, and Brent at $97.07. The U.S. has drained 14% of its Strategic Petroleum Reserve trying to ease supply pressure. As long as oil stays at these levels, the Fed cannot cut, and as long as the Fed cannot cut, macro pressure will keep weighing on the crypto market. The selloff looks closer to capitulation than the start of a new leg down. Bitcoin tested $61,500 overnight and bounced, and that level is close to the 200-week moving average, which has held as support in past bear cycles. A 13-day ETF outflow streak, $1.76 billion in liquidations in a single day, and a narrative-breaking Strategy sale are the bearish drivers weighing on the market right now. But whether they mark a bottom or signal more downside is still unclear. Despite all that, there are a couple of events coming up this month that could change the bearish sentiment in the market. The next CPI release on June 10 will show whether inflation is cooling or staying sticky. Then the FOMC meeting on June 16-17 gives the first read on how Warsh sets policy and the updated dot plot. Bitcoin is showing the worst of the market downturn. The largest cryptocurrency by market cap is now trading at $63,436, down 3.2% in 24 hours and down 22.3% on the month. The bigger picture is even worse, with Bitcoin trading more than 50% below its $126,000 all-time high.

Meanwhile, Ethereum and XRP are doing no better. ETH is trading at $1,768 after a 25.8% slide on the month, and XRP at $1.17 has hit a 15-week low, down 17.3% on the month. Both followed Bitcoin’s slide and ended up losing even more ground.

Solana took the hardest single-day hit of the four cryptocurrencies. SOL is down 4.6% in 24 hours alone and 20.9% over the past month, now trading at $68.38. High-beta altcoins like Solana and XRP amplify Bitcoin’s moves, and on the way down, that means they fall steeper than the rest of the market.

Beyond the price drops, the leverage washout was also ugly. $1.76 billion in leveraged positions got liquidated in 24 hours, with $1.50 billion of that from long positions getting forced out. Bitcoin took $773 million of the damage, Ethereum $482 million, and Solana $88 million. Traders went into this week heavily long, and the market punished them for it.

For nearly four years, Strategy (the company formerly known as MicroStrategy) was the loudest voice in Bitcoin, telling everyone to buy and never sell. The company built its corporate identity around accumulation, stacking 843,706 BTC over five years and turning Michael Saylor into the face of the institutional bullish thesis on Bitcoin. On Monday, that changed.

Strategy disclosed in an SEC 8-K filing on June 1 that it had sold 32 Bitcoin between May 26 and May 31 for $2.5 million, at an average price of $77,135. The amount represents 0.004% of the company’s holdings. That is not a number that moves markets on its own, but the signal it sent did.

That said, this was actually not panic selling. Saylor pre-announced the move on May 5, telling investors that Strategy would probably sell some bitcoin to pay a dividend just to inoculate the market and send the message that “we did it.” The 32 BTC went to fund distributions on STRC, which is the company’s perpetual preferred stock. So, the whole sequence was planned and telegraphed for weeks.

However, none of that planning protected the stock. MSTR fell nearly 6% on Monday, then dropped another 7% on Wednesday as Bitcoin slid below $62,000. Two Wall Street analysts called the sale economically immaterial, but the narrative break was the bigger damage.

For years, the “Saylor never sells” rule had been one of the arguments for holding Bitcoin through volatility. But the recent sale has made that argument look weaker, and the timing came right in the middle of the Bitcoin ETF outflow streak and a macro shock.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs were already on a record streak when last week ended, and they have now extended it further. The 10-day outflow run that closed May has stretched to 13 trading days as of June 3, deepening what was already the longest withdrawal streak since the funds launched in January 2024. The structural bid that had supported Bitcoin through every previous selloff is now selling instead of buying.

The pace has been intense. On June 3 alone, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $396.6 million, led by BlackRock’s IBIT at $342.3 million and Fidelity’s FBTC at $54.3 million. And the day before, outflows hit $519 million. Since May 20, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost over $3 billion in cumulative net outflows, or roughly 40,000 BTC by holdings.

Bitcoin ETF assets under management have dropped from around $109 billion to $85 billion during the streak, marking a 22% decline in three weeks. Ethereum ETFs have run their own parallel bleed, posting their 17th consecutive outflow day on June 3, with cumulative net inflows shrinking to $11.24 billion.

The selling is not only happening in ETFs either. According to on-chain data, whales holding between 10 and 10,000 Bitcoin sold roughly 25,000 BTC in the past week alone. So it’s not just an ETF problem, but a wider sell-off happening across the board.

Macro conditions have only made things worse for crypto. Inflation came in at 3.8% year-over-year in April, the hottest reading since May 2023, while wholesale prices jumped 6%, the largest increase since December 2022. Energy prices are up 17.9% on the year and gasoline is up 28.4%, which has pushed real wages negative for the first time since 2023.

The Federal Reserve’s response has been to hold. The April FOMC vote was 8-4 to keep rates at 3.50%-3.75%, marking the most dissents since 1992. Markets are now pricing a 68.8% probability of zero rate cuts in all of 2026, according to Polymarket . New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, sworn in on May 22, has not had time to establish his own approach yet, which adds even more uncertainty.

Then on Tuesday, June 2, Iran fired missiles at Kuwait and Bahrain, and the U.S. retaliated late that night with strikes on an Iranian military facility on Qeshm Island. Iranian drones hit Kuwait International Airport on Wednesday, killing one and injuring 63. Three days later, neither side has clarified whether the ceasefire still holds.

The result keeps the inflation loop intact. WTI crude is at $94.99, and Brent at $97.07. The U.S. has drained 14% of its Strategic Petroleum Reserve trying to ease supply pressure. As long as oil stays at these levels, the Fed cannot cut, and as long as the Fed cannot cut, macro pressure will keep weighing on the crypto market.

The selloff looks closer to capitulation than the start of a new leg down. Bitcoin tested $61,500 overnight and bounced, and that level is close to the 200-week moving average, which has held as support in past bear cycles. A 13-day ETF outflow streak, $1.76 billion in liquidations in a single day, and a narrative-breaking Strategy sale are the bearish drivers weighing on the market right now. But whether they mark a bottom or signal more downside is still unclear.

Despite all that, there are a couple of events coming up this month that could change the bearish sentiment in the market. The next CPI release on June 10 will show whether inflation is cooling or staying sticky. Then the FOMC meeting on June 16-17 gives the first read on how Warsh sets policy and the updated dot plot.

The crypto market cap stood at $2.53 trillion last Wednesday. As of this morning, it has dropped to $2.25 trillion, with Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) testing $61,500 overnight before rebounding to $63K. There’s quite a few reasons for the market plunge. Strategy broke a years-long rule and sold Bitcoin for the first time in nearly four years, while U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs are now on their longest outflow streak ever. On top of that, $1.76 billion in leveraged positions got liquidated in 24 hours, and fresh U.S. strikes on Iran have rattled the fragile ceasefire that had been holding since April. Every major coin is now down double digits on the month. Below is the breakdown of how Bitcoin, Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ), and Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ) are performing right now. Bitcoin is showing the worst of the market downturn. The largest cryptocurrency by market cap is now trading at $63,436, down 3.2% in 24 hours and down 22.3% on the month. The bigger picture is even worse, with Bitcoin trading more than 50% below its $126,000 all-time high. Meanwhile, Ethereum and XRP are doing no better. ETH is trading at $1,768 after a 25.8% slide on the month, and XRP at $1.17 has hit a 15-week low, down 17.3% on the month. Both followed Bitcoin’s slide and ended up losing even more ground. Solana took the hardest single-day hit of the four cryptocurrencies. SOL is down 4.6% in 24 hours alone and 20.9% over the past month, now trading at $68.38. High-beta altcoins like Solana and XRP amplify Bitcoin’s moves, and on the way down, that means they fall steeper than the rest of the market. Beyond the price drops, the leverage washout was also ugly. $1.76 billion in leveraged positions got liquidated in 24 hours, with $1.50 billion of that from long positions getting forced out. Bitcoin took $773 million of the damage, Ethereum $482 million, and Solana $88 million. Traders went into this week heavily long, and the market punished them for it. For nearly four years, Strategy (the company formerly known as MicroStrategy) was the loudest voice in Bitcoin, telling everyone to buy and never sell. The company built its corporate identity around accumulation, stacking 843,706 BTC over five years and turning Michael Saylor into the face of the institutional bullish thesis on Bitcoin. On Monday, that changed. Strategy disclosed in an SEC 8-K filing on June 1 that it had sold 32 Bitcoin between May 26 and May 31 for $2.5 million, at an average price of $77,135. The amount represents 0.004% of the company’s holdings. That is not a number that moves markets on its own, but the signal it sent did. That said, this was actually not panic selling. Saylor pre-announced the move on May 5, telling investors that Strategy would probably sell some bitcoin to pay a dividend just to inoculate the market and send the message that “we did it.” The 32 BTC went to fund distributions on STRC, which is the company’s perpetual preferred stock. So, the whole sequence was planned and telegraphed for weeks. However, none of that planning protected the stock. MSTR fell nearly 6% on Monday, then dropped another 7% on Wednesday as Bitcoin slid below $62,000. Two Wall Street analysts called the sale economically immaterial, but the narrative break was the bigger damage. For years, the “Saylor never sells” rule had been one of the arguments for holding Bitcoin through volatility. But the recent sale has made that argument look weaker, and the timing came right in the middle of the Bitcoin ETF outflow streak and a macro shock. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs were already on a record streak when last week ended, and they have now extended it further. The 10-day outflow run that closed May has stretched to 13 trading days as of June 3, deepening what was already the longest withdrawal streak since the funds launched in January 2024. The structural bid that had supported Bitcoin through every previous selloff is now selling instead of buying. The pace has been intense. On June 3 alone, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $396.6 million, led by BlackRock’s IBIT at $342.3 million and Fidelity’s FBTC at $54.3 million. And the day before, outflows hit $519 million. Since May 20, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost over $3 billion in cumulative net outflows, or roughly 40,000 BTC by holdings. Bitcoin ETF assets under management have dropped from around $109 billion to $85 billion during the streak, marking a 22% decline in three weeks. Ethereum ETFs have run their own parallel bleed, posting their 17th consecutive outflow day on June 3, with cumulative net inflows shrinking to $11.24 billion. The selling is not only happening in ETFs either. According to on-chain data, whales holding between 10 and 10,000 Bitcoin sold roughly 25,000 BTC in the past week alone. So it’s not just an ETF problem, but a wider sell-off happening across the board. Macro conditions have only made things worse for crypto. Inflation came in at 3.8% year-over-year in April, the hottest reading since May 2023, while wholesale prices jumped 6%, the largest increase since December 2022. Energy prices are up 17.9% on the year and gasoline is up 28.4%, which has pushed real wages negative for the first time since 2023. The Federal Reserve’s response has been to hold. The April FOMC vote was 8-4 to keep rates at 3.50%-3.75%, marking the most dissents since 1992. Markets are now pricing a 68.8% probability of zero rate cuts in all of 2026, according to Polymarket . New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, sworn in on May 22, has not had time to establish his own approach yet, which adds even more uncertainty. Then on Tuesday, June 2, Iran fired missiles at Kuwait and Bahrain, and the U.S. retaliated late that night with strikes on an Iranian military facility on Qeshm Island. Iranian drones hit Kuwait International Airport on Wednesday, killing one and injuring 63. Three days later, neither side has clarified whether the ceasefire still holds. The result keeps the inflation loop intact. WTI crude is at $94.99, and Brent at $97.07. The U.S. has drained 14% of its Strategic Petroleum Reserve trying to ease supply pressure. As long as oil stays at these levels, the Fed cannot cut, and as long as the Fed cannot cut, macro pressure will keep weighing on the crypto market. The selloff looks closer to capitulation than the start of a new leg down. Bitcoin tested $61,500 overnight and bounced, and that level is close to the 200-week moving average, which has held as support in past bear cycles. A 13-day ETF outflow streak, $1.76 billion in liquidations in a single day, and a narrative-breaking Strategy sale are the bearish drivers weighing on the market right now. But whether they mark a bottom or signal more downside is still unclear. Despite all that, there are a couple of events coming up this month that could change the bearish sentiment in the market. The next CPI release on June 10 will show whether inflation is cooling or staying sticky. Then the FOMC meeting on June 16-17 gives the first read on how Warsh sets policy and the updated dot plot. Every major coin is now down double digits on the month. Below is the breakdown of how Bitcoin, Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ), and Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ) are performing right now.

Bitcoin is showing the worst of the market downturn. The largest cryptocurrency by market cap is now trading at $63,436, down 3.2% in 24 hours and down 22.3% on the month. The bigger picture is even worse, with Bitcoin trading more than 50% below its $126,000 all-time high.

Meanwhile, Ethereum and XRP are doing no better. ETH is trading at $1,768 after a 25.8% slide on the month, and XRP at $1.17 has hit a 15-week low, down 17.3% on the month. Both followed Bitcoin’s slide and ended up losing even more ground.

Solana took the hardest single-day hit of the four cryptocurrencies. SOL is down 4.6% in 24 hours alone and 20.9% over the past month, now trading at $68.38. High-beta altcoins like Solana and XRP amplify Bitcoin’s moves, and on the way down, that means they fall steeper than the rest of the market.

Beyond the price drops, the leverage washout was also ugly. $1.76 billion in leveraged positions got liquidated in 24 hours, with $1.50 billion of that from long positions getting forced out. Bitcoin took $773 million of the damage, Ethereum $482 million, and Solana $88 million. Traders went into this week heavily long, and the market punished them for it.

For nearly four years, Strategy (the company formerly known as MicroStrategy) was the loudest voice in Bitcoin, telling everyone to buy and never sell. The company built its corporate identity around accumulation, stacking 843,706 BTC over five years and turning Michael Saylor into the face of the institutional bullish thesis on Bitcoin. On Monday, that changed.

Strategy disclosed in an SEC 8-K filing on June 1 that it had sold 32 Bitcoin between May 26 and May 31 for $2.5 million, at an average price of $77,135. The amount represents 0.004% of the company’s holdings. That is not a number that moves markets on its own, but the signal it sent did.

That said, this was actually not panic selling. Saylor pre-announced the move on May 5, telling investors that Strategy would probably sell some bitcoin to pay a dividend just to inoculate the market and send the message that “we did it.” The 32 BTC went to fund distributions on STRC, which is the company’s perpetual preferred stock. So, the whole sequence was planned and telegraphed for weeks.

However, none of that planning protected the stock. MSTR fell nearly 6% on Monday, then dropped another 7% on Wednesday as Bitcoin slid below $62,000. Two Wall Street analysts called the sale economically immaterial, but the narrative break was the bigger damage.

For years, the “Saylor never sells” rule had been one of the arguments for holding Bitcoin through volatility. But the recent sale has made that argument look weaker, and the timing came right in the middle of the Bitcoin ETF outflow streak and a macro shock.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs were already on a record streak when last week ended, and they have now extended it further. The 10-day outflow run that closed May has stretched to 13 trading days as of June 3, deepening what was already the longest withdrawal streak since the funds launched in January 2024. The structural bid that had supported Bitcoin through every previous selloff is now selling instead of buying.

The pace has been intense. On June 3 alone, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $396.6 million, led by BlackRock’s IBIT at $342.3 million and Fidelity’s FBTC at $54.3 million. And the day before, outflows hit $519 million. Since May 20, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost over $3 billion in cumulative net outflows, or roughly 40,000 BTC by holdings.

Bitcoin ETF assets under management have dropped from around $109 billion to $85 billion during the streak, marking a 22% decline in three weeks. Ethereum ETFs have run their own parallel bleed, posting their 17th consecutive outflow day on June 3, with cumulative net inflows shrinking to $11.24 billion.

The selling is not only happening in ETFs either. According to on-chain data, whales holding between 10 and 10,000 Bitcoin sold roughly 25,000 BTC in the past week alone. So it’s not just an ETF problem, but a wider sell-off happening across the board.

Macro conditions have only made things worse for crypto. Inflation came in at 3.8% year-over-year in April, the hottest reading since May 2023, while wholesale prices jumped 6%, the largest increase since December 2022. Energy prices are up 17.9% on the year and gasoline is up 28.4%, which has pushed real wages negative for the first time since 2023.

The Federal Reserve’s response has been to hold. The April FOMC vote was 8-4 to keep rates at 3.50%-3.75%, marking the most dissents since 1992. Markets are now pricing a 68.8% probability of zero rate cuts in all of 2026, according to Polymarket . New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, sworn in on May 22, has not had time to establish his own approach yet, which adds even more uncertainty.

Then on Tuesday, June 2, Iran fired missiles at Kuwait and Bahrain, and the U.S. retaliated late that night with strikes on an Iranian military facility on Qeshm Island. Iranian drones hit Kuwait International Airport on Wednesday, killing one and injuring 63. Three days later, neither side has clarified whether the ceasefire still holds.

The result keeps the inflation loop intact. WTI crude is at $94.99, and Brent at $97.07. The U.S. has drained 14% of its Strategic Petroleum Reserve trying to ease supply pressure. As long as oil stays at these levels, the Fed cannot cut, and as long as the Fed cannot cut, macro pressure will keep weighing on the crypto market.

The selloff looks closer to capitulation than the start of a new leg down. Bitcoin tested $61,500 overnight and bounced, and that level is close to the 200-week moving average, which has held as support in past bear cycles. A 13-day ETF outflow streak, $1.76 billion in liquidations in a single day, and a narrative-breaking Strategy sale are the bearish drivers weighing on the market right now. But whether they mark a bottom or signal more downside is still unclear.

Despite all that, there are a couple of events coming up this month that could change the bearish sentiment in the market. The next CPI release on June 10 will show whether inflation is cooling or staying sticky. Then the FOMC meeting on June 16-17 gives the first read on how Warsh sets policy and the updated dot plot.

Saylor cited restrictive trade, foreign, currency and monetary policies as headwinds, while pointing to a more favorable regulatory environment, faster bank adoption, tokenized securities and growth in the digital asset market as potential support.

Saylor said Bitcoin was trading 25% above its two-hundred-week moving average after briefly dipping below it. He also described the development of digital credit networks and the arrival of banking credit as favorable for the asset.
“We've got the formation of and the strengthening of digital credit networks and, of course, banking credit coming online, and all these things are very auspicious for the asset,” he said.

The forecast matters to investors because it links Saylor’s optimism to a mix of market structure and policy conditions, rather than price momentum alone. But the figures remain his outlook, not a guarantee of future performance.

I think we bounced off it. Now we're moving up into the eighties. I think we'll continue to march forward from here,” Saylor said. His view offers a sharp contrast with the pressures he said had weighed on prices in recent months. Saylor cited restrictive trade, foreign, currency and monetary policies as headwinds, while pointing to a more favorable regulatory environment, faster bank adoption, tokenized securities and growth in the digital asset market as potential support. Saylor said Bitcoin was trading 25% above its two-hundred-week moving average after briefly dipping below it. He also described the development of digital credit networks and the arrival of banking credit as favorable for the asset. “We've got the formation of and the strengthening of digital credit networks and, of course, banking credit coming online, and all these things are very auspicious for the asset,” he said. The forecast matters to investors because it links Saylor’s optimism to a mix of market structure and policy conditions, rather than price momentum alone. But the figures remain his outlook, not a guarantee of future performance. “I think that it should definitely move back into the six figures, back beyond $100,000,” Saylor said. He added that Strategy’s “long-term forecast is Bitcoin grows 20%-30% a year over the next twenty years.” He described the last twelve months as a contraction. Strategy’s own trading policy also featured in the interview. Saylor said buying and selling Bitcoin is part of the company’s regular financial activity, alongside transactions involving dollars, equity, credit, STRC and its own shares. He argued that the company needs flexibility to move among those assets and sources of capital. Saylor said that refusing to sell equity, capital or credit could degrade the company’s value, and described the ability to trade different asset pairs in either direction as a major unlock for investors.
