Bitcoin slipped slightly below its two-hundred-week moving average before recovering, according to Michael Saylor, who says the market has begun turning upward. The Strategy executive told Bloomberg Television he believes the bull market is just beginning and expects Bitcoin to move back above $100,000.
At the time of the report, BTC was trading at $83,761.77. Saylor said it had bounced from a low slightly below $60,000 and was moving into what he sees as more favorable conditions.
“I think we hit the bottom around slightly below $60,000. I think we bounced off it. Now we're moving up into the eighties. I think we'll continue to march forward from here,” Saylor said.

His view offers a sharp contrast with the pressures he said had weighed on prices in recent months. Saylor cited restrictive trade, foreign, currency and monetary policies as headwinds, while pointing to a more favorable regulatory environment, faster bank adoption, tokenized securities and growth in the digital asset market as potential support.

Saylor said Bitcoin was trading 25% above its two-hundred-week moving average after briefly dipping below it. He also described the development of digital credit networks and the arrival of banking credit as favorable for the asset.
“We've got the formation of and the strengthening of digital credit networks and, of course, banking credit coming online, and all these things are very auspicious for the asset,” he said.

The forecast matters to investors because it links Saylor’s optimism to a mix of market structure and policy conditions, rather than price momentum alone. But the figures remain his outlook, not a guarantee of future performance.

“I think that it should definitely move back into the six figures, back beyond $100,000,” Saylor said. He added that Strategy’s “long-term forecast is Bitcoin grows 20%-30% a year over the next twenty years.” He described the last twelve months as a contraction.

Strategy’s own trading policy also featured in the interview. Saylor said buying and selling Bitcoin is part of the company’s regular financial activity, alongside transactions involving dollars, equity, credit, STRC and its own shares.

He argued that the company needs flexibility to move among those assets and sources of capital. Saylor said that refusing to sell equity, capital or credit could degrade the company’s value, and described the ability to trade different asset pairs in either direction as a major unlock for investors.
Strategy bought 250 BTC last week at an average price of $86,194 per Bitcoin, bringing its total holdings to 848,250 BTC. The purchase was the company’s smallest Bitcoin buy in 2026.

Standard Chartered, a British multinational banking group, has introduced a new crypto trading service for affluent clients in the UAE. The service allows eligible customers to buy and sell Bitcoin and Ether directly through their existing bank accounts.

The bank announced the launch on October 14, saying the service would initially be available to professional investors in the UAE. The offering has received licensing approval from the Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA), and the bank plans to bring it to other markets in the future.

One of the main features is that clients will not need to open separate crypto wallets or use outside trading platforms. Standard Chartered will handle the custody and settlement of their digital assets within its banking system. The bank said this setup is designed to reduce the risks associated with third-party wallets.

The latest launch follows the bank’s earlier move into direct cryptocurrency trading for institutional clients. In July 2025, Standard Chartered began offering Bitcoin and Ether spot trading against the U.S. dollar through its UK branch.

The bank brought its institutional trading service to the UAE in September 2026 through Standard Chartered DIFC, its entity operating in the Dubai International Financial Centre under the supervision of the Dubai Financial Services Authority (DFSA). The service gives institutional clients access to BTC/USD and ETH /USD spot trading.

Clients can place trades through the bank’s existing electronic platforms, which are also used for foreign exchange transactions. They can choose their preferred custodian for settlement, including Standard Chartered’s own digital asset custody service, launched in September 2024.

With the new service, the bank is extending crypto trading beyond its institutional business to eligible wealthy clients. The move gives them a way to access Bitcoin and Ether through their existing banking relationship rather than relying on a separate crypto exchange.

The offering brings together Standard Chartered’s Wealth and Retail Banking (WRB) and Corporate and Investment Banking (CIB) businesses, alongside Zodia Markets, a digital asset trading firm backed by SC Ventures.

Eligible clients can buy and sell Bitcoin (BTC) and Ether (ETH) directly through their existing Standard Chartered bank accounts. The bank will oversee custody and settlement within its own ecosystem, removing the need for clients to manage separate wallets or rely on external exchanges.

Standard Chartered said the service complements its existing digital asset products, which include access to cryptocurrency exchange-traded funds through its cash equities platform, as well as exposure through structured products and over-the-counter derivatives.

Jio Platforms, the digital arm of Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, is seeking to raise as much as $3.2 billion in what could be India’s biggest initial public offering. The listing will test public-market appetite for a company that attracted more than $20 billion from global investors, including Google and Meta in 2020.

On Wednesday, Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing (PDF) that Jio had set a price band of ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 (about $11.19 to $11.76) per share for the offering of up to 270 million new shares (PDF). The IPO will open for subscription on October 21 and close on October 23, with bidding for anchor investors scheduled for October 19.
At the upper end of the proposed price band, the IPO would value Jio at about ₹10.3 trillion (around $108.3 billion), based on the number of shares expected to be outstanding after the offering.
In 2020, Jio was valued at up to ₹4.91 trillion ( about $65 billion at the time). Meta, then known as Facebook, invested $5.7 billion , while Google committed $4.5 billion .

Jio’s IPO is set to overtake Hyundai Motor India’s ₹278.7 billion ($3.3 billion at the time) offering in 2024, the country’s biggest to date, even if its shares are priced at the lower end of the range.

Since launching in 2016, Jio has grown into India’s largest telecom operator, with more than 524 million subscribers as of March 31, ahead of Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, and state-owned BSNL. It initially drew customers with free data and cheap plans, though its prices are now comparable to those of its rivals. Over time, Jio has grown beyond a telco and expanded into broadband , cloud services , and other digital businesses .

Jio’s IPO comes as Elon Musk has stepped up his criticism of Ambani , accusing him of trying to keep Starlink out of India. The accusation comes more than a year after Jio and rival Airtel signed deals with Musk’s SpaceX to distribute Starlink’s satellite internet service in India, subject to regulatory approvals. Indian authorities have rejected Musk’s claims .

In the quarter ended June, Jio’s revenue rose nearly 12% from a year earlier to ₹391.7 billion (about $4.1 billion), while its net profit climbed 9% to ₹77.6 billion (around $816 million), per its IPO prospectus (PDF).

Jio has set aside shares worth up to ₹25 billion (about $263 million) for eligible Reliance Industries shareholders and another ₹5 billion ($53 million) for employees, who will receive a discount of ₹54 per share.

Of the IPO proceeds, Jio plans to use up to ₹275 billion ($2.9 billion) to repay debt at its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm, with the remaining proceeds going toward general corporate purposes, per the prospectus.

On Wednesday, Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing (PDF) that Jio had set a price band of ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 (about $11.19 to $11.76) per share for the offering of up to 270 million new shares (PDF). The IPO will open for subscription on October 21 and close on October 23, with bidding for anchor investors scheduled for October 19. At the upper end of the proposed price band, the IPO would value Jio at about ₹10.3 trillion (around $108.3 billion), based on the number of shares expected to be outstanding after the offering. In 2020, Jio was valued at up to ₹4.91 trillion ( about $65 billion at the time). Meta, then known as Facebook, invested $5.7 billion , while Google committed $4.5 billion . Jio’s IPO is set to overtake Hyundai Motor India’s ₹278.7 billion ($3.3 billion at the time) offering in 2024, the country’s biggest to date, even if its shares are priced at the lower end of the range. Since launching in 2016, Jio has grown into India’s largest telecom operator, with more than 524 million subscribers as of March 31, ahead of Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, and state-owned BSNL. It initially drew customers with free data and cheap plans, though its prices are now comparable to those of its rivals. Over time, Jio has grown beyond a telco and expanded into broadband , cloud services , and other digital businesses . Jio’s IPO comes as Elon Musk has stepped up his criticism of Ambani , accusing him of trying to keep Starlink out of India. The accusation comes more than a year after Jio and rival Airtel signed deals with Musk’s SpaceX to distribute Starlink’s satellite internet service in India, subject to regulatory approvals. Indian authorities have rejected Musk’s claims . In the quarter ended June, Jio’s revenue rose nearly 12% from a year earlier to ₹391.7 billion (about $4.1 billion), while its net profit climbed 9% to ₹77.6 billion (around $816 million), per its IPO prospectus (PDF). Jio has set aside shares worth up to ₹25 billion (about $263 million) for eligible Reliance Industries shareholders and another ₹5 billion ($53 million) for employees, who will receive a discount of ₹54 per share. Of the IPO proceeds, Jio plans to use up to ₹275 billion ($2.9 billion) to repay debt at its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm, with the remaining proceeds going toward general corporate purposes, per the prospectus. extraction.body: With the end of IMSA’s 2026 season, we have thoughts about the future of the sport. The rising tide that has been the Drive to Survive effect has lifted more boats in motorsport than simply Formula 1’s. Sportscar racing is enjoying its own surge in popularity internationally at races like Le Mans in France, but also in North America in IMSA’s WeatherTech Sportscar Championship. For one thing, multi-hour, multi-class racing lends itself better to the age of streaming and second screens than it did linear broadcast TV, and fans are taking advantage of that: IMSA’s audience grew by more than a third domestically and almost a quarter internationally last year. Having some of the coolest-looking cars racing today certainly helps, whether that’s the (mostly) hybrid prototypes or the GTs, racing versions of road-going cars from Porsche, Ferrari, and others. And it definitely helps that fan access at the races is virtually unmatched, with open paddocks and grid walks that now see huge crowds get up close to the cars just before the start of each race. “I think we’re just scratching the surface,” said IMSA President John Doonan. “I think besides the people that are here on the ground, the people watching, people engaging with us on social media, I’m seeing the passion come out more. Just on the grid walk, these fans coming up and being so excited to be here.” The series has certainly been making an effort, among other things getting local high school students exposed to the industry and starting a partnership to train more mechanics with ASE. IMSA’s 2026 season wrapped up at the start of the month at Road Atlanta in Georgia. Although the 10-hour Petit Le Mans is now the regular finale, the race predates the WeatherTech series as well as its predecessor, the American Le Mans Series, first being held in 1998 after Elan Pharmaceuticals founder Don Panoz got a bright idea to invite the cars that raced at the French enduro to come here to the US. It worked and led to some classic races; no one who watched it could forget Allan McNish’s recovery drive in 2008, clawing back two laps after crashing on the way to the grid to hunt down and beat the Peugeots. (Don’t take my word for it, watch it for yourself .) 2026’s running was perhaps not quite an all-time classic. As often happens, weather played its part, suppressing the crowd size and making life complicated for the teams and drivers on track. Nearly four hours were spent neutralized behind the safety car, with 16 cautions that prevented this year’s race from ever really developing a rhythm. The first half of the race was dominated by the Acuras, and the BMWs were also strong, but in the end victory went to one of the two Porsche 963s—believe it or not, the marque’s first prototype Petit Le Mans win (although in 2015 a slower GTLM Porsche 911 RSR managed to take overall victory). This being the real world, things in sportscarland aren’t entirely easy. The war in the Middle East has disrupted both the World Endurance Championship—the series built around the 24 Hours of Le Mans—and a new Asian Le Mans series. And as always, at the top level, the sport is dependent upon manufacturer largesse, something that usually vanishes in the face of worsening economic outlooks. Porsche cut its factory prototype program in half last year , parking the two cars it had campaigned in WEC and leaving just the two cars running in IMSA. Betting heavily on an EV transition that hasn’t come to pass, plus the effect of Trump’s tariffs on US-generated profits, are mostly to blame for the decision to pull back. But Porsche is not the only one; Alpine announced earlier this year that it was retiring from the WEC at the end of this year. There were hopes that the program might be saved by Geely, the Chinese automaker that owns Lotus and Volvo. Sadly, just today it emerged that it’s unlikely to happen , and two more cars will fall off the grid at the end of the year. Acura is also calling time on its GTP program in IMSA, preferring to focus its motorsports efforts on IndyCar. In doing so, it almost certainly means there will be no Honda presence at Le Mans in the near future, something many fans had hoped to see. Then again, the end of those other programs does mean room on the grid for others to join. This year saw Genesis enter the WEC, and next year both Ford and McLaren are joining WEC as well. So the trajectory is positive. That all three factory efforts have chosen the IMSA-written LMDh technical regulations rather than Le Mans’ own Hypercar ruleset says something. Hypercar gives OEMs greater technical freedom, including the option to have all-wheel drive hybrid systems or use bespoke batteries, whereas the LMDh rules mandate common hybrid systems and gearboxes, as well as requiring each OEM to start with one of four approved carbon-fiber chassis. The lack of spec components in Hypercar was definitely a factor when Ferrari chose those rules for its 499P, as well as Toyota with the GR010 (now TR010) and Peugeot with the 9X8. Aston Martin’s road-derived Valkyrie, too . But going that route is more expensive than using some common parts, and is that extra cost even worth it when the cars all have performance balanced to roughly the same lap times anyway ? That process has just enough friction that we still haven’t seen a 499P race in IMSA despite the US being Ferrari’s largest market. “We’re fortunate that Aston Martin saw the opportunity to come [to IMSA]. I think we absolutely 100 percent need one set of regulations. I think our vision is that LMDh by sheer vote has been the choice of the OEMs,” said Doonan. “I think rules stability is really important, and this has always been a laboratory for advancement in an authentic way, but I think the more stable that we can make the platform rules-wise is only going to help its stability and longevity,” he said. The good news is that most stakeholders also agree that having two sets of regs is daft and that from 2030—when the current rulesets expire—everyone should be reading from the same sheet. “The way to go forward is to have one category. And everybody behind the scenes… there’s a lot of talks, a lot of meetings, and they’re going exactly that way,” said Urs Kuratle, head of Porsche’s prototype program. “On the other hand, with the big success sports car racing had in the past four years, we also have great races in the WEC with the Hypercars. We have record crowds, both sides of the Atlantic. So that basically proves that concept also works. And if it was the enabler, the two different congregations or regulatories or whatever, that was the way to enable the sports car renaissance, then it was a good success. If you would ask, it would have been clever to do it with one rule set from just beginning, the answer would also be yes. But it worked,” Kuratle told me. It looks likely that IMSA’s approach will win the day. “We see the next set of regulations as being an evolution of LMDH, and there’s got to be a way to have everybody see the value of what has happened with LMDH. And the OEMs did by saying, “Well, geez, I could run in the top category in a pretty cost-effective manner,” Doonan said. “Without being repetitive, stability is critical in so many areas of this right now because when headwinds that we don’t control come, my hope would be that this would be… a place where automakers can come market, Michelin and Motul can come market,” Doonan said. One reason some of us love prototype racing is that in many cases it really has improved our road cars . Direct technology transfer from the racetrack to the road is less common than it was, but still happens—Porsche’s T-hybrid engine and its electric turbocharger are directly descended from Porsche’s 919 Hybrid race car, for example. In the future, it’s more likely that software will be the place to look to see it happening. That’s something IMSA has been accelerating , offering the vast amounts of data generated during its races to researchers and developers to work with. “Now IMSA Labs has opened up this whole new opportunity to come into this space, use the data that we generate to prove out or build out new software solutions, business solutions, AI, predictive analysis. All of those things can happen here in real time, in a controlled environment, in a regulated environment,” Doonan said. “The OEMs have told me point-blank learnings from the hybrid system on the GTP cars, more so the strategy of how the hybrid is being implemented are immediately being utilized in product development for road cars, flat-out. And that’s been told to me by OEM representatives. We still have to allow things like that to be authentic and real in sportscar racing, in my opinion,” Doonan said. “It should be a technology which is also transferable to the roadcar business or for any OEM. I think that’s an important thing,” Kuratle said. “It has to be something the fans would love to see. But I make a stupid example now: whether or not you develop your own fuel pump. A fan in the grandstand doesn’t really care. So it does not matter if everybody has the same cheap pump in the cars. These are things which should be avoided in the future. But all the environmental topics have to be touched. We cannot burn shitloads of fuel on all these things,” Kuratle said. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. extraction.body: With the end of IMSA’s 2026 season, we have thoughts about the future of the sport. The rising tide that has been the Drive to Survive effect has lifted more boats in motorsport than simply Formula 1’s. Sportscar racing is enjoying its own surge in popularity internationally at races like Le Mans in France, but also in North America in IMSA’s WeatherTech Sportscar Championship. For one thing, multi-hour, multi-class racing lends itself better to the age of streaming and second screens than it did linear broadcast TV, and fans are taking advantage of that: IMSA’s audience grew by more than a third domestically and almost a quarter internationally last year. Having some of the coolest-looking cars racing today certainly helps, whether that’s the (mostly) hybrid prototypes or the GTs, racing versions of road-going cars from Porsche, Ferrari, and others. And it definitely helps that fan access at the races is virtually unmatched, with open paddocks and grid walks that now see huge crowds get up close to the cars just before the start of each race. “I think we’re just scratching the surface,” said IMSA President John Doonan. “I think besides the people that are here on the ground, the people watching, people engaging with us on social media, I’m seeing the passion come out more. Just on the grid walk, these fans coming up and being so excited to be here.” The series has certainly been making an effort, among other things getting local high school students exposed to the industry and starting a partnership to train more mechanics with ASE. IMSA’s 2026 season wrapped up at the start of the month at Road Atlanta in Georgia. Although the 10-hour Petit Le Mans is now the regular finale, the race predates the WeatherTech series as well as its predecessor, the American Le Mans Series, first being held in 1998 after Elan Pharmaceuticals founder Don Panoz got a bright idea to invite the cars that raced at the French enduro to come here to the US. It worked and led to some classic races; no one who watched it could forget Allan McNish’s recovery drive in 2008, clawing back two laps after crashing on the way to the grid to hunt down and beat the Peugeots. (Don’t take my word for it, watch it for yourself .) 2026’s running was perhaps not quite an all-time classic. As often happens, weather played its part, suppressing the crowd size and making life complicated for the teams and drivers on track. Nearly four hours were spent neutralized behind the safety car, with 16 cautions that prevented this year’s race from ever really developing a rhythm. The first half of the race was dominated by the Acuras, and the BMWs were also strong, but in the end victory went to one of the two Porsche 963s—believe it or not, the marque’s first prototype Petit Le Mans win (although in 2015 a slower GTLM Porsche 911 RSR managed to take overall victory). This being the real world, things in sportscarland aren’t entirely easy. The war in the Middle East has disrupted both the World Endurance Championship—the series built around the 24 Hours of Le Mans—and a new Asian Le Mans series. And as always, at the top level, the sport is dependent upon manufacturer largesse, something that usually vanishes in the face of worsening economic outlooks. Porsche cut its factory prototype program in half last year , parking the two cars it had campaigned in WEC and leaving just the two cars running in IMSA. Betting heavily on an EV transition that hasn’t come to pass, plus the effect of Trump’s tariffs on US-generated profits, are mostly to blame for the decision to pull back. But Porsche is not the only one; Alpine announced earlier this year that it was retiring from the WEC at the end of this year. There were hopes that the program might be saved by Geely, the Chinese automaker that owns Lotus and Volvo. Sadly, just today it emerged that it’s unlikely to happen , and two more cars will fall off the grid at the end of the year. Acura is also calling time on its GTP program in IMSA, preferring to focus its motorsports efforts on IndyCar. In doing so, it almost certainly means there will be no Honda presence at Le Mans in the near future, something many fans had hoped to see. Then again, the end of those other programs does mean room on the grid for others to join. This year saw Genesis enter the WEC, and next year both Ford and McLaren are joining WEC as well. So the trajectory is positive. That all three factory efforts have chosen the IMSA-written LMDh technical regulations rather than Le Mans’ own Hypercar ruleset says something. Hypercar gives OEMs greater technical freedom, including the option to have all-wheel drive hybrid systems or use bespoke batteries, whereas the LMDh rules mandate common hybrid systems and gearboxes, as well as requiring each OEM to start with one of four approved carbon-fiber chassis. The lack of spec components in Hypercar was definitely a factor when Ferrari chose those rules for its 499P, as well as Toyota with the GR010 (now TR010) and Peugeot with the 9X8. Aston Martin’s road-derived Valkyrie, too . But going that route is more expensive than using some common parts, and is that extra cost even worth it when the cars all have performance balanced to roughly the same lap times anyway ? That process has just enough friction that we still haven’t seen a 499P race in IMSA despite the US being Ferrari’s largest market. “We’re fortunate that Aston Martin saw the opportunity to come [to IMSA]. I think we absolutely 100 percent need one set of regulations. I think our vision is that LMDh by sheer vote has been the choice of the OEMs,” said Doonan. “I think rules stability is really important, and this has always been a laboratory for advancement in an authentic way, but I think the more stable that we can make the platform rules-wise is only going to help its stability and longevity,” he said. The good news is that most stakeholders also agree that having two sets of regs is daft and that from 2030—when the current rulesets expire—everyone should be reading from the same sheet. “The way to go forward is to have one category. And everybody behind the scenes… there’s a lot of talks, a lot of meetings, and they’re going exactly that way,” said Urs Kuratle, head of Porsche’s prototype program. “On the other hand, with the big success sports car racing had in the past four years, we also have great races in the WEC with the Hypercars. We have record crowds, both sides of the Atlantic. So that basically proves that concept also works. And if it was the enabler, the two different congregations or regulatories or whatever, that was the way to enable the sports car renaissance, then it was a good success. If you would ask, it would have been clever to do it with one rule set from just beginning, the answer would also be yes. But it worked,” Kuratle told me. It looks likely that IMSA’s approach will win the day. “We see the next set of regulations as being an evolution of LMDH, and there’s got to be a way to have everybody see the value of what has happened with LMDH. And the OEMs did by saying, “Well, geez, I could run in the top category in a pretty cost-effective manner,” Doonan said. “Without being repetitive, stability is critical in so many areas of this right now because when headwinds that we don’t control come, my hope would be that this would be… a place where automakers can come market, Michelin and Motul can come market,” Doonan said. One reason some of us love prototype racing is that in many cases it really has improved our road cars . Direct technology transfer from the racetrack to the road is less common than it was, but still happens—Porsche’s T-hybrid engine and its electric turbocharger are directly descended from Porsche’s 919 Hybrid race car, for example. In the future, it’s more likely that software will be the place to look to see it happening. That’s something IMSA has been accelerating , offering the vast amounts of data generated during its races to researchers and developers to work with. “Now IMSA Labs has opened up this whole new opportunity to come into this space, use the data that we generate to prove out or build out new software solutions, business solutions, AI, predictive analysis. All of those things can happen here in real time, in a controlled environment, in a regulated environment,” Doonan said. “The OEMs have told me point-blank learnings from the hybrid system on the GTP cars, more so the strategy of how the hybrid is being implemented are immediately being utilized in product development for road cars, flat-out. And that’s been told to me by OEM representatives. We still have to allow things like that to be authentic and real in sportscar racing, in my opinion,” Doonan said. “It should be a technology which is also transferable to the roadcar business or for any OEM. I think that’s an important thing,” Kuratle said. “It has to be something the fans would love to see. But I make a stupid example now: whether or not you develop your own fuel pump. A fan in the grandstand doesn’t really care. So it does not matter if everybody has the same cheap pump in the cars. These are things which should be avoided in the future. But all the environmental topics have to be touched. We cannot burn shitloads of fuel on all these things,” Kuratle said. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. The rising tide that has been the Drive to Survive effect has lifted more boats in motorsport than simply Formula 1’s. Sportscar racing is enjoying its own surge in popularity internationally at races like Le Mans in France, but also in North America in IMSA’s WeatherTech Sportscar Championship. For one thing, multi-hour, multi-class racing lends itself better to the age of streaming and second screens than it did linear broadcast TV, and fans are taking advantage of that: IMSA’s audience grew by more than a third domestically and almost a quarter internationally last year.

Having some of the coolest-looking cars racing today certainly helps, whether that’s the (mostly) hybrid prototypes or the GTs, racing versions of road-going cars from Porsche, Ferrari, and others. And it definitely helps that fan access at the races is virtually unmatched, with open paddocks and grid walks that now see huge crowds get up close to the cars just before the start of each race.

“I think we’re just scratching the surface,” said IMSA President John Doonan. “I think besides the people that are here on the ground, the people watching, people engaging with us on social media, I’m seeing the passion come out more. Just on the grid walk, these fans coming up and being so excited to be here.” The series has certainly been making an effort, among other things getting local high school students exposed to the industry and starting a partnership to train more mechanics with ASE.

IMSA’s 2026 season wrapped up at the start of the month at Road Atlanta in Georgia. Although the 10-hour Petit Le Mans is now the regular finale, the race predates the WeatherTech series as well as its predecessor, the American Le Mans Series, first being held in 1998 after Elan Pharmaceuticals founder Don Panoz got a bright idea to invite the cars that raced at the French enduro to come here to the US. It worked and led to some classic races; no one who watched it could forget Allan McNish’s recovery drive in 2008, clawing back two laps after crashing on the way to the grid to hunt down and beat the Peugeots. (Don’t take my word for it, watch it for yourself .)

2026’s running was perhaps not quite an all-time classic. As often happens, weather played its part, suppressing the crowd size and making life complicated for the teams and drivers on track. Nearly four hours were spent neutralized behind the safety car, with 16 cautions that prevented this year’s race from ever really developing a rhythm. The first half of the race was dominated by the Acuras, and the BMWs were also strong, but in the end victory went to one of the two Porsche 963s—believe it or not, the marque’s first prototype Petit Le Mans win (although in 2015 a slower GTLM Porsche 911 RSR managed to take overall victory).

This being the real world, things in sportscarland aren’t entirely easy. The war in the Middle East has disrupted both the World Endurance Championship—the series built around the 24 Hours of Le Mans—and a new Asian Le Mans series. And as always, at the top level, the sport is dependent upon manufacturer largesse, something that usually vanishes in the face of worsening economic outlooks. Porsche cut its factory prototype program in half last year , parking the two cars it had campaigned in WEC and leaving just the two cars running in IMSA. Betting heavily on an EV transition that hasn’t come to pass, plus the effect of Trump’s tariffs on US-generated profits, are mostly to blame for the decision to pull back.

But Porsche is not the only one; Alpine announced earlier this year that it was retiring from the WEC at the end of this year. There were hopes that the program might be saved by Geely, the Chinese automaker that owns Lotus and Volvo. Sadly, just today it emerged that it’s unlikely to happen , and two more cars will fall off the grid at the end of the year. Acura is also calling time on its GTP program in IMSA, preferring to focus its motorsports efforts on IndyCar. In doing so, it almost certainly means there will be no Honda presence at Le Mans in the near future, something many fans had hoped to see.

Then again, the end of those other programs does mean room on the grid for others to join. This year saw Genesis enter the WEC, and next year both Ford and McLaren are joining WEC as well. So the trajectory is positive.

That all three factory efforts have chosen the IMSA-written LMDh technical regulations rather than Le Mans’ own Hypercar ruleset says something. Hypercar gives OEMs greater technical freedom, including the option to have all-wheel drive hybrid systems or use bespoke batteries, whereas the LMDh rules mandate common hybrid systems and gearboxes, as well as requiring each OEM to start with one of four approved carbon-fiber chassis.

Hypercar gives OEMs greater technical freedom, including the option to have all-wheel drive hybrid systems or use bespoke batteries, whereas the LMDh rules mandate common hybrid systems and gearboxes, as well as requiring each OEM to start with one of four approved carbon-fiber chassis.

The lack of spec components in Hypercar was definitely a factor when Ferrari chose those rules for its 499P, as well as Toyota with the GR010 (now TR010) and Peugeot with the 9X8. Aston Martin’s road-derived Valkyrie, too . But going that route is more expensive than using some common parts, and is that extra cost even worth it when the cars all have performance balanced to roughly the same lap times anyway ? That process has just enough friction that we still haven’t seen a 499P race in IMSA despite the US being Ferrari’s largest market.

“We’re fortunate that Aston Martin saw the opportunity to come [to IMSA]. I think we absolutely 100 percent need one set of regulations. I think our vision is that LMDh by sheer vote has been the choice of the OEMs,” said Doonan. “I think rules stability is really important, and this has always been a laboratory for advancement in an authentic way, but I think the more stable that we can make the platform rules-wise is only going to help its stability and longevity,” he said.
The good news is that most stakeholders also agree that having two sets of regs is daft and that from 2030—when the current rulesets expire—everyone should be reading from the same sheet.

“The way to go forward is to have one category. And everybody behind the scenes… there’s a lot of talks, a lot of meetings, and they’re going exactly that way,” said Urs Kuratle, head of Porsche’s prototype program. “On the other hand, with the big success sports car racing had in the past four years, we also have great races in the WEC with the Hypercars. We have record crowds, both sides of the Atlantic. So that basically proves that concept also works. And if it was the enabler, the two different congregations or regulatories or whatever, that was the way to enable the sports car renaissance, then it was a good success. If you would ask, it would have been clever to do it with one rule set from just beginning, the answer would also be yes. But it worked,” Kuratle told me.

It looks likely that IMSA’s approach will win the day. “We see the next set of regulations as being an evolution of LMDH, and there’s got to be a way to have everybody see the value of what has happened with LMDH. And the OEMs did by saying, “Well, geez, I could run in the top category in a pretty cost-effective manner,” Doonan said. “Without being repetitive, stability is critical in so many areas of this right now because when headwinds that we don’t control come, my hope would be that this would be… a place where automakers can come market, Michelin and Motul can come market,” Doonan said.

One reason some of us love prototype racing is that in many cases it really has improved our road cars . Direct technology transfer from the racetrack to the road is less common than it was, but still happens—Porsche’s T-hybrid engine and its electric turbocharger are directly descended from Porsche’s 919 Hybrid race car, for example.

In the future, it’s more likely that software will be the place to look to see it happening. That’s something IMSA has been accelerating , offering the vast amounts of data generated during its races to researchers and developers to work with. “Now IMSA Labs has opened up this whole new opportunity to come into this space, use the data that we generate to prove out or build out new software solutions, business solutions, AI, predictive analysis. All of those things can happen here in real time, in a controlled environment, in a regulated environment,” Doonan said.

“The OEMs have told me point-blank learnings from the hybrid system on the GTP cars, more so the strategy of how the hybrid is being implemented are immediately being utilized in product development for road cars, flat-out. And that’s been told to me by OEM representatives. We still have to allow things like that to be authentic and real in sportscar racing, in my opinion,” Doonan said.

“It should be a technology which is also transferable to the roadcar business or for any OEM. I think that’s an important thing,” Kuratle said. “It has to be something the fans would love to see. But I make a stupid example now: whether or not you develop your own fuel pump. A fan in the grandstand doesn’t really care. So it does not matter if everybody has the same cheap pump in the cars. These are things which should be avoided in the future. But all the environmental topics have to be touched. We cannot burn shitloads of fuel on all these things,” Kuratle said.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

extraction.body: Flock’s founder and CEO Garrett Langley doesn’t think the risks of introducing surveillance technology at scale outweigh the rewards. “If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn’t pause progress,” Langley said, speaking on stage during a panel at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on Wednesday. During the interview, the controversial founder of the surveillance maker of license plate cameras and other recording devices deflected hard questions about the criticism Flock now faces — which has since led to cancelled contracts and even layoffs . Instead, Langley tended to respond to questions with anecdotes from conversations with police chiefs and city leaders across the United States, and tales of the supposed numerous crimes Flock has solved, rather than offer tangible solutions to people’s concerns. In doing so, Langley positioned Flock as an advance in technology that was somewhat inevitable. He stressed that if people wanted to live in a better society — that is, one with reduced crime — they would have to offer up their privacy in return. A similar argument about the trade-offs and rewards could be made for AI, which is marketed to the public as vastly improving our lives, automating tedious tasks, and making things more convenient. The flip side is the cost of sharing everything about ourselves with the makers of the AI agents themselves — and the possibility of the destruction of humanity , according to some. It’s no surprise that the AI backlash shares some overlap with Flock. Much like AI, Flock is a technology that some feel has been forced upon the public without their consent. For Langley, this is just the nature of progress, he explained. “Technology, at its core, in its definition, is just doing things better. It’s not doing things perfect,” he said. “Driverless cars, I think, is a fair analogy. Driverless cars, I think, are definitively safer than human drivers. And when there’s one accident, I don’t think the answer is to shut down driverless cars. The answer is to say, ‘Hey, let’s talk about how we prevent more accidents in the future’.” But driverless car makers don’t shrug their shoulders at crashes; the companies pause their fleets and apply fixes. Flock, meanwhile, seems to wrestle as a company with understanding when it’s the company’s responsibility to intervene. From Langley’s answers, it’s clear that the ethics around how Flock should be used is a decision he would much rather leave up to others. “We don’t want to tell city leaders how to do their job,” he noted. “We will provide recommendations, we’ll provide defaults, but we’re going to minimize the number of mandated features, functions, and policies,” he said. Among the many rebuttals to his critics that Langley raised during the interview was the idea that misinformation about Flock had led to some of its customers’ cancellations. For instance, he referenced a time when a customer ended their contract because they believed the devices performed facial recognition. While Flock cameras do not have facial recognition, they do have the ability to detect and track people . Langley also spent a fair amount of time admonishing those who think his technology, or any technology, should be perfect, attributing the quote to some unnamed community leader. “He was describing that, too often as a society we judge technology not on how it compares to the past, but how it compares to perfect. And Flock is far from perfect; I’m far from perfect — I’ve made plenty of mistakes,” Langley said. Another area of pushback was in positioning Flock as a more effective form of policing, and one that allowed police departments to do more with reduced staff. “If you look at where policing has gone over the last decade, but particularly post-COVID, law enforcement employment is declining rapidly. I think about a place like San Francisco, and there’s hundreds of open positions. They will probably never be filled,” he said, positioning Flock as the tech that would fill in those gaps. But pressed about abuse and the invasiveness of his company’s surveillance technology, Langley had no substantive answers. “I think if the idea is to curb abuse, I think there’s a way to do that that doesn’t disrupt the legal system, that doesn’t disrupt the efficacy and flow of a police department,” Langley said, without spelling out what those ideas were. For Langley, those seem to be matters of secondary importance, because his belief in Flock as a public good is so strong. “I think one of the unfortunate consequences of building a consequential company is this is the price you pay, and I think it’s worth it because there’s millions and millions of people who have a better life today because [of] Flock,” he said. “And clearly we’ve made our fair share of mistakes, and there’s some folks who disagree with what we do, but it’s worth it because one day they might be a victim,” Langley added. candidate.title: The hidden network: Inside the phishing infrastructure ecosystem powering global cybercrime - Microsoft

sources.title: The hidden network: Inside the phishing infrastructure ecosystem powering global cybercrime - Microsoft
passages: Microsoft’s research into one phishing kit unraveled a larger ecosystem, including the phishing kit developers, an infrastructure dealer, and the threat actors who buy from both.
In this blog, we examine several phishing kits marketed and sold through YAM Store, an underground marketplace tracked by Microsoft as Storm-3119.

Microsoft assesses with high confidence that these phishing kits were developed by Chinese-speaking threat actors, and, despite their distinct branding and separate Telegram-based sales channels, exhibit highly similar capabilities and functionality.

The phishing kits provide phishing templates impersonating legitimate brands and organizations (including government, financial, and logistics) worldwide, and enable criminal actors to facilitate high-volume phishing and credential stealing operations.
The similarity in their infrastructure and overlap in activity suggest either shared development origins, code reuse, or close collaboration among their developers.

Over the past year, Microsoft uncovered a Chinese-language cybercriminal ecosystem, an interconnected network of phishing kit operators, developers, and an illicit marketplace selling tools and infrastructure for large-scale phishing, enabling cybercriminal operations worldwide.
Microsoft assesses that the ecosystem is not limited to the abuse of Microsoft services and extends to other providers.
The pipeline below describes the supply side of that business: how the actor acquires, controls, and monetizes compromised environments.
Stage 1 – Reconnaissance : Storm-3119 conducts automated reconnaissance of target environments.
The actor uses Flask, a lightweight Python web framework, to covertly identify and profile cloud-enabled organizations.

The tooling is designed to discover Microsoft 365 tenants, assess enrollment opportunities, gather licensing and Azure cloud information, and perform these activities anonymously through Tor infrastructure.

Threat actors purchased and used these tools and infrastructure, including phishing kits and access to compromised or fraudulent Microsoft or Google cloud environments and related credentials, to target organizations across the healthcare, financial services, wholesale distribution, and information technology (IT) sectors in Japan, the United States, Australia, and India.
YAM Store and affiliated phishing kit companies accepted payments through cryptocurrency, including USDT and Ethereum, adding another layer to conceal illicit activity.
Most of the activity that stems from this phishing kit ecosystem consists of social engineering, phishing operations, and account and storage takeovers.
Microsoft recommends the following to mitigate the impact of Storm-3119 and Storm-2990-related threats.
The coverage below applies to the downstream activity detected by Microsoft that was identified using Storm-2990 infrastructure.
The platforms are commercially licensed phishing-as-a-service (PaaS) products.

They are designed to impersonate organizations across several industry verticals to steal information, including sign-in credentials (usernames, passwords) and financial data (credit card information), used to gain access to network environments.

In analyzed cases, the actors used similar common phishing techniques, such as urgency in the message and attaching malicious links that redirect to actor-controlled infrastructure that allows these downstream threat actors to perform the following activities:
Protect your people, data, and infrastructure with AI-powered, end-to-end security from Microsoft.
YAM Store is an initial access broker (IAB) that sells infrastructure using compromised or fraudulently obtained environments in providers like Microsoft and Google.
The marketplace offers a variety of infrastructure based on age, subscription type, and environment types such as education (.edu) or non-profit (.org).
Storm-3119 uses automation to identify expired environment or organization names and leverages legitimate customer information associated with them to help circumvent existing detections.
Stage 4 – Phishing and DNS infrastructure support : The threat actor maintains dedicated infrastructure to support and manage phishing operations on behalf of their customers.
A custom DNS management platform enables centralized control of phishing domains, SSL certificates, and domain-routing configurations through Cloudflare.
The Iron Man System phishing kit panel is predominately hosted on China-based hosting providers, with a smaller number of panels found on hosting providers in other countries.
The fully featured, multi-tenant phishing kit uses the GoFrame application development framework, an open-source Go framework with roots in the Chinese developer ecosystem.

This platform is a separate set of administrative panels (implemented in PHP, Java/Spring, and Cloudflare Workers) that lets the operator maintain, monetize, and expand access using stolen application credentials.

Leveraging the compromised environment’s client secret through an application-only authentication flow, the panel performs full directory control: it resets passwords silently (without forcing a change at next sign-in), assigns education licenses, and grants privileged attributes that the actor can later monetize.
Because this access is application-level rather than tied to a single user session, the resulting persistence is more durable, more scalable, and harder to detect.

In addition to targeting existing tenants, Storm-3119 also separately creates fraudulent organizations and supporting web presence to establish tenants on Microsoft’s platform, likely using AI-generated content and forged documentation to make the fabricated entities appear legitimate.

In one case, the actor created an environment, likely using AI, named “Jewish Choice” under the guise of a nonprofit organization and associated it with jewishchoice[.]org , a domain registered only within the past several months that did not appear to represent a legitimate organization.

This confirms that the kit supports live, interactive phishing where the operator monitors each victim’s progress and manually controls what the victim sees next, a hallmark of sophisticated PaaS platforms.
The attacker then harvests the information to use in follow-on fraudulent financial activities.
This restriction adds a layer of obfuscation by limiting site access to paying customers.

Threat actors purchased and used these tools and infrastructure, including phishing kits and access to compromised or fraudulent Microsoft or Google cloud environments and related credentials, to target organizations across the healthcare, financial services, wholesale distribution, and information technology (IT) sectors in Japan, the United States, Australia, and India. In collaboration with law enforcement agencies and other partners worldwide, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit (DCU) facilitated a disruption of the ecosystem’s primary developers and infrastructure . Microsoft’s research into one phishing kit unraveled a larger ecosystem, including the phishing kit developers, an infrastructure dealer, and the threat actors who buy from both. In this blog, we examine several phishing kits marketed and sold through YAM Store, an underground marketplace tracked by Microsoft as Storm-3119. We share our analysis of the technical aspects of this Chinese-language phishing kit ecosystem, the shared infrastructure, provisioning methods, and downstream activity by threat actors using these tools. Microsoft, alongside industry partner Resecurity , identified three phishing kits sold through the YAM Store that make up this Chinese-language cybercriminal network: CoGUI (also known as NX or FA), Haozi (also known as Phoenix), and Iron Man System. Microsoft tracks the cluster of activity and the developers behind all three phishing kits as Storm-2990. Since January 2026, the threat actors behind these kits have been responsible for facilitating the sending of over one billion phishing emails and SMS messages to over 75 thousand organizations worldwide. Microsoft assesses with high confidence that these phishing kits were developed by Chinese-speaking threat actors, and, despite their distinct branding and separate Telegram-based sales channels, exhibit highly similar capabilities and functionality. The phishing kits provide phishing templates impersonating legitimate brands and organizations (including government, financial, and logistics) worldwide, and enable criminal actors to facilitate high-volume phishing and credential stealing operations. The similarity in their infrastructure and overlap in activity suggest either shared development origins, code reuse, or close collaboration among their developers. These phishing kits have been advertised through YAM Store, first CoGUI and Haozi, followed by Iron Man System starting in June 2026. YAM Store and affiliated phishing kit companies accepted payments through cryptocurrency, including USDT and Ethereum, adding another layer to conceal illicit activity. The scale and proliferation of this ecosystem demonstrate how readily available criminal infrastructure can lower the barrier to entry, enabling less skilled cybercriminals to target organizations at scale and contribute to fraud losses. By mapping the relationship between YAM Store and these phishing kits, we provide insight into the commercial infrastructure that supports modern phishing operations. YAM Store is an initial access broker (IAB) that sells infrastructure using compromised or fraudulently obtained environments in providers like Microsoft and Google. The marketplace offers a variety of infrastructure based on age, subscription type, and environment types such as education (.edu) or non-profit (.org). The YAM Store marketplace provides cybercriminals with a platform to purchase fraudulently acquired Microsoft and Google domains associated with legitimate, expired, or previously used organization numbers, allowing actors to use seemingly legitimate infrastructure and obtain workspaces at relatively low cost. Storm-3119 uses automation to identify expired environment or organization names and leverages legitimate customer information associated with them to help circumvent existing detections. During this investigation, Microsoft uncovered a five-stage attack pipeline often used in Storm-3119’s operations. YAM Store functions as an access broker, an intermediary that hijacks Microsoft 365 and Azure for Education tenants and resells the stolen accounts, licenses, and storage as a service to downstream operations, including the phishing kits tracked as Storm-2990. The pipeline below describes the supply side of that business: how the actor acquires, controls, and monetizes compromised environments. Stage 1 – Reconnaissance : Storm-3119 conducts automated reconnaissance of target environments. The actor uses Flask, a lightweight Python web framework, to covertly identify and profile cloud-enabled organizations. The tooling is designed to discover Microsoft 365 tenants, assess enrollment opportunities, gather licensing and Azure cloud information, and perform these activities anonymously through Tor infrastructure. Stage 2 – Environment takeover and app-only admin panels : Once a viable environment is identified, the threat actor centralizes associated information in an actor-controlled platform used to administer compromised Microsoft 365 environments. This platform is a separate set of administrative panels (implemented in PHP, Java/Spring, and Cloudflare Workers) that lets the operator maintain, monetize, and expand access using stolen application credentials. Leveraging the compromised environment’s client secret through an application-only authentication flow, the panel performs full directory control: it resets passwords silently (without forcing a change at next sign-in), assigns education licenses, and grants privileged attributes that the actor can later monetize. Because this access is application-level rather than tied to a single user session, the resulting persistence is more durable, more scalable, and harder to detect. Stage 3 – Storage and resource abuse : With the stolen privileged credentials, the threat actor signs in to a compromised Global Administrator account and self-provisions the PnP Management Shell service principal, which represents the actor’s application inside the compromised tenant. Through this service principal, the threat actor grants themselves broad Microsoft Graph permissions, including read and write access to directory data and AppCatalog.ReadWrite.All, along with full control over the SharePoint API. The actor then abuses the compromised tenant’s SharePoint and OneDrive as bulk hosting and converts the hijacked storage into a sellable product. Stage 4 – Phishing and DNS infrastructure support : The threat actor maintains dedicated infrastructure to support and manage phishing operations on behalf of their customers. A custom DNS management platform enables centralized control of phishing domains, SSL certificates, and domain-routing configurations through Cloudflare. Stage 5 – Storefront and monetization : Storm-3119 resells the hijacked accounts, licenses, and storage through an automated storefront, operating as the access broker that supplies these resources to downstream operations. Payment is accepted through Alipay, WeChat Pay, and USDT (TRC20), and the storefront supports a sub-reseller tier. Telegram is used for order notifications and buyer contact rather than as the primary sales channel. In addition to targeting existing tenants, Storm-3119 also separately creates fraudulent organizations and supporting web presence to establish tenants on Microsoft’s platform, likely using AI-generated content and forged documentation to make the fabricated entities appear legitimate. In one case, the actor created an environment, likely using AI, named “Jewish Choice” under the guise of a nonprofit organization and associated it with jewishchoice[.]org , a domain registered only within the past several months that did not appear to represent a legitimate organization. This activity indicates that Storm-3119 likely established the website and associated domain to lend credibility to the fabricated nonprofit identity and facilitate tenant creation. YAM Store sells its illicitly acquired infrastructure, as well as the prominent phishing kits tracked as Storm-2990, to other threat actors. The platforms are commercially licensed phishing-as-a-service (PaaS) products. They are designed to impersonate organizations across several industry verticals to steal information, including sign-in credentials (usernames, passwords) and financial data (credit card information), used to gain access to network environments. Iron Man System’s customers purchase a subscription that provides access to the kit’s license server, with the domain hard-coded into the kit. This restriction adds a layer of obfuscation by limiting site access to paying customers. The kits allow attackers to steal money by abusing the stolen credit card information. After the target provides the sensitive information (sign-in details, credit card info), the phishing kit collects it using a WebSocket, offering customers real-time victim interaction through Telegram notifications during credential harvesting. This confirms that the kit supports live, interactive phishing where the operator monitors each victim’s progress and manually controls what the victim sees next, a hallmark of sophisticated PaaS platforms. The attacker then harvests the information to use in follow-on fraudulent financial activities. The Iron Man System phishing kit panel is predominately hosted on China-based hosting providers, with a smaller number of panels found on hosting providers in other countries. The fully featured, multi-tenant phishing kit uses the GoFrame application development framework, an open-source Go framework with roots in the Chinese developer ecosystem. Microsoft observed downstream activity by threat actors using infrastructure affiliated with the Storm-2990 phishing kits. In analyzed cases, the actors used similar common phishing techniques, such as urgency in the message and attaching malicious links that redirect to actor-controlled infrastructure that allows these downstream threat actors to perform the following activities: The threat actors using the phishing kits conduct phishing campaigns at scale whether it is a missing toll payment or a traffic citation. The following screenshots show email or SMS phishing lures used in Storm-2990 phishing kits. This interconnected network of Chinese-language phishing kit operators and developers operates as an enabling ecosystem, providing infrastructure and services that facilitate criminal activity rather than functioning as a standalone malware tool. Microsoft assesses that the ecosystem is not limited to the abuse of Microsoft services and extends to other providers. While Microsoft notes that the identified organizations impacted by attacks stemming from Storm-3119 or Storm-2990 operations include financial, healthcare, and IT companies, the activity conducted by threat actors using these tools are common attacks that could affect any organization. Most of the activity that stems from this phishing kit ecosystem consists of social engineering, phishing operations, and account and storage takeovers. Microsoft recommends the following to mitigate the impact of Storm-3119 and Storm-2990-related threats. Hardening credentials and cloud identities is also necessary to defend against phishing attacks, which seek to gain valid credentials and access tokens. As an initial step, use passwordless solutions like passkeys and implement multifactor authentication (MFA) throughout your environment: Microsoft Defender customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog. The coverage below applies to the downstream activity detected by Microsoft that was identified using Storm-2990 infrastructure. Microsoft Security Copilot is embedded in Microsoft Defender and provides security teams with AI-powered capabilities to summarize incidents, analyze files and scripts, summarize identities, use guided responses, and generate device summaries, hunting queries, and incident reports. Customers can also deploy AI agents , including the following Microsoft Security Copilot agents , to perform security tasks efficiently: Security Copilot is also available as a standalone experience where customers can perform specific security-related tasks, such as incident investigation, user analysis, and vulnerability impact assessment. In addition, Security Copilot offers developer scenarios that allow customers to build, test, publish, and integrate AI agents and plugins to meet unique security needs. Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following threat analytics reports in the Defender portal (requires license for at least one Defender XDR product) to get the most up-to-date information about the activity and techniques discussed in this blog. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments. Microsoft Security Copilot customers can also use the Microsoft Security Copilot integration in Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence, either in the Security Copilot standalone portal or in the embedded experience in the Microsoft Defender portal to get more information about the activity discussed in this blog. To hear stories and insights from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community about the ever-evolving threat landscape, listen to the Microsoft Threat Intelligence podcast . extraction.body: Discover what’s coming to Microsoft Ignite, Nov 17-20, 2026. Register now. Over the past year, Microsoft uncovered a Chinese-language cybercriminal ecosystem, an interconnected network of phishing kit operators, developers, and an illicit marketplace selling tools and infrastructure for large-scale phishing, enabling cybercriminal operations worldwide. Threat actors purchased and used these tools and infrastructure, including phishing kits and access to compromised or fraudulent Microsoft or Google cloud environments and related credentials, to target organizations across the healthcare, financial services, wholesale distribution, and information technology (IT) sectors in Japan, the United States, Australia, and India. In collaboration with law enforcement agencies and other partners worldwide, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit (DCU) facilitated a disruption of the ecosystem’s primary developers and infrastructure . Microsoft’s research into one phishing kit unraveled a larger ecosystem, including the phishing kit developers, an infrastructure dealer, and the threat actors who buy from both. In this blog, we examine several phishing kits marketed and sold through YAM Store, an underground marketplace tracked by Microsoft as Storm-3119. We share our analysis of the technical aspects of this Chinese-language phishing kit ecosystem, the shared infrastructure, provisioning methods, and downstream activity by threat actors using these tools. Microsoft, alongside industry partner Resecurity , identified three phishing kits sold through the YAM Store that make up this Chinese-language cybercriminal network: CoGUI (also known as NX or FA), Haozi (also known as Phoenix), and Iron Man System. Microsoft tracks the cluster of activity and the developers behind all three phishing kits as Storm-2990. Since January 2026, the threat actors behind these kits have been responsible for facilitating the sending of over one billion phishing emails and SMS messages to over 75 thousand organizations worldwide. Microsoft assesses with high confidence that these phishing kits were developed by Chinese-speaking threat actors, and, despite their distinct branding and separate Telegram-based sales channels, exhibit highly similar capabilities and functionality. The phishing kits provide phishing templates impersonating legitimate brands and organizations (including government, financial, and logistics) worldwide, and enable criminal actors to facilitate high-volume phishing and credential stealing operations. The similarity in their infrastructure and overlap in activity suggest either shared development origins, code reuse, or close collaboration among their developers. These phishing kits have been advertised through YAM Store, first CoGUI and Haozi, followed by Iron Man System starting in June 2026. YAM Store and affiliated phishing kit companies accepted payments through cryptocurrency, including USDT and Ethereum, adding another layer to conceal illicit activity. The scale and proliferation of this ecosystem demonstrate how readily available criminal infrastructure can lower the barrier to entry, enabling less skilled cybercriminals to target organizations at scale and contribute to fraud losses. By mapping the relationship between YAM Store and these phishing kits, we provide insight into the commercial infrastructure that supports modern phishing operations. YAM Store is an initial access broker (IAB) that sells infrastructure using compromised or fraudulently obtained environments in providers like Microsoft and Google. The marketplace offers a variety of infrastructure based on age, subscription type, and environment types such as education (.edu) or non-profit (.org). The YAM Store marketplace provides cybercriminals with a platform to purchase fraudulently acquired Microsoft and Google domains associated with legitimate, expired, or previously used organization numbers, allowing actors to use seemingly legitimate infrastructure and obtain workspaces at relatively low cost. Storm-3119 uses automation to identify expired environment or organization names and leverages legitimate customer information associated with them to help circumvent existing detections. During this investigation, Microsoft uncovered a five-stage attack pipeline often used in Storm-3119’s operations. YAM Store functions as an access broker, an intermediary that hijacks Microsoft 365 and Azure for Education tenants and resells the stolen accounts, licenses, and storage as a service to downstream operations, including the phishing kits tracked as Storm-2990. The pipeline below describes the supply side of that business: how the actor acquires, controls, and monetizes compromised environments. Stage 1 – Reconnaissance : Storm-3119 conducts automated reconnaissance of target environments. The actor uses Flask, a lightweight Python web framework, to covertly identify and profile cloud-enabled organizations. The tooling is designed to discover Microsoft 365 tenants, assess enrollment opportunities, gather licensing and Azure cloud information, and perform these activities anonymously through Tor infrastructure. Stage 2 – Environment takeover and app-only admin panels : Once a viable environment is identified, the threat actor centralizes associated information in an actor-controlled platform used to administer compromised Microsoft 365 environments. This platform is a separate set of administrative panels (implemented in PHP, Java/Spring, and Cloudflare Workers) that lets the operator maintain, monetize, and expand access using stolen application credentials. Leveraging the compromised environment’s client secret through an application-only authentication flow, the panel performs full directory control: it resets passwords silently (without forcing a change at next sign-in), assigns education licenses, and grants privileged attributes that the actor can later monetize. Because this access is application-level rather than tied to a single user session, the resulting persistence is more durable, more scalable, and harder to detect. Stage 3 – Storage and resource abuse : With the stolen privileged credentials, the threat actor signs in to a compromised Global Administrator account and self-provisions the PnP Management Shell service principal, which represents the actor’s application inside the compromised tenant. Through this service principal, the threat actor grants themselves broad Microsoft Graph permissions, including read and write access to directory data and AppCatalog.ReadWrite.All, along with full control over the SharePoint API. The actor then abuses the compromised tenant’s SharePoint and OneDrive as bulk hosting and converts the hijacked storage into a sellable product. Stage 4 – Phishing and DNS infrastructure support : The threat actor maintains dedicated infrastructure to support and manage phishing operations on behalf of their customers. A custom DNS management platform enables centralized control of phishing domains, SSL certificates, and domain-routing configurations through Cloudflare. Stage 5 – Storefront and monetization : Storm-3119 resells the hijacked accounts, licenses, and storage through an automated storefront, operating as the access broker that supplies these resources to downstream operations. Payment is accepted through Alipay, WeChat Pay, and USDT (TRC20), and the storefront supports a sub-reseller tier. Telegram is used for order notifications and buyer contact rather than as the primary sales channel. In addition to targeting existing tenants, Storm-3119 also separately creates fraudulent organizations and supporting web presence to establish tenants on Microsoft’s platform, likely using AI-generated content and forged documentation to make the fabricated entities appear legitimate. In one case, the actor created an environment, likely using AI, named “Jewish Choice” under the guise of a nonprofit organization and associated it with jewishchoice[.]org , a domain registered only within the past several months that did not appear to represent a legitimate organization. This activity indicates that Storm-3119 likely established the website and associated domain to lend credibility to the fabricated nonprofit identity and facilitate tenant creation. YAM Store sells its illicitly acquired infrastructure, as well as the prominent phishing kits tracked as Storm-2990, to other threat actors. The platforms are commercially licensed phishing-as-a-service (PaaS) products. They are designed to impersonate organizations across several industry verticals to steal information, including sign-in credentials (usernames, passwords) and financial data (credit card information), used to gain access to network environments.
